These differences represent integrated responses of the contrasting irrigation-history and cultivar–site combinations rather than an independently quantified effect of irrigation duration. However, higher soil concentrations were not accompanied by proportional increases in berry concentrations. All studied elements exhibited a consistent distribution pattern, with the highest concentrations in leaves, intermediate concentrations in stems, and the lowest concentrations in berries. BAC values for berries remained low for all elements, indicating limited transfer from soil to harvested products. High BFI values indicated pronounced differences in trace-element concentrations between leaves and berries, consistent with restricted accumulation in reproductive organs. Zinc showed preferential accumulation in plant tissues, whereas Mn was characterized by stronger physiological regulation and Mo displayed intermediate behavior. PCA revealed a clear organ-related structure in the trace-element concentration data. The results indicate that trace-element partitioning in the studied irrigated viticultural systems reflects the combined influence of soil geochemical conditions and plant-mediated processes. The observed organ-specific partitioning was associated with substantially lower Mn, Zn, and Mo concentrations in grape berries than in vegetative organs, despite differences in total soil concentrations.

title: Experimental study on the contribution of microbial-induced carbonate precipitation to carbon sequestration in soil from the northern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Lingjie Huang, Xuelin Li, Shuang Li, Xuefen Sheng, Xinyuan Guo, Baitang Li, Ruoyu Hu, Fuchun Li
abstract: Soil inorganic carbon (SIC) plays a critical role in global carbon cycling; however, the contribution of microbial-induced carbonate minerals (CMs) to the SIC pool remains poorly explored. There is no definitive method for distinguishing between microbial-induced and chemical CMs in soil nor a calculation of the ratio between the two. To fill this gap, a soil profile at a depth of 110 cm, located in the alpine grassland of the northern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP), was examined. Incubation experiments were conducted using mixed microbes isolated from soil. Our analysis encompassed vertical variation along the profile in soil organic carbon (SOC), SIC, and Ca2+, as well as the carbon isotopic composition (δ13C) of CMs, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), and SOC. X-ray diffraction and field-emission scanning electron microscopy equipped with energy-dispersive analysis were used to characterise the CMs in the soil. The close negative correlation between microbial biomass and δ13CCMs in both soil samples and incubation experiments suggests that soil microorganisms actively participate in CM formation. To quantify the proportion of microbial-induced CMs in soil, we established an empirical relationship between δ13Ccalcite and δ13CCO2(g) through incubation experimencts. This relationship allowed us to estimate the δ13C of the microbial-induced CMs (δ13CMCMs) using the δ13CCO2(g). Thereby, the calculated average δ13CCO2(g) for the upper soil layer was −36.2‰, corresponding to an estimated δ13CMCMs value of −26.5‰. Based on the above δ13CCMs, the estimated proportion of microbial-induced CMs in the total CM content is calculated, ranging from 43.7% to 4.0% with depth. Consequently, microbial-induced CMs are estimated to contribute approximately 20.2% to the SIC pool within the upper 1-m soil profile at Laohugou. These findings provide a novel framework for quantifying the contribution of microbially induced carbonate minerals to SIC sequestration using carbon isotopes. They highlight a pathway for transferring soil-derived CO2 into relatively stable inorganic carbon pools, with implications for understanding carbon cycling under changing environmental conditions.

title: Returned concrete as a new sustainable feedstock for enhanced weathering: Carbon dioxide removal potential and methodological recommendations
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Rémi Rateau, Ruadhán Magee, Frank McDermott, Maurice Bryson
abstract: Returned concrete is a cumbersome by-product generated by the ready-mix concrete industry. A new potentially sustainable market for the estimated 42 ± 19 Mt yr−1 of limestone-rich crushed returned concrete produced globally is its deployment as a pH-adjusting enhanced weathering feedstock for carbon dioxide removal in agricultural soils. However, its variable mineralogical composition presents methodological challenges that are not addressed by existing protocols and carbon credit registries. Based on literature review and limited but new observations at concrete plants, a model-based tiered methodological approach is proposed to address these challenges. Our methodology is based on measurements of bicarbonate in soil water, assuming that the bicarbonate originates entirely from calcite weathering, coupled with a calculation of additional carbonation-driven CO2 uptake that takes account of the potential and realized carbonation of hydrated cement paste in concrete at the post-milling stage. With the simple Tier 1 approach, a stochastically modelled carbonation uptake value of 0.032 ± 0.007 (1σ) t CO2 t−1 returned concrete spread is suggested, which should be added to enhanced weathering-derived carbon dioxide removal calculated in the field using a soil water-based approach. In cases where more complete local data are available, Tier 2 methods are suggested for improved accuracy. The methodology described here estimates carbonation-driven carbon dioxide removal that is additional, as it takes into account the CO2 removal that occurred during storage of the returned concrete before milling and also subtracts the counterfactual removal that would have occurred had the returned concrete remained un-milled and used as buried road base aggregate.

title: Geochemical controls on natural arsenic variability in Arctic tundra soils: Implications for regional geochemical baselines and environmental assessment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Evgeny Lodygin
abstract: Reliable regional geochemical baseline values are essential for distinguishing natural variability in trace elements from anthropogenic pollution, particularly in Arctic environments where pedogenic processes create pronounced spatial heterogeneity. However, information on the natural distribution of arsenic (As) in tundra soils of the European Russian Arctic remains limited. This study examined As concentrations in representative background soils of the Vorkuta district (Komi Republic, Russia) to identify the main factors controlling its distribution and establish regional geochemical baseline values for environmental assessment. A total of 280 soil samples representing ten WRB soil groups and their genetic horizons were analyzed for total As content, as well as for selected physicochemical properties. Statistical evaluation included Spearman correlation analysis, principal component analysis (PCA), and calculation of the upper 95% confidence limit (UCL95%) for individual soil groups. Arsenic concentrations varied significantly between soil types and horizons, reflecting substantial pedogenic and geochemical variability in soils without identified local anthropogenic sources. The lowest mean concentrations were observed in sandy Podzols, while loamy hydromorphic and cryogenic soils consistently had higher values. The PCA analysis revealed that the main factors influencing arsenic distribution differ between organic and mineral horizons. In organic horizons, As variability was primarily associated with soil pH, whereas organic carbon represented a separate source of variability. In mineral horizons, As concentrations were primarily associated with the fine mineral fraction and Fe2O3 and Al2O3 contents. These contrasting relationships explain the pronounced vertical differentiation of arsenic in tundra soil profiles. Calculated UCL95% values also differed substantially between soil groups, indicating that a single regional background concentration cannot adequately reflect the natural geochemical variability of Arctic tundra soils. The results indicate that regional geochemical baseline values should be established separately for major soil groups and genetic horizons. The proposed baseline values provide a scientifically sound basis for environmental assessment and geochemical mapping in the European Russian Arctic and can serve as a guide for long-term monitoring of trace element behavior in permafrost-affected landscapes.

title: Primary mineral assemblage controls cation release and carbonation pathways in shallow basaltic reservoirs
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Lizi Liao, Yijun Zheng, Shichen Duan, Tian Liang, Rong Xue, Yongchun Fan, Zhiqiang Yu, Ping'an Peng
abstract: Shallow basaltic formations are promising reservoirs for geological CO2 storage by mineral carbonation, yet the role of primary mineral assemblage in controlling cation release and carbonation pathways under shallow-burial conditions remains poorly constrained. We conducted 60-day batch CO2–H2O–basalt experiments at 30 °C and 2 MPa on six basalts from the Leizhou Peninsula, South China, spanning altered, alkaline, transitional and tholeiitic lithologies. Time-resolved fluid chemistry was combined with mineralogical, spectroscopic and thermal characterization of reacted solids and of the precipitates recovered from the filtrates. Cation release varied systematically with mineral assemblage. Peak dissolved Ca followed the ordering of modal pyroxene abundance, ranging from 29 to 195 mg/L, whereas plagioclase and olivine abundances gave no comparable ordering. Transitional basalts exhibited the lowest molar (Ca + Mg)/Si release ratios and approached amorphous-silica saturation only after Day 30, too late to explain their low Ca fluxes. The montmorillonite-rich altered basalt released anomalously high Mg (149 mg/L) decoupled from Si; extraction experiments and thermal analysis indicate that exchangeable Mg and dissolution of pre-existing magnesite together account for no more than one quarter of this inventory, and that most mobilized Mg remained in solution rather than being converted to carbonate. Carbonate precipitates recovered from filtrates formed after depressurization and storage, and cannot be interpreted as in situ mineralization. Primary mineral assemblage, rather than bulk oxide composition, therefore controls not only cation release but also cation partitioning among aqueous and solid sinks (e.g., incorporation into Fe-(oxy)hydroxides versus carbonate phases), and recovered fluids require analytical-purpose-specific preservation.

title: Beyond expert weighting: A data-knowledge driven COBRAC-Fuzzy RAWEC framework for mineral prospectivity mapping
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Mahnaz Mahboobi, Homayoon Katibeh, Yousef Bahrami, Amin Beiranvand Pour
abstract: The inherent subjectivity of expert-driven weighting schemes remains a major limitation in mineral prospectivity mapping, often introducing cognitive bias and reducing predictive reliability in geologically complex environments. This study presents a novel, data- and knowledge-driven multi-criteria decision-making framework that integrates COBRAC (Comparisons Between Ranked Criteria) and Fuzzy RAWEC (Fuzzy Ranking of Alternatives with Weights of Criteria) for mineral prospectivity mapping, which, to the best of our knowledge, represents the first application of these methods to mineral exploration. COBRAC objectively derives internally consistent weights for criteria and subcriteria directly from Prediction-Area (P-A) performance and mineral occurrence frequencies, reducing subjective weighting bias while capturing nonlinear and non-monotonic relationships between evidential intensity and mineralization probability that conventional expert-based weighting schemes often overlook. Fuzzy RAWEC incorporates uncertainty through statistically derived triangular fuzzy numbers and a deviation from reference ranking mechanism, supporting false-positive reduction, mitigating rank reversal, and generating more stable suitability rankings under heterogeneous exploration conditions. The framework was applied to porphyry copper prospectivity mapping in the Shahr-e-Babak district of the Kerman Copper Metallogenic Belt, Iran, using seven evidential layers comprising UHK (UMAP-Hypergraph-Kmeans) geochemical anomalies, volcanic lithologies, phyllic, argillic, propylitic, and FeO/OH alteration zones, as well as fault structures. These layers were standardized using a logistic transformation and classified using the fractal C-A model. The proposed CFR framework achieved the highest prediction rate (82%), outperforming the robust BWM-ARAS (78%) and conventional AHP-TOPSIS (72%) models. This performance hierarchy (CFR > BWM-ARAS > AHP-TOPSIS) was demonstrated by the P-A analysis and corroborated by the success-rate curves, supporting the comparative effectiveness of CFR within this study area. A key advantage of the proposed approach lies in its data-driven weighting strategy, which objectively captures non-monotonic relationships between evidential intensity and mineralization probability. In several cases, intermediate anomaly classes exhibited higher P-A rates, and consequently greater predictive significance, than extreme classes. This characteristic enables CFR to accommodate spatially complex patterns and statistically dispersed extreme values without assuming a strictly linear relationship between evidence intensity and mineral occurrence. The proposed framework provides an objective, uncertainty-aware, and reproducible alternative to conventional Multiple-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) approaches, enhancing exploration targeting in the study area while offering a potentially transferable methodology for mineral prospectivity mapping in other geological settings.

title: Effects of low-molecular-weight organic acids on phosphate release from partially oxidized vivianite
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Qian Wang, Peng Zhang, Zhang Wen
abstract: Vivianite dissolution and precipitation play important roles in regulating phosphate (PO4-P) dynamics in subsurface environments. However, under redox-dynamic conditions, vivianite is readily oxidized to form partially oxidized vivianite, which exhibited a reduced dissolution rate. Despite its environmental significance, the influence of co-existing low-molecular-weight organic acids (LMWOAs) on the release of PO4-P from partially oxidized vivianite remains poorly understood. In this study, PO4-P release from partially oxidized vivianite (10 g/L) was systematically investigated in the presence and absence of LMWOAs. The results showed that LMWOAs significantly enhanced PO4-P release across a broad pH range (pH 5–9). For instance, in the absence of LMWOAs, the cumulative dissolved PO4-P concentration reached 0.11 mM within 10 h at pH 7, whereas the presence of LMWOAs increased PO4-P release by a factor of 2.3–6.5. The enhancement of PO4-P release strongly depended on the type and concentration of LMWOAs, solution pH and the oxidation extent of vivianite. Enhancement effects increased with higher stability constants of LMWOAs toward Fe2+ and Fe3+ and with a higher Fe(II) fraction in vivianite, but decreased with increasing solution pH. The LMWOA-induced enhancement of PO4-P release was mainly attributed to ligand complexation, which lowered the energy barrier for mineral dissolution and inhibited secondary precipitation reactions between phosphate and iron. These findings provide new insights into PO4-P dynamics in redox-dynamic environments and suggest an alternative strategy for enhancing PO4-P availability from vivianite in agricultural soils.

title: Selective separation and recovery of rare earth elements using adsorbents for urban mining: Design of functional groups, porous materials, and desorption strategies
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Young Gun Ko
abstract: The accelerating deployment of advanced electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems has intensified global demand for rare earth elements (REEs), while conventional mining faces escalating environmental and geopolitical constraints. Urban mining has therefore emerged as a strategic secondary resource, yet its highly complex and dilute leachates impose formidable challenges for selective REE recovery. Among available technologies, adsorbent-based processes offer unique advantages in terms of tunable selectivity, operational simplicity, and reusability. Although ion-imprinted and ligand-functionalized adsorbents can preferentially bind specific REEs under controlled conditions, sufficiently high REE-to-REE selectivity remains difficult to achieve in realistic multicomponent leachates containing chemically similar lanthanides and large excesses of competing species. Consequently, practical REE fractionation is unlikely to rely on a single adsorbent alone. This review therefore proposes an integrated strategy that combines adsorbents with complementary selectivity profiles and hierarchical porous structures in sequential adsorption and desorption stages.

title: NICKEL ADSORPTION-DESORPTION ON AN ILLITE-SMECTITE CLAY
description: Publication date: Available online 25 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Soumya Das, M. Jim Hendry, Peter E.R. Blanchard
abstract: Nickel (Ni2+) adsorption-desorption on illite-smectite mixed-layer clay was evaluated in batch experiments across pH ∼2–11 using ∼10 mg/L Ni2+ in deionized water (DI; I = 0.005 M) and coal mine drain water (I = 0.08 M). In both waters, percent Ni2+ sorbed increased with pH and decreased with ionic strength. In DI water, ∼58% of Ni2+ was sorbed under acidic conditions with the sorption edge inflection point at pH ∼4.8; in mine water, basal surface sorption was suppressed by competing cations, shifting the inflection point to pH ∼6.3. Desorption was hysteretic in both waters, with greater Ni2+ retention in DI water (∼83%) than mine water (∼34%). Ni K-edge EXAFS analyses show that at low pH, Ni2+ adsorbs via outer-sphere complexation at permanent basal charge sites, evidenced by a Ni-O first-shell scattering path (2.05–2.07 Å; CN ∼6) with negligible second-shell contributions. At higher pH, inner-sphere complexation at variable-charge edge sites dominates, reflected in multiple Ni-Al/Si scattering paths (∼2.95, ∼3.10, ∼3.25 Å). Ni-Al layered double hydroxide (LDH) formation occurred only at high pH in DI water. Compared to kaolinite (companion study, identical experimental conditions), illite-smectite sorbs Ni2+ at lower pH (inflection points ∼1.5–2 units lower), consistent with its greater surface area (∼57 vs. ∼13 m2/g) and cation exchange capacity. EXAFS spectral differences between the two clays demonstrate that XAS can distinguish Ni2+ adsorption mechanisms in mixed-clay systems. These findings have direct implications for predicting Ni2+ mobility in clay-rich coal mine waste rock and natural environments.

title: Fluorine Occurrence, Leaching Behavior, and Environmental Enrichment in Coal-bearing Strata of Eastern Yunnan, China
description: Publication date: Available online 25 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Yuxuan Zhu, Piaopiao Duan, Wenfeng Wang, Tian Fu, Jihang Zhang, Moran Cao, Dongyan Liu
abstract: Complex tectono-sedimentary and magmatic processes resulted in widespread enrichment of fluorine (F) in Late Permian coal-bearing strata of Southwest China. Coal gangue accumulation and coal combustion may be sources of fluorine in the environment, yet F mobilization from coal gangue and F enrichment in surrounding media (e.g., soils, plants) remain poorly understood. Late Permian coal and coal gangue from eastern Yunnan were investigated using static immersion and dynamic leaching experiments, combined with F concentrations in soils, plants, and coal-dried crops. Geochemical characterization of the samples showed that F concentrations ranged from 39 to 149 μg/g in coal and 549 to 720 μg/g in coal gangue, with fluorapatite as the primary F-bearing phase. Leaching experiments revealed that F release was controlled by pH, particle size, and occurrence mode, with the initial stage being most critical. Acidic conditions and finer particle sizes promoted sustained release, whereas coarser fractions exhibited surface depletion followed by internal dissolution. Elevated F concentrations were observed in some soils and plant roots around the studied coal mines, as well as in coal-dried crops. The present observations, together with previous studies, suggest that weathering–leaching of coal gangue and coal combustion emissions may contribute to environmental F enrichment. F released from gangue during rainfall leaching and weathering may enter adjacent soils through surface runoff and leachate infiltration, while gangue-derived dust may provide an additional input. Bioavailable F in soils may subsequently be taken up by plant roots. Concurrently, F-bearing gases and particulates generated during coal combustion may deposit onto coal-dried crops, potentially increasing dietary F exposure.

title: Systematic evaluation of the state of knowledge on iodine, neptunium and technetium sorption in the context of deep geological nuclear waste disposal
description: Publication date: Available online 23 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Thimo Philipp, Guido Bracke, Torben Weyand, Christoph Borkel
abstract: Sorption of radionuclides on mineral surfaces is a key process limiting radionuclide transport in deep geological repositories. As sorption behavior is strongly controlled by the environmental conditions, a comprehensive coverage of different potentially relevant systems is essential. Motivated by the enormous complexity of this task, this work provides a systematic evaluation of the state of knowledge for the retention of I(-I), Np(V), Np(IV), Tc(VII) and Tc(IV). Literature was compiled and categorized according to solid phase, environmental conditions, data type and applied methods. Thereby, less explored systems could be identified based on the number of references. The evaluation shows that the coverage of the different systems is highly uneven. Sound knowledge exists for near-neutral pH, low ionic strength, room temperature and solutions containing carbonate and calcium. Knowledge gaps persist mainly for elevated temperatures, high ionic strengths, high pH, dissolved silicon, organic molecules and microbial activity. The relevance of the knowledge gaps depends on the radionuclide and its oxidation state. For I(-I), most relevant gaps concern sorption at high ionic strengths and temperature as well as the effect of organic molecules. Highly relevant gaps for Np(V) are the effect of elevated temperature, dissolved silicon and microbial activity. For Np(IV), most relevant deficiencies are the lack of studies on the effects of dissolved silicon and organic molecules. For Tc(VII), gaps related to microbial activity are most relevant and For Tc(IV), the most relevant gap concerns the influence of organic molecules. Future studies should focus more on thermodynamic data, spectroscopic investigations and in-situ studies.

title: Mineralogical control on metal(loid) mobility in ultramafic rocks and soils: implications for surface water contamination in New Caledonia
description: Publication date: Available online 14 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Chloé Dubernet, Aurélie Barats, Christophe Renac, Maximilien Mathian, France Pattier, Sylvain Gallet, André Mexias, Peggy Gunkel-Grillon
abstract: While ultramafic rocks cover only 1% of the Earth's surface, they outcrop over more than a third of New Caledonia. Their weathering and leaching, whether natural or accelerated by anthropogenic activities, release metals into rivers, posing a significant risk to primary domestic water resources. This study investigates how the mineralogical composition of typical ultramafic rocks and derived soils controls the mobility of Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn, Co, and As. Mineralogical characterization revealed a clear transition from parent rocks dominated by serpentine, pyroxene and chromite, to soils primarily composed of Fe- and Mn-oxides that are enriched in metal(loid)s. The combination of mineralogical identification and chemical analyses during sequential extractions demonstrates that metal(loid)s are strongly retained within crystalline phases, most notably in Fe-oxides, phyllosilicates (for Ni), and chromite (for Cr). Conversely, Mn and Co, and to a lesser extent Ni and As, are highly mobile due to under acidic and reducing conditions and the dissolution of Mn-oxides. Although Fe, Ni, As, and Cr are largely sequestered, their extreme total concentrations still permit substantial transfer to solution via desorption and the minor dissolution of Fe-oxides under moderately acidic conditions. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that water quality in ultramafic watersheds is highly vulnerable to degradation driven by fluctuations of pH or redox potential, targeted metal(loid)s and by specific mineral phases.

title: Integrated hydrochemical-isotopic ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) tracers and Bayesian-ML models constrain groundwater salinity sources and controls in a semi-arid plateau basin: Implications for sustainable groundwater management
description: Publication date: Available online 14 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Zhuo Zhang, Sheming Chen, Futian Liu, Chuanshun Zhi, Yubo Xia, Wanjun Jiang, Jing Zhang, Hang Ning, Hailan Xie, Qinghua Meng, Wengang Liu, Huaming Guo
abstract: Groundwater salinization poses a growing threat to water security in arid and semi-arid inland basins. However, quantitative studies on its mechanism remain critically limited. This study investigates the sources and controlling factors of groundwater salinity in the Chahanur Basin, Inner Mongolia, China, using an integrated approach of hydrochemical analyses, strontium isotopes (87Sr/86Sr ratio), bayesian mixing models, and statistical modeling. Total dissolved solids (TDS) in groundwater range from 324 to 5,440 mg/L, with more than half of the samples exceeding the WHO aesthetic-based drinking water guideline of 1,000 mg/L. Salinity increases from mountainous recharge zones toward the basin center and generally decreases with depth. Hydrochemical facies are dominated by Na-Cl and mixed Na-Ca types. Ionic ratios and saturation indices indicate that silicate weathering and evaporite dissolution are the major natural sources of dissolved salts. Strontium isotopic signatures further confirm the dominance of halite dissolution and the influence of precipitation and anthropogenic inputs. Quantitative apportionment using a MixSIAR model shows that silicate weathering contributes to averagely 42.5% of groundwater salinity, followed by halite dissolution (26.6%) and anthropogenic inputs (18.9%). Generalized linear and random forest models identify evaporation as the dominant control on groundwater TDS, with secondary influences from cation exchange, elevation, proximity to saline lakes, and aquifer type. This study provides a scientific basis for sustainable groundwater management in arid inland basins.

title: Testing the bio-additionality hypothesis for enhancing the alkalinity production via Enhanced Weathering
description: Publication date: Available online 6 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Lukas Rieder, Mathilde Hagens, Tullia Calogiuri, Reinaldy Poetra, Anna Neubeck, Abhijeet Singh, Harun Niron, Sara Vicca, Siegfried E. Vlaeminck, Jens Hartmann
abstract: Natural silicate weathering is considered one of the most important natural CO2 sinks on geological time scales. Accelerating this natural process to capture more CO2 also on human timescales is known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW). This can be done, for example, by spreading crushed rock on agricultural soils, where it can sequester CO2 and have beneficial effects as a mineral nutrient fertilizer. Previous studies have shown that specific bacteria, fungi, and earthworms enhance mineral dissolution. The interaction of all these biotic components and whether this can be optimized through specific species mixtures is not yet well understood. In this study, we investigate how the addition of biota, including bacteria (Bacillus subtilis), the endogeic earthworm Aporrectodea caliginosa [Savigny], and the fungus Aureobasidium pullulans, to a wheat-straw and crushed-tephrite substrate affects rock dissolution. The effect of biota on a low-inorganic-carbon tephrite-straw mixture was studied in a flow-through column setup lasting 56 days. Groundwater was used to irrigate these columns daily. Leachate water was collected and analyzed for total alkalinity (TA), dissolved inorganic and organic carbon, pH, electrical conductivity (EC), major anions, and major cations to assess the impact of biota on these parameters. The addition of biota to the straw–tephrite rock mixture did not increase the equivalent amount of TA, cations, or anions over the 56-day experimental period. The addition of straw itself might have increased the dissolution of the tephrite. It is likely that the CO2 generated during straw decomposition increased the local CO2 partial pressure, thereby lowering the pH and promoting the dissolution of minerals. The added microbes were unable to colonize the substrate, and earthworm survival was low (36 ± 24 %), with small activity (38 ± 42 %) observed. Although inoculated biota did not enhance weathering in this case, the addition of wheat straw helped to increase the leached amounts of K and Na.

title: Geochemistry of CO 2 and CH 4 in CO 2 -rich fluids from the Okinawa Trough and Mariana Arc
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Koudai Taguchi, Shinsuke Kawagucci, Takazo Shibuya, Yohei Matsui, Junichi Miyazaki, Masayuki Miyazaki, Tomoko Takahashi, Eiji Tasumi, Shuya Tan, Shotaro Tagawa, Ken Takai
abstract: We examine the chemical and isotopic compositions of various types of CO2-rich fluids, including liquid CO2 (L-CO2) fluids, CO2-rich gas bubbles, and hydrothermal fluids, collected from hydrothermal fields in the Okinawa Trough and Mariana Arc. Carbon isotopic composition of CO2 is similar regardless of the fluid type within each field, indicating a common CO2 source predominantly derived from subducted carbon through magmatic processes. The venting CO2 is more depleted in 13C in the Okinawa Trough than in the Mariana Arc, potentially reflecting compositional differences in subducted carbon, with a greater contribution of organic carbon at the Ryukyu Trench than at the Mariana Trench. In the Okinawa Trough, CH4 associated with L-CO2 fluids is in hydrogen isotopic equilibrium with H2O at hydrothermal temperatures, suggesting that it originated in hot subseafloor environments and experienced extensive interaction with H2O. The chemical compositions of hydrothermal fluids indicate subseafloor phase separation and generation of a CO2–CH4-rich vapor phase, which may have subsequently cooled and condensed to form CH4-bearing L-CO2 fluids. In contrast, CH4 associated with CO2-rich fluids and CO2-rich gas bubbles at the Mariana Arc is likely to be in hydrogen isotopic disequilibrium with H2O. This unusual isotopic composition of CH4, which have not previously been reported in subseafloor hydrothermal systems, could be consistent with either an early-stage thermogenic origin or an abiotic CH4 formation via the Sabatier reaction. Comparison of multiple fields in the Okinawa Trough and Mariana Arc provides new insights into common and setting-dependent processes controlling the geochemistry of CO2-rich fluids.

title: Selenium cycling in recent upwelling sediments
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Philipp Böning, Hans-Jürgen Brumsack
abstract: Selenium (Se) is an essential trace element for the growth of organisms. It occurs in many species in the marine environment, is actively taken up by marine plankton and becomes enriched in reducing sediments. However, the present Se data base for upwelling sediments is essentially non-existent, and therefore its oceanic mass balance remains less well constrained. This may also be due to limited knowledge of the sedimentary enrichment mechanisms for Se, which may be biogenic particle flux and/or diffusion of dissolved species across the sediment water interface (SWI) and subsequent reduction at depth. To better constrain the enrichment and accumulation mechanisms, chemical data (Se, Al, Ni and total organic carbon, TOC) are presented for recent sediments from the upwelling areas of Northern Chile and Peru from within and below their respective oxygen minimum zones (OMZ) and a comparison with published data from Southern Chile and the Arabian Sea. The results show that highest enrichments (up to 28 mg kg−1) and highest accumulations (up to 442 μg m−2 yr−1) of Se occur in Peruvian and North Chilean OMZ sediments, likely due to a combination of high biogenic matter flux and severe oxygen depletion. While Se is only variably associated with TOC it is strongly and linearly correlated with Ni (r2 = 0.97) a robust productivity indicator. The correlation between Se and Ni corresponds to the marine planktonic Se/Ni ratio, which favors the biogenic particulate input of Se to upwelling sediments as primary Se enrichment mechanism. Selenium may be used as productivity indicator based on the apparent preservation of an upper water column signal (as has been found for Ni). For future studies the analysis of Se along with Ni is encouraged to discuss deviations from the marine particulate Se/Ni trend, which may help establish Se and Ni as productivity proxies.

title: Electron-beam-induced non-bridging oxygen hole center (NBOHC) growth in quartz: SEM-CL constraints from diverse geological samples
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Șerban-Constantin Grecu, Stephen J. Mojzsis, Mihai N. Ducea, Johan De Grave, Alida Timar
abstract: Despite being one of the stoichiometrically purest minerals (ideal formula SiO₂), quartz exhibits various intrinsic and impurity-related defects that contain important genetic information. We report scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with cathodoluminescence (CL) wavelength-resolved spectroscopy on quartz from different rock types spanning a wide range of geological settings and ages to investigate defect phenomena. All samples show two main emissions: a red band at ~1.93 eV (~643 nm), attributable to non-bridging oxygen hole centres (NBOHC) defects, and a blue band at ~2.7 eV (~450 nm), explained by Ti-related defects. The origin of NBOHCs is relatively well understood and may result from intrinsic mechanisms or extrinsic pathways involving radiolysis of passivated precursor sites such as hydroxyl-related defects. Radiation-damage experiments under controlled electron irradiation in SEM provide a tool to study defect formation dynamics. We investigate the evolution of the NBOHC defect at different irradiation times. CL acquired during SEM irradiation shows monotonic growth of the ~1.9 eV emission described by the sum of two saturating exponentials, interpreted as coexistence of hydroxyl-mediated defect generation and intrinsic rupture of Si–O–Si bridges or peroxy Si–O–O–Si linkages. The fitted parameters vary among quartz samples from different geological contexts, suggesting potential provenance-related information. The initial CL intensity may reflect the natural balance among α-radiation damage, thermal resetting, and hydrogen passivation. Overall, these findings highlight the potential relevance of NBOHC-related CL to quartz provenance and thermochronology, warranting further investigation and experimental validation.

title: SOLWCAD*: Computation of multi-component volatile saturation in the system H 2 O-CO 2 -silicate melts
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Paolo Papale, Deepak Garg
abstract: Volatile saturation in silicate melts is a primary driver of magmatic evolution and volcanic dynamics. This study presents SOLWCAD*, a major re-evaluation of H2O-CO2 saturation modelling calibrated against an expanded global database of over 2300 experimental determinations – approximately doubling the size of previously available datasets. By integrating fully non-ideal thermodynamics with robust statistical regression, the model extends its reach from natural magmas to industrial silicate melts, covering pressures from 2 GPa to atmospheric conditions and temperatures up to 2000 K. A central focus is the trade-off between model complexity and predictive robustness. While standard information criteria (AIC/BIC) favour formulations with pressure-dependent binary interaction coefficients, out-of-sample R2 analysis and parameter covariance analysis reveal that such complexity leads to over-parameterization and reduced generalizability. We therefore prioritize predictive parsimony, selecting a robust 23-parameter constant-coefficient model that employs a hierarchical optimization of the CO2 reference state to maximize precision. SOLWCAD* provides high-precision computations for H2O and CO2 solubility and saturation, including exsolved gas properties, making it a versatile tool for petrological, volcanological, and industrial applications. SOLWCAD* is freely available at gitlab.com/paolo_papale/SOLWCADstar, allowing quick computations over a number of computational modes (including P − T loops, closed vs. open conditions, construction of isobars) and adding single phase and multiphase properties from largely employed literature models; all of the above, with or without confidence intervals and error bars.

title: In situ mica Rb-Sr geochronology resolves a short-lived magmatic–hydrothermal Li-mineralization event at Yifeng–Fengxin, South China
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Keqing Zong, Jionghui Wang, Jixiang Li, Xinshui Wang, Zaicong Wang, Linqing Jia, Jialin Li, Zhaoxian Zhu, Xi Zhang, Fanghua Zhang, Jie Lin
abstract: Constraining the temporal relationship between extreme magmatic differentiation and lithium (Li) mineralization is critical for ore-genetic models of rare-metal granites, yet remains challenging where zircon U-Pb data record protracted or composite magmatic–hydrothermal histories. Here, we apply in situ mica Rb-Sr geochronology using femtosecond laser-ablation inductively coupled plasma tandem mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS/MS) to the Ganfang granitic complex, the principal host of the world-class Yifeng–Fengxin Li deposit in South China. Biotites from two samples of the adjacent Neoproterozoic Jiuling basement granites yield Rb-Sr isochron ages of 808.9 ± 4.3 Ma (1σ, MSWD = 0.59, n = 30) and 810.5 ± 5.1 Ma (1σ, MSWD = 1.2, n = 30), in agreement with the known formation age of the Jiuling batholith. These results confirm that the Rb-Sr isotopic system in mica remained closed despite the subsequent intrusion of the Mesozoic Ganfang complex. In contrast, micas from all facies of the Li-fertile Ganfang complex, including muscovite monzogranite, Li-muscovite albite granite, lepidolite albite granite, and felsite, yield indistinguishable Rb-Sr isochron ages ranging from 135.7 ± 1.5 Ma to 137.8 ± 1.2 Ma (ten isochrons). This temporal coherence is accompanied by progressive whole-rock enrichment in Li2O (from 0.06 to 1.41 wt%), Rb, Cs, and Be, coupled with a systematic decrease in the Zr/Hf ratio, and by a parallel evolution of mica from muscovite to lepidolite with increasing Li2O (from 0.22 to 6.71 wt%), F, Rb, and Be, indicating that extreme differentiation and Li enrichment occurred during a short-lived episode at ca. 137 Ma. The mica Rb-Sr ages overlap published U-Pb ages of cassiterite, columbite-group minerals, and apatite, as well as muscovite 40Ar-39Ar ages, thereby directly linking Li-mica formation to the principal magmatic–hydrothermal and ore-forming interval. By contrast, published zircon U-Pb ages scatter from 153 to 102 Ma and systematically decrease with increasing zircon U + Th contents, a pattern consistent with radiation-damage-enhanced Pb loss. Our results demonstrate that the principal Li enrichment at Yifeng–Fengxin was confined to a brief interval at ca. 137 Ma and establish in situ mica Rb-Sr geochronology as a robust tool for dating rare-metal mineralization in granite- and pegmatite-hosted systems.

title: Contrasting rubidium and potassium isotope fractionation during chemical weathering
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Colin Z. Lin, Nicole X. Nie, Zhe Zhang, Roberta L. Rudnick, Sarah Aarons
abstract: Rubidium and potassium both exhibit heavier isotopic compositions in seawater relative to bulk silicate Earth (BSE), yet the mechanisms responsible for this fractionation remain poorly understood. We present coupled Rb and K isotopic measurements of a well-characterized metadiabase weathering profile in Cayce, South Carolina, which spans a continuum of weathering intensity from unweathered parent rock to strongly weathered saprolite (with chemical index of alteration from 45 to 95). Both Rb and K elemental and isotopic compositions show systematic transitions, from addition to leaching of heavy isotopes, coinciding with changes in clay mineralogy, indicating that clay mineral formation is the primary control on Rb and K mobilization and isotope fractionation. Rubidium isotopic compositions vary by ~0.26‰ across the profile, much larger than the variation in K isotopic compositions (~0.08‰), demonstrating that continental weathering fractionates Rb isotopes more strongly than K isotopes. Rayleigh distillation modeling for this and previously reported weathering profiles yields fluid-clay isotopic fractionation factors of +0.04‰ to +0.28‰ for Rb and 0 to +0.07‰ for K, indicating enrichment of heavier isotopes in weathering fluids relative to clay minerals. A steady-state box model incorporating Monte Carlo simulations confirms that reproducing the seawater–BSE isotopic offsets requires larger Rb isotope fractionation than that of K during continental weathering, consistent with weathering profile observations. However, the box model also reveals a paradox: while continental weathering fractionates Rb more strongly than K, reverse weathering must fractionate K more strongly than Rb in order to explain the seawater-BSE isotopic offsets, despite both processes involving fluid–clay isotope fractionation. This could reflect different structural preferences for Rb and K in clay minerals in continental weathering versus reverse weathering settings.

title: Fifty years of hydrochemical data link groundwater to bradyseism at Campi Flegrei caldera
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Marcello Liotta, Monica Piochi
abstract: Among volcanic calderas, Campi Flegrei stands out for its high-enthalpy geothermal reservoirs and long-lived bradyseism, both extensively investigated and monitored. While bradyseism is regarded as a potential eruption precursor, geothermal fluids play a fundamental role in driving unrest and triggering eruptions. Despite decades of investigation, the integration of long-term hydrochemical records remains limited. We reassess 50 years of chemical and isotopic analyses of surface and subsurface waters, systematically compiling and verifying original datasets to refine the geochemical framework of the caldera's hydrothermal system and to clarify its relationship with bradyseismic crises. We document the broad compositional variability of brines sampled by deep geothermal drilling in the 1970s and 1980s—a feature oversimplified in previous works—and provide chemical, isotopic, and mineralogical constraints on the shallow hydrothermal system that mediates fluid discharge from depth. Deep brines discharge mainly within the well-known central solfataric areas of Solfatara and Pisciarelli, where ground deformation, seismicity, and fumaroles are most intense. Long-term hydrochemical records from repeatedly studied sites in this sector reveal a previously unrecognized connection with bradyseismic phenomena. By reconstructing hydrochemical time-series and integrating them with independent geophysical and geochemical records spanning two main bradyseisms occurring during the drilling campaigns, we show that small but clear changes in water chemistry parallel ground deformation over multi-decadal timescales, without substantially altering the hydrogeological facies. These changes provide the first long-term evidence of a close coupling between bradyseismic activity and intra-caldera hydrothermal circulation. Our findings highlight the value of integrating multi-decadal hydrochemical observations into geochemical monitoring strategies.

title: Zinc isotope fractionation during cadmium substitution in sphalerite under variable salinity
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Lisheng Gao, Xinran Yan, Guangshu Yang, Chuanwei Zhu, Hui Yin, Yuxu Zhang, Haifeng Fan, Hanjie Wen
abstract: Zinc (Zn) isotopes are increasingly used to trace Zn cycling in geological and geochemical systems, yet Zn isotope fractionation during metal substitution in sulfide minerals remains poorly constrained. Here, we investigate Zn isotope fractionation associated with Cd substitution for Zn in sphalerite (ZnS) through batch experiments conducted under anoxic conditions at pH 5.5, with variable Cd concentrations and salinity. Zinc release increases systematically with Cd uptake, whereas elevated salinity suppresses both Cd uptake and Zn release, consistent with changes in aqueous Cd speciation associated with chloride complexation and competitive surface interactions. Kinetic experiments further show that Zn isotope compositions evolve toward relatively stable values during both Zn adsorption and Cd-Zn exchange. The magnitude of Zn isotope fractionation depends on both the ZnS phase and solution salinity. For ZnS synthesized at 100 °C, Δ66Znsolid–solution values are −0.26 ± 0.02‰ in ultrapure water and − 0.33 ± 0.04‰ in 10% NaCl solution. In contrast, ZnS synthesized at 250 °C exhibits substantially smaller fractionation in ultrapure water (−0.10 ± 0.01‰) but a stronger salinity dependence, with Δ66Znsolid–solution reaching −0.29 ± 0.04‰ in 10% NaCl solution. These results indicate that intrinsic differences between the ZnS phases influence the magnitude of Zn isotope fractionation, whereas aqueous chemistry further modulates its dependence on salinity. The enrichment of heavy Zn isotopes in solution is consistent with the preferential retention of light Zn through secondary adsorption of Zn released during Cd-Zn substitution. The experimentally constrained fractionation values obtained here provide new constraints on Zn isotope behavior during metal substitution in sulfide minerals and improve the interpretation of Zn isotope signatures in sphalerite–bearing geological systems.

title: Crystallographic reconstruction of fluid-disrupted zircon
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Albert Chang-sik Cheong, Hyeong Soo Kim, Sang Sub Han, Yong-Hyun Kim, Shinae Lee, Wonhee Lee, Yeongmin Kim, Keewook Yi, Jeongmin Kim, Youn-Joong Jeong, Seungsoon Choi, Jae Hyuck Jang, Ji-In Park, Ji-Hyun Lee, Naoya Sakamoto, Jaeyong Shin, Sugeun Jo
abstract: Fluids profoundly reshape minerals, yet how exactly crystallographic information governs such multistage processes remains unclear. Here we document hydrothermal destruction and subsequent lattice-coherent reconstruction within individual zircon grains from the Namsan ferroan granite of southeastern Korea under subvolcanic magmatic–hydrothermal conditions. The zircon cores contain c-axis-aligned thorite inclusions and cavities surrounded by successive radiation-damage zones and locally infilled by secondary phases enriched in fluid-transported elements, recording channelized fluid–mineral interaction. These disrupted features are pseudomorphically replaced by compact zircon rims that truncate the internal cavity–inclusion network and develop chemical zoning independent of the core fabric. Transmission electron microscopy nonetheless shows continuous atomic columns across the core–rim interface, with no amorphous interlayer or grain boundary. We infer that preferential dissolution of metamict domains contributed Zr and Si, while interface-coupled dissolution–reprecipitation and epitaxial precipitation into cavities collectively extended the inherited lattice during net zircon growth. The resulting internally porous yet coherent single-crystal architecture demonstrates persistent crystallographic control over mineral reconstruction spanning more than four orders of magnitude in length scale, with implications for zircon archival fidelity and the long-term preservation of reconstructed crystal structures.

title: Equilibrium germanium isotope fractionation between minerals: Implications for isotope effects and their applications
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Haochen Duan, Fang Huang
abstract: Germanium (Ge) isotopes have significant potential for tracing geochemical and cosmochemical processes involving Ge, but the equilibrium Ge isotope fractionation mechanism between Ge oxides, hydroxides, and sulfides remains unexplored. Here, we investigate the reduced partition function ratios (103 ln X/70 β, X = 72, 73, 74, and 76) of Ge isotopes in Ge-bearing minerals using first-principles calculations. The results show that 103 ln X/70 β decreases in the following sequence of krieselite > otjisumeite > bartelkeite > brunogeierite > schaurteite > stottite > fleischerite > argutite > argyrodite > Ge-Vacancy-doped sphalerite > barquillite > catamarcaite > renierite > Ge-Cu-doped sphalerite > germanite > briartite > putzite > colusite. The minerals with GeO bonds have larger 103 ln X/70 β values, shorter bond lengths, and lower coordination numbers (CN) and electronegativities than minerals with GeS bonds. These findings indicate that 103 ln X/70 β is negatively correlated with Ge CN and bond lengths, as well as the electronegativity of neighboring cations and anions. Although Ge is not a variable-valence element, the large variation in 103 ln X/70 β between oxides and sulfides indicates that Ge can be sensitive to the redox state. Our results show that when multiple elements are coupled and incorporated into minerals, a shorter distance between them increases the stability of doped minerals, indicating that trace element incorporation and compensation in minerals prefer a short-range-order principle. This mechanism provides a theoretical explanation for the phenomenon that Ge separates from sphalerite as independent Ge minerals during recrystallization processes. Our results indicate that differences in element electronegativity drive the composition isotope effect, in which systems with high electronegativity tend to enrich heavy isotopes. Meanwhile, we observed a significant difference in 103 ln X/70 β between low- and high-Ge sphalerite, indicating that trace element systems should account for the concentration isotope effect. Ge isotope fractionation factors provide a theoretical foundation for Ge isotope applications, indicating that they have the potential to constrain planetary core-mantle differentiation, ore-formation conditions, and the later effects of recrystallization on sphalerite.

title: Heat transport, carbon mass balance and fluids origin in the Matese Massif chain (southern Italian Apennine) inferred from chemical and isotopic data
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Francesco Rufino, Renato Palmieri, Luigi Marfella, Emilio Cuoco, Alessandro Santi, Rosario Avino, Martina Avella, Thomas H. Darrah, Dario Tedesco, Stefano Caliro
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive hydrogeochemical characterization of the Matese Massif carbonate aquifer system (Southern Apennines, Italy), based on original field samples collected during the 2018–2020 period. Hydrochemical and isotopic analyses were carried out on 109 groundwater samples (springs and wells) to quantify heat discharge and flux of endogenous carbon (Cdeep). The heat flux discharged by the aquifer system was estimated at ~250 MW with the primary contribution originating from basal discharge zones. Thermal anomalies, defined by the difference between infiltration and discharge temperatures, indicate a mean geothermal warming of ~2.2 °C, consistent with geothermal gradient interactions during circulation. The deep CO2 flux was estimated at approximately 540 tons/day, underscoring the magnitude of deep degassing in tectonically active non-volcanic settings. Isotopic signatures (δD, δ18O) confirm the meteoric origin of the Matese Massif groundwater, while δ13C and noble gases isotope reveal mixing processes between shallow meteoric/atmospheric components and deep-seated crustal/mantle fluids. Specifically, emissions in the northwestern sector of the Matese Massif exhibit isotopic signatures similar to the Roman Magmatic Province, whereas the south-eastern sector aligns with the Campanian Magmatic Province. These findings identify the Matese Massif as a structural and geochemical pivot separating two distinct regional degassing domains. We propose that the Quaternary extensional regime, superimposed on the Apennine subduction structural framework, controls the upwelling of mantle-derived fluids along major lithospheric discontinuities. The carbon and heat budgets of the Matese Massif provide critical quantitative constraints for better understanding the deep degassing mechanisms within active carbonate orogens.

title: Palygorskite facilitates proto-dolomite precipitation in dilute solutions at low temperatures
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Xiangjie Cui, Huan Liu, Juan Li, Jiani Chen, Xiancai Lu
abstract: The dolomite problem has attracted wide attention for over one century and is still full of mysteries. Recent studies have shown that clay minerals can facilitate proto-dolomite precipitation at room temperature. Here, we investigated the effects of palygorskite on proto-dolomite precipitation at 30–150 °C and solution Mg2+/Ca2+ molar ratios of 0 to 20. The results show that palygorskite promoted Mg incorporation into calcite, and induced proto-dolomite precipitation with Mg2+/Ca2+ ≥ 4 at 150 °C, Mg2+/Ca2+ ≥ 14 at 30 °C, and with intermediate Mg/Ca ratios and temperatures. The Mg content of carbonate precipitates increased linearly with the initial solution Mg2+/Ca2+ ratio and also increased with reaction temperature. FTIR and TEM analyses indicate that proto-dolomite formation involves two stages: precipitation of amorphous Ca-Mg carbonate (ACMC), with 61–63 mol% MgCO3 and minor Si, on palygorskite surfaces, followed by its crystallization into proto-dolomite with about 54 mol% MgCO3. Palygorskite surfaces promote the precipitation of ACMC, while Si released from palygorskite contributes to the transformation of ACMC into high-Mg calcite (HMC) and proto-dolomite. Meanwhile, the initial solution Mg2+/Ca2+ ratio strongly influences the Mg content in ACMC, while temperature mainly influences the Mg preservation during the ACMC crystallization. These results disclose a possible mechanism for dolomite formation and the influences of various factors. Further, these findings demonstrate that clay minerals function not only as passive substrates for heterogeneous nucleation, but also as active regulators of mineral evolution by influencing precursor formation, stabilization, and transformation.

title: Geochronology and trace element geochemistry of allanite and apatite reveal protracted ore deposit formation due to multiple fluid pulses at the Mary Kathleen REE–U Deposit, NW Queensland
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Alanis Olesch-Byrne, Bruno Vieira Ribeiro, Melanie A. Finch, Brandon Mahan, Andrew G. Tomkins
abstract: Hydrothermal ore systems commonly record repeated mineral growth, fluid infiltration, and isotopic re-equilibration, making it difficult to distinguish continuous ore formation from superimposed mineralising events. Petrochronology of fluid-sensitive accessory minerals can link mineral ages, textures, and trace-element signatures to resolve these overprinted histories. Here we integrate microtextural observations, in situ UPb geochronology, and trace-element geochemistry of allanite and apatite from the Mary Kathleen REE–U deposit, northwest Queensland, to test whether mineralisation reflects a single continuous event or multiple discrete fluid pulses. Allanite records four age populations between 1575 and 1487 Ma, indicating episodic REE–U mineralisation over ~90 Myr rather than continuous growth. Younger allanite domains are U-rich and generally more concordant, whereas older domains are U-poor and show stronger reverse discordance. Th/U and Eu/Eu* vary systematically with age, but we interpret these changes as recording evolving uranium mobility and fluid chemistry rather than a unique redox signal. Together with apatite UPb data, these results support repeated REE–U remobilisation during the Isan Orogeny and demonstrate the value of allanite–apatite petrochronology for reconstructing overprinted hydrothermal histories in complex metasomatic systems.

title: Distinct roles of sediment electron-accepting and electron-donating capacities in long-term oxidant consumption and contaminant degradation during in situ chemical oxidation
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Chenglong Yu, Lijun Fan, Hao Wang, Jianyuan Chen, Chuanzhiheng Luo, Shengyan Pu
abstract: The persistence and activation of oxidants in aquifers are critical for the performance of in situ chemical oxidation of contaminated groundwater but are largely constrained by aquifer chemical heterogeneity. However, the links between chemical heterogeneity of sediments and oxidant consumption and contaminant degradation remain unclear. Using a recently developed modified chemical probe method, we characterized the chemical heterogeneity of sediments from two contaminated aquifers by quantifying their electron-accepting capacity (EAC) and electron-donating capacity (EDC). We then investigated persulfate (S2O8 2−) consumption regulated by sediment EAC/EDC over 7–15 days. Results showed that S2O8 2− consumption correlates well with sediment EAC rather than EDC. Further analysis revealed that the initial fast kinetics were driven by oxidation of reactive EDC in expandable Fe-bearing phyllosilicates and the hidden cycling of EAC–EDC in Fe(III) oxides. In contrast, the subsequent slow kinetics were controlled by EAC–EDC cycling of structural Fe(III) associated with both Fe(III) oxides and expandable phyllosilicates. Although S2O8 2− consumption was governed by EAC, contaminant degradation was controlled by EDC. This is because reactions of S2O8 2− with EDC generate highly reactive oxidants (e.g., •OH and SO4•−), whereas reactions with EAC produce weak or negligible oxidants. Overall, these findings demonstrate the distinct roles of sediment EAC and EDC in oxidant consumption and activation, thereby providing quantitative insights for designing low-oxidant-consumption remediation strategies.

title: Aftermath of the Great Oxidation and Lomagundi–Jatuli Events: Geochemical and Isotopic Constraints on Earth's Early Habitability
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Abhisikta Goswami, Yirang Jang, Sanghoon Kwon, M. Santosh, Sarada Prasad Mohanty, Jiyoung Choi
abstract: In Earth's early history, the Lomagundi–Jatuli Event (LJE) represents a major carbon cycle perturbation associated with the later stages and aftermath of the Paleoproterozoic Great Oxidation Event (GOE), marked by enhanced marine carbon cycling and atmospheric oxygen accumulation. The Aravalli Supergroup (ca. 2.3–1.9 Ga) of Rajasthan, India, preserves an extensive sedimentary archive of these transitions. Previous studies documented carbon isotope perturbations, phosphogenesis, and redox evolution within these metasediments but lacked an integrated multi-proxy comparison of the geochemical and isotopic characteristics. The present study compares the geochemical and isotopic compositions of carbonaceous phyllites from two contrasting domains: the non-phosphoritic Umra sub-basin and the phosphorite-associated Udaipur domain. Integrated analyses of major and trace elements, chemical indices, redox-sensitive elements (Cr, Ni, U, Cu, V), REE + Y systematics, and stable isotopes (δ13Corg and δ15N) reveal variable depositional environments. The Umra sub-basin exhibits geochemical and isotopic variability, with fluctuating redox proxies, REE + Y anomalies, and carbon and nitrogen isotopic signatures indicating differences in depositional conditions and organic matter preservation. In contrast, the Udaipur domain records geochemical characteristics consistent with reducing conditions, including enrichment in redox-sensitive elements and depleted δ13Corg (V-PDB) values, following the LJE. These findings demonstrate environmental heterogeneity between the successions and support investigating relationships between phosphorite-associated sedimentation, nutrient cycling, and marine redox variability during the LJE and the GOE interval. The results contribute to understanding Paleoproterozoic carbon cycling and surface-environment evolution within the published geological framework, without independently establishing the relative depositional ages of the two successions.

title: Quartz as a recorder of the magmatic-hydrothermal transition in highly peraluminous rare-metal granites: evidence from the Beauvoir granite (French Massif Central)
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Océane Rocher, Christophe Ballouard, Antonin Richard, Lorenzo Tavazzani, Cyril Chelle-Michou, Patrick Carr, Alexandre Tarantola, Nicolas Esteves, Nordine Bouden, Julien Mercadier
abstract: Magma degassing is a ubiquitous process in granitic systems, particularly pronounced in highly peraluminous rare-metal granites (PRMGs), that influences crystallisation dynamics, metal transport, and ore deposition. In this study, we investigate the magmatic-hydrothermal transition in the Beauvoir leucogranite, a world-class PRMG and major lithium resource from the French Paleozoic Variscan belt, by integrating detailed petrographic observations of magmatic quartz and associated fluid inclusions with microthermometry and in situ analyses of quartz trace-element compositions and oxygen isotopes. The high H₂O contents of the Beauvoir melts (ca. 3.6–7.3 wt.%) favoured early H₂O saturation and magmatic volatile phase (MVP) exsolution during crystallisation, likely close to the liquidus. Early stages remained largely melt-dominated, with quartz cores recording increasing Li and Al contents across the granite units, consistent with progressive magmatic differentiation. In contrast, crystal rims exhibit a systematic depletion in Li and Al, reflecting increasing fluid influence on crystallisation dynamics, possibly combined with crystallisation of late-stage Li-bearing phases. In the apical and most evolved magmatic unit (B1), snowball-textured quartz overgrowths record catastrophic, high-intensity MVP exsolution events, likely triggered by rapid decompression and associated with strong undercooling and disequilibrium crystallisation. Cs fractionation modelling places these events at a late stage of evolution, corresponding to approximately 84–98% crystallisation. Snowball quartz is further characterised by a marked decrease in δ18O values from quartz cores to snowball rims of approximately 4.8–7.8‰, interpreted as the result of kinetic oxygen isotopic fractionation under disequilibrium conditions. Beyond its impact on quartz crystallisation, high-intensity MVP exsolution might have promoted the re-equilibration of pre-existing metal-bearing minerals, while strongly modifying the physicochemical conditions of the system, including its oxidation state, potentially enhancing the late-stage crystallisation of cassiterite (SnO₂) and columbite-group minerals.

title: Continental subduction transfers carbon and niobium‑tantalum to the deep mantle: Evidence from Nb Ta enriched orogenic peridotites
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Chun-Peng Xia, Ren-Xu Chen, Yong-Fei Zheng, Zhuang-Zhuang Yin, Guo-Chao Sun, Bing Gong, Xiang-Ping Zha
abstract: Continental subduction can deliver carbonate-bearing crustal material into the deep mantle to generate carbonate melts, but their migration, storage, and role in mass transfer within continental subduction zones remain poorly understood. We present an integrated petrological and geochemical investigation of orogenic peridotites from the Dabie–Sulu orogenic belt, combining whole-rock and mineral compositions, clinopyroxene Sr isotopes, rutile UPb ages, and comprehensive zircon analyses (cathodoluminescence imaging, UPb dating, trace elements, HfO isotopes and inclusion analyses). The garnet peridotites represent residues of the subcontinental lithospheric mantle (SCLM) that experienced variable degrees of metasomatism. Carbonate minerals, diagnostic clinopyroxene geochemical signatures (high Ca/Al, (La/Yb)N ratios and low Ti/Eu ratios) and P-T constraints provide multiple lines of evidence for carbonated silicate melt metasomatism. Elevated 87Sr/86Sr ratios in clinopyroxene and carbonate (0.7081–0.7106), together with high δ18O values (up to 14.1‰) and enriched Hf isotopic compositions in magnesite-bearing Triassic zircon domains, indicate that the metasomatic melt was derived from the deeply subducted South China Block. Most studied garnet peridotites have higher Nb and Ta contents than those of the Depleted Mantle. All have contents exceeding those of the modeled residue after 20% batch melting, and several samples show suprachondritic Nb/Ta ratios. This confirms that the metasomatized SCLM can act as a local high-Nb/Ta reservoir. Whole-rock and mineral compositions reveal that Ti-clinohumite is the dominant host of Nb and Ta. Ti-clinohumite inclusions in Triassic zircon domains and Triassic rutile UPb ages suggest that NbTa enrichment resulted from the same carbonate metasomatic event. Collectively, our results suggest that the continental subduction triggers carbonate metasomatism that transfers both carbon and high field strength elements from the subducting slab into the overlying SCLM, enriching it in volatiles and locally elevating its Nb/Ta ratios. These metasomatic domains may later be tapped by post-collisional magmatism, contributing to a protracted recycling pathway that operates on timescales longer than those in oceanic subduction zones.

title: Experimental diagenetic transformation of biogenic aragonite to calcite in sulfate and/or phosphate-bearing fluids
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Amalia Jiménez, Joel Marcelo Coronel, José Manuel Astilleros
abstract: The transformation of biogenic aragonite to calcite in phosphate or phosphate-sulfate bearing fluids was investigated through hydrothermal experiments at 60–80 °C up to 90 days. A phosphate-only system (BF) and a phosphate-sulfate system (BFS) were characterized by XRD, FTIR, and aqueous geochemical analyses supported by PHREEQC modelling. In both series, the reaction proceeded via an interface-coupled dissolution–precipitation mechanism, producing a two-stage sequence: hydroxylapatite (HAp) precipitation followed by calcite, consistent with the higher supersaturation of the fluid with respect to HAp. Variations in unit cell parameters are consistent with incorporation of HPO₄2− into HAp and oxyanions into secondary calcite. The contraction of the HAp c-axis and the decrease in dissolved sulfate (11.3% at 90 days), which may involve surface adsorption, are consistent with SO₄2− incorporation into the HAp lattice. Although dissolved P removal was similar in both series, calcite formed earlier and more extensively in BFS system (>83 vs. <30 wt% at 90 days), a difference not explained by the bulk saturation with respect to calcite. We hypothesize an indirect effect of sulfate, through the HAp intermediate and the Ca budget of the system, rather than a direct effect on calcite nucleation. Dissolved phosphate modifies the aragonite-to-calcite reaction pathway by introducing HAp as a reactive intermediate whose non-stoichiometric crystal chemistry may couple mineral replacement kinetics to fluid composition. Carbonate phosphatization may alter primary geochemical signatures in diagenetically altered carbonates from phosphate-rich environments and carbonate-to-apatite replacement is a potential pathway for P sequestration during carbonate diagenesis.

title: A multi-isotopic study to constrain groundwater geochemistry - case study of a quaternary sand and gravel aquifer in Cardiff, UK
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Zhe Dong, Katharine Hendry, David Boon, Ashley Patton, Jamie Lewis, Hong Chin Ng, Fiona Whitaker, Tong Wang, Xiaoning Liu, Tom Kibblewhite
abstract: Chemical alteration of groundwaters has implications for elemental fluxes into rivers, estuaries and coastal oceans. Individual isotope systems offer strong process constraints, while integrating multiple isotopes adds complementary insight that reveals the complexity of coupled geochemical processes. Here, we use multiple stable isotopic systems to investigate the physical and chemical controls on groundwater composition in a Quaternary sand and gravel coastal aquifer from Cardiff, UK. Stable isotopic compositions of silicon (Si), magnesium (Mg), and strontium (Sr), along with radiogenic Sr isotopes reveal significant impacts of anthropogenic interventions on the groundwater system, particularly the construction of a barrage and groundwater extraction. The saltier coastal groundwaters likely reflect contributions from saline estuarine/seawater-derived water and/or localized seepage from the underlying Triassic bedrock. This influx of saline water, combined with reducing conditions, has facilitated calcite precipitation that has removed substantial amounts of dissolved calcium (Ca) from the groundwater. The mechanisms controlling dissolved silicon (DSi) dynamics in the groundwater are complex. In coastal regions, silica precipitation predominantly influences DSi concentrations and isotopic composition, whereas vegetation uptake is the primary control on DSi concentrations and isotopic signatures in inland groundwaters. These findings are crucial for understanding the intricate interplay between natural processes and human interventions in shaping groundwater geochemistry, offering valuable insights for managing coastal water resources and mitigating anthropogenic impacts. By providing a multi-isotopic framework for investigating groundwater systems, this study provides a clearer perspective on the factors controlling modern and palaeo groundwater chemistry and can aid in predicting solute fluxes from groundwater to the ocean.

title: Coupled redox reactions in solution enable incorporation of labile ruthenium in iron (oxyhydr)oxides
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Sebastian T. Mergelsberg, Libor Kovarik, Elaine D. Flynn, Duo Song, Jeffrey G. Catalano, Eugene S. Ilton
abstract: Platinum group elements (PGEs) are substantially enriched in laterite soils formed over ultramafic terrains, where they correlate strongly with Fe and concentrate in Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides. However, the redox kinetics and structural fate of Ru during Fe oxide crystallization remain poorly characterized. Here we combine UV–Vis spectroscopy, high-energy X-ray diffraction, TEM, pair distribution function analysis, and Ru K-edge XANES and EXAFS spectroscopy to probe the coupled behavior of Ru and Fe during the formation and aging of ferrihydrite and goethite. Ferrozine titrations show that dissolved Fe(III) rapidly oxidizes lower-valent aqueous Ru species to Ru(IV) within minutes. Co-precipitation at pH 6.8 and 11 incorporates Ru(IV) into ferrihydrite as a dilute substituent at octahedral Fe sites, with no evidence of RuO₂. Subsequent conversion to goethite via aging at 21 °C (100 days) or 60 °C (3 days) retains Ru(IV) in the solid phase, where it maintains a ferrihydrite -like local coordination environment within the goethite host. Further, STEM shows that Ru is homogeneously distributed through goethite and discrete phases do not form. These results establish that structural incorporation of Ru into Fe (oxyhydr)oxides is both thermodynamically and kinetically accessible under conditions relevant to laterite formation and provide mechanistic constraints on the enrichment of Ru in the Fe oxyhydroxide fraction.

title: Rodingites as archives of Ca-Mg-Fe metasomatism and trace element mobility: Constraints from Mount Orliakas (Pindos Ophiolite, Greece)
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): L. Tsiarsioti, C. Karkalis, A. Sideridis, H. Tsikos, P. Mason, P. Petrounias, P. Pomonis, A. Rogkala, P. Koutsovitis
abstract: Rodingites serve as critical archives of fluid-rock interaction in mafic-ultramafic complexes. In the Mount Orliakas massif (Pindos Ophiolite, Greece), rodingitization of gabbronoritic protoliths occurred through distinct multi-stage Ca-metasomatism within serpentinized ultramafics. Notably, the dykes preserve nearly unaltered gabbroic cores, providing a direct reference for quantifying metasomatic fluxes without relying on extrapolated protolith compositions. Stage-1 (~370 °C, 3–5 kbar) formed prehnite and grossular, while Stage-2 (~300 °C, final exhumation) developed (hydro)andradite, Ti-rich garnet, and vesuvianite. Geochemical trends reveal a two-stage fluid evolution: initial Ca-enrichment coupled with Si, Mg, and Fe depletion (Stage-1), followed by distinct Mg and Fe enrichment in advanced Stage-2 rodingites. This reversal marks a shift to Mg-Fe-rich fluids driven by extensive interaction with surrounding serpentinizing ultramafics. Alkali depletion reflects plagioclase replacement by garnet. Trace elements show early REE depletion and late re-enrichment; Th, Ta, Nb, Cr, and Ni were depleted, while Zr was enriched. Highly mobile elements (Ba, Pb, Cs, U, As) were largely removed. Notably, Ti was immobile in shallow Group-A but mobilized at depth in Group-B rodingites, while Nb and Y showed inverse enrichment, reflecting pressure-dependent fluid mobility. Thermodynamic modeling results (PERPLE_X) validate the P-T path, constraining the Stage-1 to Stage-2 transition as a shift towards oxidizing, low-CO₂, Fe-Mg-rich fluids. These findings highlight rodingitization as a key process in element mobility within mafic-ultramafic complexes, controlled by protolith depth, redox conditions, and evolving fluid composition.

title: Experimental mineral carbonation of three ultramafic rocks in a simplified CO 2 -H 2 O system: Implications for Ni, Co, and Cr mobility
description: Publication date: 20 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 728 Author(s): Błażej Cieślik, Anna Pietranik, Alicja Lacinska, Keith Bateman, Krzysztof Turniak, Jakub Kierczak
abstract: Ex situ single-stage aqueous mineral carbonation experiments were conducted on three ultramafic rocks (UMR), including two serpentinized peridotites (SP I and SP II) and one serpentinite (S), in a simplified CO2-H2O-UMR reaction system at 50 °C and 20 bar CO2, and 185 °C and 150 bar CO2. We examined carbonation efficiency, fluid chemistry, and Ni, Co, and Cr mobility. At 50 °C, Mg-silicate dissolution dominated, but limited carbonate precipitation resulted in negligible CO2 sequestration. At 185 °C, magnesite precipitation yielded carbonation efficiencies up to 43% after 48 h. Although SP I and SP II initially contained similar olivine proportions (≈ 45 and 48 wt%), their carbonation efficiencies differed markedly (≈ 11% and 43%, respectively). The slightly more Fe-rich and Ni-poor olivine in SP II may have promoted dissolution, while inherited alteration may also have influenced reactivity. The olivine-free serpentinite achieved carbonation efficiency comparable to SP I. Fluid compositions showed MgSi decoupling: Mg accumulated during low-temperature dissolution but decreased as magnesite precipitated at 185 °C, whereas dissolved Si increased despite calculated supersaturation with respect to amorphous silica. Ni and Co were mobilized during Mg-silicate dissolution, but their aqueous concentrations were not directly proportional to Mg release. Measured Ni concentrations were lower than estimates based on olivine Ni/Mg ratios; retention in secondary reaction products is plausible but unconfirmed. Chromium concentrations in recovered fluids remained very low, consistent with limited release from Cr-bearing spinels. These findings highlight the importance of reaction conditions and feedstock characteristics for CO2 storage and trace-metal mobility.

title: Corrigendum to “Investigating pressure effects of Ti and Zr partitioning into zircon, quartz, and rutile at crustal temperatures” [Chem. Geol. 673 (2025) 122518]
description: Publication date: 5 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 727 Author(s): Heather M. Kirkpatrick, Dustin Trail, T. Mark Harrison, Elizabeth A. Bell

title: Fractionation of sulfide and platinum-group minerals in Macquarie Island magmas: Implications for platinum-group element systematics during mid-ocean ridge magma differentiation
description: Publication date: 5 January 2027 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 727 Author(s): Gyuchan Park, Jung-Woo Park, Vadim S. Kamenetsky, Jiwon Hwang
abstract: Platinum-group element (PGE) behavior in mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) magmas is commonly interpreted to reflect the segregation of immiscible sulfide liquid. Nonetheless, experimental studies suggest that under the reduced redox conditions of MORB systems, discrete platinum-group minerals (PGMs) may become stable and influence PGE budgets. However, direct constraints from natural samples on their role during MORB magma differentiation remain limited. Here, we investigate cogenetic MORB glasses and olivine-rich lavas and dykes (picrites) from the Macquarie Island ophiolite (SW Pacific) to evaluate the relative roles of immiscible sulfide liquid and PGMs during early MORB magma evolution.
