This study proposed an RFF-DNN model and developed a field–UAV–satellite collaborative framework for TOC retrieval, improving agreement between TOC predictions and field measurements. Comparisons across multiple scales further highlighted the importance of modeling-scale selection for retrieval accuracy, providing methodological support for detailed spatial mapping of TOC in water bodies.

title: Characterizing field-scale hydrology over tile-drained farmland with high-resolution integrated surface–subsurface hydrological modeling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Haoyuan Yu, Bin Peng, Saubhagya S. Rathore, Scott L. Painter, Phong V.V. Le, Bo Gao, Kaiyu Guan, Jiawei Fan, Mengqi Jia, Carl Bernacchi, Evan DeLucia, Michael D. Masters
abstract: Subsurface tile drainage strongly alters water movement, soil moisture, and nutrient transport in agricultural landscapes, but field-scale representation of tile drains in integrated surface–subsurface hydrological models (ISSHMs) remains challenging. Here, we developed and evaluated two spatially explicit tile-drain representations in the Advanced Terrestrial Simulator (ATS): a seepage-based method (SBM) and an equivalent drainage-zone method (DZM). SBM represents tile drainage as a pressure-dependent seepage sink applied to tile-designated cells. DZM represents tile drains as equivalent drainage-zone cells and improves upon conventional high-conductivity layer methods by modifying permeability, porosity, and water-retention parameters, which improves drain-zone representation and limits unrealistic drainage below the tile depth. The two methods were applied to two tile-drained Miscanthus x giganteus fields in the Midwestern United States. In field M1 both methods reproduced tile flow with comparable performance (SBM: NSE = 0.57, mKGE = 0.73; DZM: NSE = 0.57, mKGE = 0.77), and well captured seasonal ET dynamics (mKGE = 0.75). Validation in the M2 field showed strong transferability of the model, with tile-flow performance remaining satisfactory for both methods (SBM: NSE = 0.59, mKGE = 0.75; DZM: NSE = 0.55, mKGE = 0.65). Spatial resolution had limited effects on aggregated hydrological responses after parameter adjustment, but finer-resolution meshes improved heterogeneous surface ponding and subsurface-flow patterns. Microtopography, soil properties, and tile configuration caused representation-dependent drainage responses. SBM provided similar aggregated hydrological performance with lower computational cost, whereas DZM represented organized drain-zone flow pathways and tile-layer Darcy velocity patterns. These findings provide guidance for selecting tile-drain representations in ISSHMs and establish a hydrological foundation for investigating biogeochemical reactions and nutrient-transport processes in tile-drained landscapes.

title: Raindrop size distribution retrieval using X-band phased array radar: A New–generation radar application in China
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Duanyang Ji, Qiang Dai, Linyao Dong, Ningyuan Jia, Hui Li, Jingxuan Zhu, Tongxiao Zeng, Tiesheng Guan
abstract: The raindrop size distribution (DSD) is the fundamental descriptor characterizing rainfall microphysical properties, which is crucial for revealing rainfall formation mechanisms. Guangdong Province of China has successively deployed an X-band phased array radar (XPAR) network, with nearly 30 radars now forming a collaborative adaptive observing system over the Greater Bay Area. Despite the superior spatiotemporal resolution of XPAR, there remains a research gap in its application regarding the systematic transition from advanced hardware capabilities to refined microphysical characterization. To fill this gap, this study establishes an XPAR-based DSD retrieval framework with two models, namely RDEM-ER (Radar DSD Estimation Model using Empirical Regression) and RDEM-RF (Radar DSD Estimation Model using Random Forest). It also introduces a multi–temporal aggregation scheme to investigate DSD characteristics at different temporal resolutions derived from high-resolution XPAR observations. The results show that both models perform stably across temporal scales, while RDEM-RF exhibits superior overall retrieval performance. Specifically, the minute-scale model-based retrieval R2 of D0 and log10Nw both reach 0.90, and the R2 of μ is significantly improved from 0.33 (RDEM-ER) to 0.78 (RDEM-RF). The radar-retrieved DSD parameters show significant scale dependence, while the proposed framework maintains consistent retrieval performance across temporal scales. Collectively, this study offers an innovative framework for advancing XPAR-based rainfall microphysical studies, with great potential to underpin operational weather forecasting and hydrological modelling in future practical applications.

title: Hydrograph response spectra reveal representative flood modes and long-term changes in peak discharge and recession in a semi-arid urbanizing loess basin
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Fanglei Niu, Yixuan Wang, Xiaomin Liu, Ruizhong Gao, Limin Duan, Tingxi Liu, Ping Miao, Hongli Ma, Shiming Bai
abstract: Event-scale flood responses in semi-arid urbanizing basins vary with storm forcing, antecedent wetness, and land-surface change, yet the multidimensional morphology of event hydrographs remains underrepresented in flood-response diagnosis. We applied an eight-signature hydrograph response-spectrum framework to 51 independent flood events (1996–2023) in the Ulan Moron River Basin, a semi-arid urbanizing loess basin in China. Four principal components explained 87.20% of signature variance, and K-means clustering identified three representative modes: high-yield peaked, flashy low-yield, and buffered broad modes. These modes captured contrasting hydrograph characteristics, with moderate resampling stability (mean bootstrap adjusted Rand index = 0.538). In exploratory comparisons, rainfall amount and maximum 1-h intensity exhibited the strongest environmental contrasts among modes, suggesting a potential role for storm forcing. Although mode composition showed no detectable shift across the study periods, annual-median unit-area peak direct discharge and the fitted recession coefficient declined (Sen’s slopes: −0.00189 m3 s-1 km-2 yr-1 and −0.00736 h-1 yr-1, respectively), indicating lower event peaks and slower fitted recession. The gray-development index was positively associated with sample-based hydrograph concentration after adjustment for selected storm and antecedent-wetness variables (coefficient = 0.243; year-clustered p = 0.0019). This association weakened under time-consistent concentration definitions and was difficult to distinguish from concurrent temporal changes. Overall, these findings demonstrate that flood-response modes may show no detectable compositional shift while continuous hydrograph characteristics evolve, highlighting the value of multidimensional hydrograph analysis for identifying changes that categorical classification alone may overlook.

title: A continual learning framework for karst spring discharge forecasting: Cross-spring and cross-stage knowledge transfer
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Huiqing Hao, Yonghong Hao, Chunmei Ma, Shuai Gao, Quanrong Wang, Meihong Ma, Tian-Chyi Jim Yeh
abstract: Building upon the previously developed Temporal-Spatial Fusion Graph Neural Network (TSF-GNN), this study integrates drift detection, replay memory, and Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) into a continual learning framework for karst spring discharge forecasting. Through sequential learning, this framework continuously accumulates, transfers, and updates hydrological knowledge across multiple spring systems and hydrological stages. It treats multiple karst spring systems as sequential learning tasks, allowing the model to capture task-specific differences while reusing transferable hydrological knowledge from previously learned spring systems. It also treats successive hydrological stages within each spring system as sequential tasks, enabling the model to adapt to evolving relationships between recharge and discharge while preserving previously learned hydrological knowledge. In the framework, drift detection is employed to identify key distributional shifts in precipitation inputs and spring discharge responses, replay memory preserves representative historical hydrological conditions, and EWC constrains excessive parameter drift to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning. The framework was evaluated using three representative karst spring systems in the upper Haihe River Basin, China. Results show that the framework maintained stable predictive performance in both cross-spring and cross-stage learning tasks, as indicated by testing Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values ranging from 0.73 to 0.96. Drift analysis revealed pronounced spatial variability in precipitation recharge input distributions, particularly for precipitation stations located in mountain-front transition zones and areas with strong topographic variability. Meanwhile, replay memory progressively achieved broad temporal coverage while preferentially retaining dry-season and low-flow conditions, indicating that historical groundwater-storage-controlled regimes were preserved during sequential learning. Overall, the results suggest that the investigated karst spring systems are well suited to a continual learning framework because their recharge and discharge relationships evolve across spatially heterogeneous spring systems and temporally changing hydrological stages. This study provides a knowledge-driven framework for groundwater forecasting under changing environmental conditions. It highlights the potential of continual learning for hydrological prediction in non-stationary groundwater systems.

title: Regulatory chloride thresholds delay early detection of coastal aquifer salinization
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Seyed Mostafa Biazar
abstract: Coastal aquifers face growing saltwater intrusion, yet operational detection still relies on a single regulatory chloride threshold, the U.S. secondary drinking-water standard of 250 mg L−1, which flags contamination only once it has arrived. Whether intrusion could be detected earlier within existing networks has not been tested at scale. We assembled 218,181 chloride measurements from 44,990 wells in 17 U.S. coastal states and identified 145 wells with sustained fresh-to-saline transitions, most of them in coastal aquifers affected by lateral seawater intrusion, upconing or relict saline water. Classical early-warning signals of critical slowing down were weak (Cliff’s δ ≈ 0.1; area under the curve [AUC] ≈ 0.56), and a power analysis at the observed sampling times showed that even a simulated fold would reach an AUC of no more than about 0.64. Chloride instead rose gradually, often accelerating most strongly in the freshest wells, yet no trend-based forecast made at the moment of decision was significantly more accurate than a naive baseline, and linear extrapolation missed the arrival by a median of 9 years. The decision threshold, in contrast, mattered greatly: a warning threshold of 150 mg L−1 would have given a median lead time of about 2 years, a conservative estimate given left-censoring, at a false-positive rate below 10% (AUC 0.89). A counterfactual monitoring simulation shows that the threshold largely sets the lead time, whereas sampling frequency mainly determines how many transitions are caught. Earlier warning is therefore achievable chiefly through threshold redesign, without necessarily expanding routine sampling.

title: Simultaneous characterization of irregular non-point contaminant sources and non-Gaussian hydraulic conductivity fields using advanced data assimilation methods
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Wenyan Dou, Jiangjiang Zhang, Lei Yao, Chenglong Cao, Tongchao Nan
abstract: In groundwater modeling, effective identification of contaminant source and hydraulic conductivity parameters is essential for reliable prediction. However, most groundwater inverse modeling studies assume point contaminant sources and/or log-Gaussian hydraulic conductivity fields. In reality, irregular non-point contaminant sources and non-Gaussian hydraulic conductivity fields are commonly observed in groundwater systems. In this study, we design a series of complex cases involving the characterization of single to dual irregular non-point contaminant sources and channelized hydraulic conductivity fields, and further consider the presence of prior model misspecification. Their simultaneous characterization constitutes a high-dimensional inverse problem with 6,642 unknown parameters, marked by pronounced nonlinearity, non-Gaussianity and equifinality. Despite its practical significance, this challenging problem has not been investigated. To fill this gap, we propose and evaluate three advanced data assimilation methods: the ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation (ES-MDA), the iterative local updating ensemble smoother (ILUES), and the ensemble smoother with deep learning-based update (ES(DL)). The results show that ES-MDA is constrained by its underlying Gaussian assumption, which limits its ability to recover non-Gaussian structures in both contaminant source and hydraulic conductivity parameters. ILUES partially mitigates equifinality and can identify key regions of contaminant sources and high-conductivity zones, but it struggles to obtain accurate inversion results. In contrast, ES(DL) learns nonlinear mappings from the observation innovation to the parameter update, leading to superior performance in reconstructing contaminant source distributions, recovering non-Gaussian parameter structures, and reproducing observational data. These findings provide valuable insights into the simulation and characterization of complex groundwater systems.

title: Rainfall-driven submarine groundwater discharge reveals contrasting controls on reactive nitrogen and silicon in a subtropical semi-enclosed bay
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Manhua Luo, Gang Li, Yasong Li, Shujie Zhang, Hailong Li
abstract: Semi-enclosed bays are dynamic land–sea interfaces where rainfall-driven groundwater renewal can regulate submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) and coastal nutrient cycling, yet the coupling between these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated seasonal variations in SGD and nutrient dynamics following prolonged rainfall in Shenshan Bay, a subtropical semi-enclosed bay, by integrating radium isotopes (223Ra and 224Ra), stable isotopes (δ2H and δ18O), nutrient measurements, and an SGD mass-balance model. Results showed that sustained rainfall enhanced groundwater renewal and increased total SGD by 116%, primarily driven by a 2.3-fold increase in recirculated saline SGD. Despite this enhanced SGD, NH4 +–N concentrations and SGD-derived NH4 +–N fluxes declined markedly, whereas dissolved silicate (DSi) remained elevated. Multi-tracer evidence demonstrated that rainfall-driven groundwater renewal altered source contributions and mixing regimes. This process promoted NH4 + depletion and transformation along flow paths under modified hydro-biogeochemical conditions, whereas DSi remained predominantly controlled by groundwater transport and water–rock interactions. Consequently, rainfall shifted the exported nutrient signature from a “high NH4 +–high DSi” to a “low NH4 +–high DSi” regime, resulting in pronounced wet-season NH4 +-Si decoupling. Direct precipitation became the dominant NH4 +–N source to the bay, whereas SGD remained a major source of DSi. These findings highlight that rainfall controls coastal nutrient export not only by modifying groundwater fluxes but also by altering subsurface nutrient transformations, underscoring groundwater renewal as a critical hydrological link between precipitation variability and coastal biogeochemical processes.

title: Hourly stable isotopes reveal dynamic fog evolution and moisture source transitions in the Namib Desert
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Carlynn Diersing, Yue Li, Eugene Marais, Lixin Wang
abstract: Fog can be a critical component of the hydrological cycle in drylands, but its short-term evolution and moisture–source variability remain poorly resolved at sub-daily timescales. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first hourly-resolution stable isotope (δ18O and δ2H) investigation of fog evolution and moisture source transitions in the central Namib Desert. This analysis is based on 360 fog water samples collected across 129 fog events at the Gobabeb Namib Research Institute during 2022–2023, integrated with surface meteorological observations and satellite-based fog detection. Fog water δ18O and δ2H varied substantially within individual events, revealing pronounced sub-daily isotopic evolution. Paired pre- and post-sunrise comparisons showed significant isotopic enrichment after sunrise, with a mean increase of 4.1‰ for δ2H and 0.7‰ for δ18O (both p < 0.01). At the event level, increases in fog water amount during terrestrial-moisture fog were associated with decreases in both δ18O and δ2H, whereas no statistically detectable relationship was found for the more sparsely sampled ocean-moisture fog events. Moisture-source contributions also evolved within events: 45% of events were predominantly terrestrial moisture and 22% predominantly oceanic moisture, while approximately one-third exhibited ocean-to-terrestrial, terrestrial-to-ocean, or two-directional source transitions. Isotope trajectories were similarly diverse, with 40% of events showing progressive enrichment, 23% progressive depletion, and 37% bidirectional changes, demonstrating that moisture-source transitions and isotope evolution were not linked through a simple one-to-one relationship. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the overall trajectory classification was robust to analytical uncertainty, although temporal sampling density influenced the ability to resolve within-event reversals. Satellite- and isotope-based classifications agreed for 84% of fog-hour identifications (non-mixed fog types). Overall, these findings demonstrate that fog in the central Namib Desert undergoes substantial within-event changes in moisture-source contribution and isotope composition. High-frequency isotopic measurements therefore reveal dynamic fog evolution that is largely obscured by event-integrated sampling.

title: Pore-scale simulation of gas–water-liquid sulfur three-phase relative permeability in carbonate rocks
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Zhilin Cheng, Rui Zhang, Tong Li, Zheng Li
abstract: Water invasion coupled with liquid sulfur precipitation can substantially alter multiphase transport in heterogeneous carbonate porous media by redistributing wetting films, modifying interfacial topology, and reducing phase connectivity. Here, a modified color-gradient three-phase lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) was used to investigate gas–water-liquid sulfur flow and relative permeability in representative two-dimensional carbonate pore structures. The effects of initial liquid sulfur saturation (Ss ), initial water saturation (Sw ), and capillary number (Ca) on fluid distribution, interfacial area, sulfur retention, and gas connectivity were examined. At low Ca, liquid sulfur showed low mobility and was retained mainly as droplets, clusters, or slugs in pore corners, throats, and fracture junctions, enlarging the sulfur-gas interface and disrupting connected gas pathways. Within the present 2D domains, when Ss increased from 0.1 to 0.2, the gas cutoff point in the intergranular-pore model (P1) shifted to Sw approximately 0.35, while the peak gas relative permeability in the matrix-fracture model (F1) decreased from about 0.32 to 0.10. The stronger response of F1 suggests that fracture junctions and abrupt aperture transitions enhance local sulfur retention and phase disconnection in the simulated structure. The effects of Sw and Ca were strongly structure dependent. In P1, water-film lubrication and higher Ca promoted sulfur detachment and widened the three-phase co-flow window. In F1, however, water bridging and sulfur entrainment enhanced structural trapping and produced a non-monotonic gas relative permeability response. The generalized Corey model reproduced the liquid-sulfur relative permeability trend at fixed Sw , whereas the Stone II and Baker correlations showed structure-dependent agreement with the present 2D simulations, with substantially larger deviations in F1 where gas mobility was strongly affected by junction-scale phase disconnection. These results provide pore-scale evidence for three-phase flow impairment caused by coupled sulfur deposition and water invasion, with implications for production evaluation and drawdown control in high-sulfur carbonate gas reservoirs, as well as for understanding water-controlled transport, retention, and remobilization of immiscible phases in fractured carbonate aquifers and other subsurface hydrological systems.

title: How causal-prior embedding strategies affect generalization in deep learning models for groundwater level prediction
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Xingyu Zhu, Xiaoling Su, Haijiang Wu, Taishan Wang, Hanwen Yan
abstract: Causal priors can improve deep learning models for hydrological prediction, yet how embedding strategies translate this information into transferable predictive skill remains unclear. We used convergent cross mapping (CCM) to derive well-specific priors encoding inferred causal strengths and response lags of meteorological influences on groundwater levels. Using a common Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) backbone and shared training and evaluation settings, we compared six embedding mechanisms that varied where and how causal priors entered model computation, including three newly developed variants for prior-guided attention, gate modulation, and loss regularization. Capacity controls and prior shuffling tested the contribution of well-specific prior information, while noise perturbations assessed sensitivity to prior errors. Models were evaluated using weekly observations from 118 groundwater wells in Germany under in-sample (IS), out-of-sample (OOS), and multi-step forecasting settings. The predictive value of these priors depended on how they were embedded. Compared with the dynamic-input-only baseline, three strategies using separate representation fusion or recurrent conditioning improved mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) by 7.6%–9.9% (IS), 2.6%–4.8% (OOS), and 7.8%–10.6% (6-week horizon). Input concatenation, prior-guided attention, and loss regularization yielded limited gains. The dual-branch fusion strategy achieved the best overall performance at modest additional computational cost. Further analyses confirmed that the improvements depended on informative, station-aligned priors rather than increased model capacity alone. However, some wells showed performance deterioration, revealing sensitivity to prior reliability and local groundwater-response heterogeneity. These findings show that the usefulness of inferred causal priors depends on both information content and embedding strategy, providing practical guidance for balancing predictive accuracy and generalization.

title: Basin-specific storage persistence and atmospheric–groundwater drought associations across Ethiopia
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Mekash S. Kifelew, Xianfang Song, Lihu Yang, Dongmei Han, Hongmei Bu, Ying Ma
abstract: Atmospheric and land-surface drought indicators may not reliably represent groundwater-storage drought because terrestrial stores respond at different timescales. We assessed seven drought pathways across 12 Ethiopian basins (2003–2024), linking precipitation (SPI), climatic water balance (SPEI), soil moisture (SSMI), runoff (SRI), and GRACE/GRACE-FO-derived groundwater-storage drought (SGDI). Lag associations were evaluated with detrending, first differencing, 9,999 phase-randomized lag-search surrogates, Benjamini–Yekutieli (BY) correction, bootstrap, storage-component sensitivity, event matching, and secondary teleconnection analyses. Atmospheric–soil-moisture associations peaked near one month and soil-moisture–runoff associations near zero lag, whereas no groundwater-ending pathway survived primary BY correction after detrending or differencing. Multi-scale groundwater-ending surfaces increased toward the upper accumulation boundary: 24 months was selected in 43/48 original searches, and extending the search to 36 months moved 44/48 maxima to that new boundary. A detectability simulation showed that lag-search inference was approximately calibrated under resampled storage noise but had low power for weak synthetic coupling, so non-significance is interpreted as limited identifiability rather than absence of climatic influence. A conservative three-region spatial sensitivity retained all 18 upper-cascade BY results and 0/24 groundwater-ending results. The first two SSA-reconstructed components had a national reconstruction variance ratio of 93.1% in the original equal-basin SGDI series and 52.1% after linear detrending. These results support basin-specific, multi-season storage monitoring without interpreting selected scale–lag maxima as fixed physical response times.

title: Process-informed feature engineering improves LSTM streamflow predictions in snow-affected watersheds
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Mohamed M. Fathi, Mukesh Kumar, Kaustubh Anil Salvi, Steven J. Burian
abstract: Accurate streamflow prediction in snow-affected catchments remains challenging due to the nonlinear and temporally evolving nature of snow accumulation and melt processes. While Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models have shown considerable promise for streamflow prediction, their performance is fundamentally driven by the quality and informativeness of input features. This study assesses whether LSTM-based streamflow predictions could be further improved by incorporating additional process-informed inputs, derived solely from the same standard meteorological forcings already used by the LSTM. To this end, we feature-engineer inputs including rain-snow partitioning, approximate snow water equivalent, and antecedent gross snowfall, and evaluate their added value within local and regional LSTM frameworks across 88 snow-affected catchments in the US. Results revealed substantial improvements, particularly for the local model, for which the 25th (50th) percentile Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) increased from 0.50 (0.71) using standard meteorological inputs to 0.62 (0.76) when incorporating engineered features. The improvements were most pronounced during the snowmelt period, when streamflow is strongly influenced by antecedent snow storage. For regional models, the benefit scaled inversely with training-data availability: median NSE increased from 0.74 to 0.80 when models were trained on restricted datasets (four independent subsets of 22 catchments), but only from 0.82 to 0.83 when trained on the full 88-catchment dataset. As progressively more informative snow-related inputs were introduced, the performance gap between local and regional models narrowed substantially. Collectively, the results indicate that process-informed feature engineering improves streamflow prediction by providing information on snow storage dynamics that would otherwise need to be inferred implicitly from long sequences of daily meteorological forcings. These findings highlight the critical role of process-informed feature engineering in advancing streamflow prediction in snow-affected catchments.

title: Warming increases world’s population exposure to water scarcity risk
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Senlin Tang, Qiang Zhang, R. Iestyn Woolway, Fubao Sun, Yao Feng, Chong-Yu Xu, Vijay P. Singh, Jingchun Fang, He Sun, Ziwei Li, Likun Han
abstract: Water is a critical resource, and approximately 80% of the world’s population faces significant threats to water security. Compounding the threat is the uncertainty of global water resources caused by their variability, which hinders effective management. Here, data-driven deep learning techniques were coupled with a physics-informed hydrological model to better represent climate-change-induced changes in water resources and improve the reliability of future water-resource projections. Our findings indicated a reduction in the area of water-scarce regions from 41.4 ± 1.3 million km2 during the historical period (1995–2014) to 39.5 ± 2.1 and 38.3 ± 2.2 million km2 during 2015–2100 under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, respectively. Despite this spatial decline, population exposure to water scarcity increased from 4.31 ± 0.06 billion people during 1995–2014 to 5.84 ± 0.11 and 5.18 ± 0.13 billion people under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, respectively. The response of water resources to climate change can be classified into three patterns: exacerbated decrease, minimal change, and accelerated increase. Substantial reductions in water availability were identified in South Australia/New Zealand, in contrast to projected increases in North Asia and relatively moderate changes in Western South America. By providing a comprehensive assessment of global water resources, the study offers a scientific basis for more sustainable and rational water-resources management.

title: Time-varying causality in karst spring discharge under groundwater overexploitation and causality-informed LSTM for multi-step prediction
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Juan Zhang, Yonghong Hao, Quanrong Wang, Qi Wang, Jiyang Tian, Xiaoyang Li, Tian-Chyi Jim Yeh
abstract: Long-term groundwater overexploitation may alter how precipitation drives spring discharge in karst aquifers, but traditional recession- and correlation-based methods assume time-invariant drivers and cannot capture such changes. We used causal inference to examine how exploitation-induced groundwater-level decline reshapes precipitation–discharge causality, redistributes subsurface flow contributions, and affects discharge predictability in the Niangziguan Springs basin. The results showed that heavy extraction weakened the causal influence of precipitation on discharge by about one order of magnitude, whereas the time-lag structure remained largely unchanged. The dominant flow component shifted from fast to intermediate flow, and fast flow was the most sensitive to groundwater-level drawdown. Under overexploitation, self-causality became the largest component of the causal contribution to discharge variability (60%–72% of the normalized information flow). In addition, the seven precipitation records contributed synergistically, i.e., each station carried more causal information on discharge when analyzed jointly with the other stations than on its own. We injected the diagnosed causal structure into a long short-term memory (LSTM) network at the input, encoder, and architecture levels. Over the 2001–2022 testing period, the architecture-level multi-branch model (M3) performed best and most stably for one-month-ahead prediction (NSE = 0.854 ± 0.006; RMSE = 0.249 m3/s) and significantly outperformed all other designs at every lead time (1–3 months), whereas input- and encoder-level fusion improved on the baseline only at the three-month lead. Groundwater overexploitation weakens recharge control and reorganizes karst spring dynamics. The gain of M3 is attributed mainly to its multi-branch separation of time scales.

title: Constraining binary alpine karst spring recharge using Ensemble Rainfall-Runoff analysis (ERRA) and artificial tracer tests
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Jasper F.D. Lammers, Martin Masten, Thomas Wagner, Ralf Benischke, Simon Seelig, Wolfgang Schöner, Gerfried Winkler
abstract: Karst systems sustain a substantial share of global freshwater supply, yet their internal discharge dynamics are difficult to characterize because conduit networks are often inaccessible to direct observation. Fluorescent tracer tests can quantify recharge-area-to-spring connections and travel times, but only under the conditions at the time of testing. Rainfall-runoff deconvolution methods such as Ensemble Rainfall-Runoff Analysis (ERRA) offer a complementary, data-driven approach resolving nonlinear, non-stationary discharge responses across catchment wetness and precipitation intensity. We apply ERRA alongside 14 years of tracer test data to the binary Etzbach karst spring (Austrian Alps) to quantify discharge response across antecedent wetness and precipitation intensity conditions, determine whether contributing subcatchments share governing controls, and test consistency between ERRA-derived dynamics and tracer-constrained transit times. Results show wetness-dependent response timing and magnitude, driven by two thresholds acting on the same storage deficit in the allogenic region: a connectivity threshold, saturating by mid-wetness, and a contributing-area threshold, which continues to rise into wet conditions. Tracer tests confirm a minimum two-hour travel time from the fastest-responding subcatchment, accelerating under wetter, more intense conditions, with infiltration-excess overland flow emerging at the highest wetness and intensity combined. A second subcatchment connects independent of wetness, activating only during highest intensities — indicating structurally different triggers. The Normalized Response Function further reveals a recurrent discharge signal whose ∼50-hour travel time aligns with a gradient-controlled velocity relationship, hinting at a third contributing subcatchment. These findings establish ERRA, combined with tracer validation, as a robust method for resolving multi-origin, nonlinear binary karst discharge dynamics.

title: The influence of planning horizon on the importance of streamflow parameter uncertainty in reservoir analyses
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Natasha Ballis, Rory Nathan, Murray Peel, Benjamin J. Henley, Thomas McMahon
abstract: Longer streamflow records allow us to calculate streamflow model parameters with greater certainty. There is a common assumption that this reduction in parameter uncertainty is of practical benefit to the design and operation of water resource systems. Here we explore this assumption by considering the uncertainty in estimates of reservoir reliability based on streamflow records of different lengths. We consider stationary first-order autoregressive synthetic streamflows with example annual variabilities, skewnesses and autocorrelations reflective of a broad range of hydrological regimes in reservoir behavior analyses. We also consider a range of reservoir planning horizons. We find that the reduced parameter uncertainty gained from a longer record ( ≥ 30 years) translates into appreciably more certain reliability estimates only when planning horizons are sufficiently long, in the order of 100 years or more. For shorter planning horizons, in the order of 10–30 years, reduced parameter uncertainty has little impact on estimates of reliability. Rather, these analyses are dominated by aleatory uncertainty. Therefore, we suggest that for the design and operation of water resource systems under the assumption of a stationary climate, the practical benefit of reduced parameter uncertainty gained from longer records depends on the length of the reservoir planning horizon.

title: Uncovering hidden residential water use patterns in an arid city
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Peyman Yousefi, Rubab Saher
abstract: Managing residential water demand in arid regions requires not only knowing how each household distributes its water use across the year but also assessing whether households maintain that pattern over time. This study combines annual clustering, transition probability analysis, and entropy analysis to uncover residential water-use patterns and their temporal stability among approximately 281,000 single-family households over six years, and a two-part hurdle model to examine which household characteristics are associated with changes in that pattern. We identified five annual water use patterns, ranging from a nearly uniform year-round consumption (C2, 53.4%) to a sharp July summer peak (C3, 38.0%), with smaller shares following a fall-peaking (C1, 7.4%), a spring-to-summer (C4, 0.5%), and a summer-to-fall (C5, 0.6%) pattern. We showed that 34.2% of households never changed their pattern, while 50.3% changed twice or more, revealing a behavioral divide within the residential sector. Structural property characteristics showed the strongest detectable associations with that change, although the model explained little of its variation. Pool ownership was associated with both a lower probability of complete stability (OR = 0.79) and greater switching magnitude (beta = +0.019), whereas living area was associated only with switching magnitude (beta = +0.018) and plumbing fixtures with greater stability (OR = 1.13). Because membership persisted in 68.2% of adjacent-year transitions, a single year of billing data supports a one-year-ahead seasonal-pattern assignment and can inform short-horizon demand forecasting, whereas multi-year targeting requires periodic reassessment, with structural characteristics serving as group-level indicators of where it is most needed.

title: Extreme rainfall intensification in the Mexico Valley, a warming and expanding tropical megalopolis
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Rodrigo Muñoz-Sánchez, Miguel Angel Altamirano del Carmen, Francisco Estrada, Bernardo A. Bastien-Olvera, Oscar Calderón Bustamante, Alma Mendoza-Ponce
abstract: Increasing atmospheric temperature is expected to lead to higher moisture-holding capacity and the potential for stronger storms. Urban regions are heating both due to global climate change and the urban heat island effect, particularly in the understudied tropics with growing populations and where deforestation and urbanization rates remain high. Models and observations have concluded that sub-daily extreme rainfall is highly sensitive to temperature increases. However, little is known about the compounding effects of climate change and urbanization in urban rainfall intensification. In this paper, we analyze extreme precipitation intensification in the Mexico Valley megalopolis, an expanding tropical megalopolis and one of the largest in the world. We use a Regional Convection Permitting Model under a high greenhouse gas emissions and rapid urban growth scenario. We found that urbanization would be responsible for 67.5% of the increase in mean precipitation by midcentury, and for up to 34.3% of the increase in rainfall intensity. The median increase in rainfall intensity, due to the overall temperature increase, all over the megalopolis would be 16%/°C, more than twice the Clausius-Clapeyron rate, with stronger intensification occurring in shorter duration and longer return period storms. Conversely, higher-elevation regions might see a reduction in extreme rainfall intensity, particularly for longer return period events. Finally, we derive spatially explicit, grid-cell-level relationships to understand the spatial structure in changes in extreme rainfall intensity and for them to be estimated as a function of local temperature anomalies, where the largest increases happen in newly urbanized areas.

title: Heavy metal migration pathways in the contaminated canal sediment–soil–aquifer system
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Marina Ćuk Đurović, Maja Todorović, Igor Jemcov
abstract: This study develops an integrated approach of heavy metal transport in a canal sediment–soil–surface water–groundwater system, linking contaminant sources, hydrogeochemical processes, hydrogeological environment, and transport pathways to groundwater as the primary receptor. Multivariate factor analysis identified three distinct geochemical associations controlling metal distribution in canal sediments, which act as long-term sinks and potential secondary sources of contamination: (F1) Zn, Ni, and Cu associated with organic matter and mobility in groundwater; (F2) Cd and As characterized by vertical persistence and occurrence in canal sediment and the geological environment; and (F3) Pb and Cr dominated by canal sediment accumulation and limited vertical transfer. Complementary assessment methods, including the pollution index (Pi), geoaccumulation index (Igeo), and potential ecological risk index (PERI), were applied to evaluate contamination intensity and ecological risk. The study further demonstrates that meaningful interpretation of contaminant migration requires integration of hydrogeological and hydrochemical evidence. Field hydraulic obseravtions and hydrochemical similarities indicate potential connectivity between the shallow unconfined and deeper confined aquifer, highlighting the importance of future investigations and monitoring of synchronous groundwater-level fluctuations as a possible indicator of hydraulic connectivity within the aquifer system. Overall, the proposed integrated methodology provides a robust framework for linking sediment-based risk assessment with contaminant transport behavior across interconnected environmental compartments. The results identify Zn as the most mobile element and the only metal currently detected in groundwater. In contrast, Cd exhibits vertically persistent accumulation within sediments and soils, indicating a greater tendency for long-term retention under present conditions. These findings emphasize the importance of multi-compartment approaches for identifying both current contamination patterns potential long-term groundwater vulnerability at historically contaminated sites.

title: Video-based river velocity estimation using natural tracers
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): S.S. Mandipe, A.J. Wade, N. Everard, D.P. Brass, P. Rameshwaran
abstract: Accurate stream flow measurements, especially during floods or at ungauged sites, are essential to progress hydrological understanding. Quantitative Image Velocimetry (QIV) helps to address this need using video-based flow measurements. Here, we compare surface velocity error across three configurations: (1) oblique imagery with ground control points (GCPs) elevated above the water surface, (2) oblique imagery with GCPs placed at the water surface, and (3) nadir imagery acquired using an uncrewed aerial system without GCPs. In each case, surface velocity was estimated using Particle Image, Particle Tracking and Space-Time Image Velocimetry. Error estimates were determined using controlled flume experiments and five field surveys in the River Tweed; a site used as a model for upland UK rivers. Benchmarked against kinematic current meter data, the lowest errors (<5%) from the field surveys were achieved using oblique view GCPs positioned adjacent to the water surface. Surface velocities estimated from a nadir view, without GCPs, could sometimes achieve errors below 20%. Similar outcomes were observed under controlled flume conditions. The results show that QIV can yield acceptable surface flow estimates in complex upland environments with natural tracers. By using naturally occurring river surface tracers, this work extends QIV beyond simplified reach set-ups and artificial tracers, contributing to an advancement in methodology for measuring stream flows.

title: Extreme precipitation reorganizes nutrient responses from source to transport: Evidence from 90 catchments
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Mengyu Wang, Zhao Wang, Lifeng Wu
abstract: Increasing hydroclimatic extremes cause abrupt fluctuations in river nutrient concentrations that challenge watershed management. Yet it remains unclear how extreme precipitation alters driver structures across different nutrient species beyond isolated sites and events. We compared the responses of total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP) and ammonia nitrogen (NH3-N) to extreme and ordinary precipitation events across 90 catchments in the Haihe River Basin. Interpretable machine learning was combined with concentration–discharge (C–Q) relations and event-window export estimates to relate predictive attribution to observed transport responses. The analyses showed that median nutrient concentration responses under extreme conditions were approximately 4.3–7.4 times those under ordinary conditions. Predictive attribution showed a source-to-transport shift across all three nutrients. Transport-related shares increased by 16.7, 15.4 and 7.2 percentage points for TN, TP and NH3-N, respectively. At the analyzed measured-discharge sections, C–Q slopes generally became more positive, and event-window runoff and nutrient export increased. Higher runoff and nutrient export also persisted after normalization by actual window duration. For TN, higher export coincided with greater runoff without a consistent rise in flow-weighted concentration, whereas TP and NH3-N showed increases in both runoff and flow-weighted concentration. These patterns are consistent with stronger hydrological connectivity during intense rainfall and distinct source and transport constraints among nutrients. The findings can provide insights into nutrient-specific export responses during extreme rainfall and inform event-scale monitoring alongside continued nutrient source reduction.

title: Transient disruption of the seasonal rainfall–groundwater level coupling following a near field earthquake
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Wenxu Zhang, Hongbiao Gu, Yao Yang, Mingqian Li, Zujiang Luo
abstract: Groundwater level (GWL) is widely used to probe earthquake-related hydrogeological changes in the crust. However, the interpretation of these changes relies almost entirely on the cyclic components of the GWL, such as tides and barometric pressure. Conversely, seasonal component controlled by precipitation is often overlooked as a confounding factor, limiting the interpretation of the response of rainfall-sensitive aquifers to seismic. This study treats rainfall as a diagnostic signal for the response of GWL to earthquakes, using a proposed dual validation framework and records from a well following a near field earthquake. During the first rainy season after the earthquake, the well produced GWL anomaly: although rainfall was slightly above the long-term average, the GWL exhibited a trend contrary to the expected seasonal rise (67.92% lower than the average). The dual validation framework attributes the changes through two independent lines of evidence—one testing external forcing, the other the aquifer’s own response. The former, combined with rainfall-scenario analysis, confirmed that the GWL anomaly resulted from a reduction in the actual contribution of precipitation (∼78.05%), caused by increased discharge. The latter indicated that the increase in discharge was most likely due to enhanced hydraulic connectivity within the groundwater system caused by the earthquake. There was also a statistically significant causal relationship between this enhanced connectivity and the earthquake (placebo test; p < 0.01). We argue that taking rainfall into account can enhance the detection of hydrogeological and GWL changes following earthquakes and other abrupt disturbances.

title: Assessing lateral inflows to a sub-arctic stream using distributed temperature sensing, terrain metrics, and process-based modeling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Parsa Parvizi, Jari-Pekka Nousu, Danny Croghan, Samuli Launiainen, Pertti Ala-Aho, Ilkka Martinkauppi, Hannu Marttila
abstract: Groundwater–surface water interactions regulate streamflow persistence and thermal regimes by linking catchment subsurface water storage to surface hydrology. However, mapping locations of groundwater discharge remains challenging, particularly in high-latitude catchments with strongly seasonal hydrological cycle. We used high-resolution distributed temperature sensing (DTS) to monitor stream temperature at 2 m spatial and 30 min temporal resolution along a 2 km boreal headwater stream in northern Finland. Seasonal gradient-based thermal patterns were used to identify stream sections dominated by groundwater discharge. In addition, snowmelt periods were used to detect surface and near-surface flow contributions to the stream. We then compared DTS-derived patterns with terrain-based hydrological metrics (upslope contributing areas and topographic wetness index) and SpaFHy-2D hydrological model simulations to assess their ability to predict groundwater discharge and surface water inflow locations. Terrain-based predictions showed limited spatial agreement with DTS (17–40% recall), whereas SpaFHy-2D showed higher recall (83%) but limited spatial overlap (Jaccard index = 0.21). Modelled inflow discharge locations remained spatially consistent across seasons, while inflow magnitudes varied seasonally and were highest during snowmelt. DTS effectively detected groundwater–surface water interactions and exposed limitations of terrain metrics and hydrological models. In this peatland-esker sub-arctic catchment, groundwater discharge appeared to be influenced by hydrogeological heterogeneity that was not fully captured by surface topography, while a peatland drainage ditch enhanced lateral connectivity between peatlands and the stream.

title: From static to dynamic parameter regionalization for process-based evapotranspiration modelling through differentiable parameter learning
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Mingming Xie, Jianyun Zhang, Zhenxin Bao, Guoqing Wang, Junliang Jin, Cuishan Liu, Jie Wang, Xiaoxiang Guan
abstract: Accurate evapotranspiration (ET) estimation in ungauged regions remains challenging because conventional parameter regionalization assumes that process-model parameters vary across sites but remain constant over time. This assumption is limited because many parameters implicitly represent changing vegetation physiological states and environmental controls. To address this limitation, we developed a physics-informed dynamic parameter regionalization framework for the Penman-Monteith-Leuning (PML) ET model. The framework is implemented through differentiable parameter learning (dPL), in which an entity-aware Long Short-Term Memory network estimates PML parameters from dynamic environmental forcing and static site attributes, while the differentiable PML process module constrains parameter learning through ET observations. Its performance was evaluated at 103 FLUXNET2015 sites using leave-one-site-out cross-validation and compared with vegetation-type and regression-based regionalization approaches. Results showed substantial spatial heterogeneity of PML parameters among and within vegetation types, while static attributes explained only part of this variability. Compared with conventional static approaches, the proposed dynamic parameterization framework improved ET estimation, increasing the median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) from 0.64 to 0.74, with consistent improvements across vegetation types, seasons, and environmental states. The learned dynamic parameters exhibited physically plausible seasonal variations and environmental associations, with temporal variability in the stomatal conductance coefficient ( m ) and soil evaporation constraint factor ( f soil ) contributing most to the performance improvement. Additional evaluation using gross primary productivity (GPP) provided independent support for the consistency of the learned parameterization with coupled carbon–water processes. Long-term simulations at 63 sites showed broad consistency with existing ET products. These results demonstrate that dynamic parameter regionalization provides a transferable and interpretable framework for process-based ET modelling.

title: A physics-enhanced index reveals drought–flood abrupt alternation dynamics and hydroclimatic controls
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Zheng Wang, Xiran Li, Xuan Zhang, Fanghua Hao, Yongshuo Fu
abstract: Climate warming has intensified the hydrological cycle and increased the likelihood of compound drought–flood abrupt alternation (DFAA) events, posing growing challenges to water security in river basins. However, widely used precipitation-based indices often do not adequately represent the non-linear effects of antecedent soil moisture and intra-day precipitation concentration, which can weaken the correspondence between meteorological anomalies and hydrological responses. To address this limitation, we developed a physics-enhanced Hydrological Standardized Weighted Average Precipitation (H-SWAP) to better characterize effective hydrological input. Independent validation showed that H-SWAP increased the mean correlation with runoff from 0.55 to 0.58 and the correlation with soil moisture from 0.168 to 0.171 relative to the Standardized Weighted Average Precipitation (SWAP). Based on H-SWAP, DFAA events in the Yangtze River Basin were characterized by increasing frequency and intensity, shortening duration, and earlier occurrence over the study period. Spatial analysis further indicates a divergence in risk centers, with high-intensity areas tending to shift upstream and high-frequency areas concentrating in downstream regions. Random Forest was used to capture nonlinear and interacting climatic controls, while SHAP and Structural Equation Modeling revealed dominant local moisture effects and indirect influences of Nino3.4 and NAO through local hydroclimatic pathways. Overall, this study provides an improved framework for identifying DFAA events and advances understanding of their multi-scale drivers, with implications for basin-scale risk assessment and water-resources management.

title: Role of moisture transport and land–atmosphere feedbacks in meteorological drought formation over Inner Mongolia
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Xiaolan Yu, Zhiming Han, Limin Duan, Chao Gao, Ziyi Yan, Wenrui Zhang, Jianan Wang, Zhi Li
abstract: Understanding moisture-source contributions and land–atmosphere feedbacks associated with meteorological drought is crucial for early prediction. This study extends meteorological drought analysis beyond precipitation deficits to atmospheric moisture supply and associated moisture-source processes. By integrating monthly analyses with assessments of six representative droughts during 1991–2022, we investigated drought development in Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region (IMAR) from perspectives of atmospheric moisture-source dynamics and large-scale climate modes. Approximately 92.7% of the multi-year mean precipitation moisture over IMAR originated from terrestrial sources, including 19.9% from locally recycling and 72.8% from external terrestrial regions, whereas oceanic sources contributed only 7.3%. Significant spatial associations between drought severity and locally recycled moisture deficits occurred in four representative events (Moran’s I = 0.42–0.61, p < 0.01). During two long-duration droughts, locally recycled moisture deficits contributed more than 120% of net total moisture deficit because increased moisture from other sources partially compensated for local deficit, whereas local and external terrestrial moisture jointly contributed more than 90% during four short-duration droughts. The contribution of locally recycled moisture increased from −24% during mild droughts to 57% under the most severe conditions, indicating a shift from compensation to drought amplification. Cross-wavelet analysis identified the strongest standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index covariability with arctic oscillation highlighting the importance of mid-to-high-latitude circulation for IMAR drought variability. These findings provide a scientific basis for drought risk assessment and early warning in IMAR, offering a moisture-source perspective on associations between meteorological drought and land–atmosphere feedback in arid and semi-arid regions.

title: A three-step hydrogeochemical approach for designing groundwater-based monitoring networks in seismically active regions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Lorenzo Chemeri, Marco Taussi, Jacopo Cabassi, Marino Domenico Barberio, Davide Fronzi, Alberto Renzulli, Orlando Vaselli
abstract: Hydrogeochemical monitoring of groundwater systems is increasingly recognized as a powerful tool for investigating crustal processes and for the potential identification of geochemical precursors associated with seismic activity. However, the lack of standardized procedures to select and validate suitable monitoring sites still limits the comparability and effectiveness of the existing networks. This study proposes a three-step hydrogeochemical approach aimed at identifying the most appropriate and suitable sampling sites to be included in water monitoring networks for seismic surveillance. The approach was tested in the Pesaro-Urbino (PU) Province (northern Apennines, Italy) that was selected as the pilot-site due to the moderate-to-high seismicity occurring in the area. The characterization phase enabled the definition of four main geochemical facies and the identification of sites potentially affected by deep fluid circulation. The (subsequent) assessment phase integrated chemical and isotopic parameters (δ13C–TDIC, δ34S–SO4, δ11B, 87Sr/86Sr), highlighting deep and structurally controlled flow systems related to the Triassic Anhydrite Burano Formation, located in the area at a depth of at least 620 m. The monitoring phase on selected sites evaluated temporal stability and geochemical resilience, identifying a subset of stable and structurally influenced sites as the most suitable for inclusion in a long-term hydrogeochemical surveillance network. This approach, combining multi-parametric datasets and reproducible criteria, provides a flexible and transferable framework that can be applied to a wide range of geological and geodynamic contexts to support the design of permanent groundwater monitoring systems for seismic research.

title: Exploring the mutual interactions among population, income and water resource availability using a coupled socio-hydrological model
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Elena Cristiano, Carlotta Atzori, Roberto Deidda, Günter Blöschl, Francesco Viola
abstract: Throughout human history, water availability and societal development have been tightly interconnected, mutually influencing one another. Population size and economic prosperity tend to increase when water is not a limiting factor. Conversely, as the population grows, the corresponding water demand rises. To support sustainable water resource management, a socio-hydrological model that includes the interactions among climate, population and wealth is here proposed to represent these complex dynamics. Differently from previous socio-hydrological models, we explicitly couple water availability with both demographic and economic dynamics through two key bidirectional feedback mechanisms. The aim of the model is to explore how water availability influences long-term economic and population dynamics with a particular focus on the consequences of investments in hydraulic infrastructure. Through the analysis of different initial conditions of population density, average income and mean annual rainfall, the evolution of the socio-economic variables and water availability is explored. Results reveal a strong interdependence between water availability and socio-economic dynamics, highlighting the importance of incorporating mutual feedback mechanisms in the model. Mean annual precipitation strongly structures long-term population, income and infrastructure investment, while initial socio-economic conditions modulate the resulting trajectories. Increasing mean annual precipitation from approximately 400 to 1,000 mm yr−1 increases median population density from approximately 50 to 220 inh km−2, while reducing median per-capita infrastructure investment by approximately 60%, largely as a consequence of the inverse relationship between per-capita capital and population density under full water-resource exploitation. The model also identifies combinations of rainfall, population density and income compatible with steady conditions, whose comparison with country-level observations provides a qualitative real-world consistency check.

title: Stratification and mixing alter the response of chlorophyll-a regime to physical constraints in a shallow ice-covered lake
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Wen Zhao, Ming Li, Wenfeng Huang, Georgiy Kirillin, Youpeng Wang, Zhijun Li
abstract: Under-ice phytoplankton biomass and community composition are critical to winter lake ecosystem and can mediate subsequent spring bloom, but their responses to physical constraints remain poorly understood, particularly in mid-latitude cold-arid regions. Using chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) as an indicator of algal biomass, field observations were conducted in a shallow ice-covered lake on the Mongolian Plateau to investigate stratification and aquatic habitats dynamics, and Chl-a’s response. Results indicated that local mixing is primarily governed by rapid changes in thermal structure, while salinity exerts a slower, stabilizing influence on the water column, jointly regulating the vertical position of the deep chlorophyll-a maximum (DCM). Two mixing modes were detected: 1) long-term mixing associated with a temperature dichotomy, which promoted a persistent DCM right beneath the ice; and 2) short-term mixing triggered by abrupt cooling, which produced temporary algal blooms followed by rapid dissolved oxygen (DO) drawdown. Compared to the open-water season, metabolic rate estimation shows that algae require substantially lower irradiance to experience photoinhibition during ice-covered period. Mixing relieves the photoinhibition under cold water just beneath the ice as well as reshapes Chl-a profiles via suspension and settling. Elevated pre-recovery respiration may delay net algal growth by offsetting photosynthetic gains. These findings reveal favorable conditions for under-ice temperature dichotomy, mixing, and algal growth in shallow lakes of temperate arid regions, and clarify the specific role of local mixing in shaping the winter algal dynamics.

title: Quantifying preferential-flow evolution in seasonally frozen irrigated soils under coupled freeze-thaw controls: evidence from the Ningxia Yellow River Irrigation District
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Chunying Wang, Juanjuan Wu, Wangcheng Li, Mingtang Chai, Juanjuan Yu, Yu Zhang
abstract: Preferential flow in seasonally frozen ground exerts a critical control over water and nutrient transport within irrigation districts and underlying groundwater systems. However, quantitative assessments of how interacting environmental drivers govern this process under freeze–thaw conditions remain scarce. To address this knowledge gap, soil profiles from the Ningxia Yellow River Irrigation District—a typical seasonally frozen region in China—were selected for investigation. A Box-Behnken design (BBD) coupled with dye-tracing techniques was employed to visualize preferential flow morphology features, and response surface methodology (RSM) was subsequently used to elucidate the interactive effects of initial water content (IWC), freeze–thaw cycles (FTC), and freezing temperature (FT) on preferential flow metrics. The five fitted response-surface models captured relationships between freeze–thaw factors and target variables, yet predictive performance varied across models. IWC exerted the dominant control over preferential flow development; specifically, low IWC significantly promoted the formation of deep preferential flow pathways. A nonlinear interaction was observed between FTC and FT. Model outputs showed that high FTC combined with less‑negative freezing temperatures generated larger infiltration extents and a higher preferential flow proportion (PFP). Finally, laboratory-based multi-objective optimization yielded the mathematically optimal freeze–thaw parameter combination for preferential flow formation within the parameter range of this experiment. This study offers theoretical insights into preferential flow behavior under multi-factor freeze–thaw coupling and provides tentative references for regional water-resource management and soil ecological improvement.

title: Multi-horizon early warning of harmful algal blooms in cascade reservoirs using mechanistic data augmentation and machine learning
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Sungjin Kim, Sewoong Chung
abstract: Hydrologic regulation and variability influence cyanobacterial blooms in cascade reservoirs, yet sparse monitoring and infrequent bloom events constrain early warning. We developed a hybrid framework coupling CE-QUAL-W2 simulations with machine-learning classifiers to predict bloom alerts across multiple horizons in a Korean cascade reservoir system. Mechanistic augmentation increased training data resolution from weekly to daily while preserving physically plausible hydrodynamic, thermal, and water-quality dynamics. Recall reached 0.89 and 0.76 at 1-day and 2-day horizons, respectively, exceeding persistence baselines of 0.68 and 0.58. At 3 days, recall approached persistence, indicating limited additional predictive skill. Because predictions used observed meteorological inputs, performance represents a retrospective upper bound on operational forecasting skill. External validation using held-out observations from two independent bloom years with contrasting hydrologic regimes yielded caution-level recall of 0.60–0.71 at 1 day and 0.50–0.71 at 2 days. These estimates, reported with 95% confidence intervals, provide preliminary evidence of transferability given the small numbers of observed alert events (10 and 7). Explainable artificial intelligence identified water temperature, residence time, and discharge as dominant predictors, linking warning skill to thermal and hydrologic controls. Mechanistic augmentation outperformed non-mechanistic interpolation, whereas synthetic oversampling degraded performance, potentially through physically implausible samples. The findings demonstrate the value of process-informed data augmentation for bloom early warning under sparse monitoring. Using routinely monitored variables, the framework could support intensified monitoring and assessment of coordinated upstream flow regulation within a 1–2-day warning window, with transfer to other cascade reservoirs requiring site-specific recalibration and evaluation using forecast meteorological inputs.

title: A multiscale equivalent porous media method for simulating flow and solute transport in fractured media
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Lei Tian, Litang Hu, Jianchong Sun, Junchao Zhang
abstract: Multiscale fracture networks are common in fractured porous media (FPM), yet their complex geometries and interactions with the rock matrix remain difficult to characterize. This complexity poses a major challenge for accurately simulating groundwater flow and solute transport in FPM systems. Here, we develop a multiscale equivalent porous media (MEPM) method for simulating flow and solute transport in coupled fracture–matrix systems. In the MEPM framework, small-scale fractures are implicitly incorporated into a synthetically enhanced matrix through permeability tensors, whereas medium- and large-scale fractures are explicitly mapped onto refined grids to represent their geometries and hydraulic controls. Numerical experiments show that, relative to a conventional equivalent porous media (CEPM) model, the MEPM model more accurately reproduces complex solute distribution patterns, particularly preferential flow caused by heterogeneous and anisotropic fracture hydraulics. Compared with the discrete fracture network (DFN) model, the MEPM approach reduced the computational time from 2,200 to 8 min. The corresponding root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) for flow and solute transport were 0.18 m and 0.05–0.08 mg/L, respectively, demonstrating a substantial improvement in computational efficiency without a significant loss of accuracy. The MEPM model also captured mass exchange between the fracture and matrix domains. Neglecting the enhancement of the matrix by small-scale fractures led to differences of 21.70–65.40 m in the predicted solute migration distance. In addition, simulations of solute transport involving different adsorption and attenuation processes successfully reproduced spatiotemporal concentration differences between the fracture and matrix domains. These results demonstrate that the MEPM method provides an efficient and accurate framework for simulating groundwater flow and solute transport in multiscale fractured porous media while maintaining a practical computational burden.

title: A physically based event model coupling litter interception, lateral drainage and dynamic surface-seal conductivity on afforested loess slopes
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Changkun Ma, Jiayi Lu, Quanjiu Wang, Xiaoxu Jia
abstract: The forest-floor litter layer has long been known to protect the soil surface from raindrop impact, yet litter-specific event models typically treat the layer as an interception or storage deduction that leaves the infiltration capacity of the soil beneath it unchanged. We show that, of the three litter processes examined here, omitting this protective function is the largest structural source of error in predicting storm infiltration and the outlet hydrograph on afforested loess slopes, and correct it with a Green–Ampt model extended by three interface processes: litter interception, lateral drainage within the saturated litter, and a surface conductivity that decays with the raindrop kinetic energy transmitted through the litter. The model was tested with a simulated-rainfall factorial (30–120 mm h−1 × 10–30° × bare versus litter-covered soil; 96 runs) and natural-rainfall runoff plots (2023–2024) in a Robinia pseudoacacia plantation on the Chinese Loess Plateau. Litter held event-end surface conductivity at 15.1–16.9 mm h−1, near the uncrusted 18.2 mm h−1, whereas bare surfaces sealed to 3.6–6.4 mm h−1, with diminishing returns above about 0.6 kg m−2 of litter within the tested range. Cover consequently raised infiltration by up to 78%, delayed runoff onset by 4.9–12.5 min and lowered peak discharge significantly at ≥ 60 mm h−1 but not at 30 mm h−1, while litter interflow carried 14–52% of outlet discharge, rising with slope. The coupled model reached a validation NSE of 0.87 (KGE 0.88), against 0.64 for an interception-deduction model and 0.38 for bare soil. Removing the seal-suppression term lowered NSE by 0.16 and caused a 17% underestimate of storm infiltration, whereas omitting lateral drainage overestimated infiltration and underestimated discharge on steeper slopes. On these surfaces the litter layer matters less for the water it stores than for the sealing it prevents. Within the bounds of plot scale, two rainfall seasons and one soil type, the model supports event-runoff and precipitation-resource assessment in loess plantations.

title: Changes in drought transition dynamics under future climate in Great Britain: A Markov chain analysis using SPI and SSI
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Nishant Gaur, Encarni Medina-Lopez, Lindsay Beevers
abstract: Drought in Great Britain (GB) has received increasing attention following recent events, including those of 2018–2019 and 2022. Previous studies based on UKCP18 climate projections and the enhanced Future Flows and Groundwater dataset (eFLaG) have reported increasing drought frequency, duration, and severity across much of GB. However, these conventional drought characteristics do not fully describe how drought states evolve over time. This study addresses that gap by quantifying projected changes in drought transition dynamics across 133 parent catchments in GB using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Standardized Streamflow Index (SSI). Drought frequency and severity were evaluated for baseline, near-future, and far-future periods. First-order Markov chain transition matrices were constructed for meteorological and hydrological drought states and compared between baseline and future periods using a non-parametric permutation test. The matrices were then decomposed into downward mobility, upward mobility, dry-to-dry persistence, and wet-to-wet persistence metrics. Results reveal a clear south-east to north-west contrast in future drought transition behaviour. Southern and south-eastern catchments show stronger increases in downward mobility and dry-state persistence, indicating a greater tendency towards drying and weaker recovery towards wetter states. In contrast, north-western catchments show more heterogeneous responses, including simultaneous increases in dry-to-dry and wet-to-wet persistence. Directional change and persistence do not peak in the same regions, indicating that future drought intensification may arise through different transition mechanisms across GB. These findings provide a process-based perspective on future drought evolution, with implications for drought-risk assessment and long-term water management.

title: A nonstationary index reveals intensifying global dry–wet abrupt alternation events and their climate drivers
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Pengcheng Xu, Shuchang Luo, Dong Wang, Yuankun Wang, Xiaolei Fu
abstract: As global water cycles become more erratic, the sudden flip from drought to flood is putting immense pressure on ecosystems and water security worldwide. However, how the trend-induced nonstationarity within the water balance series modulates the evolution of dry-wet abrupt alternation (DWAA) events remains poorly understood, especially as climate change fundamentally alters the atmospheric supply–demand balance. With the help of Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS), this study introduces a nonstationary standardized DWAA ( I NSDWA ) index to investigate how often and how intensely regions flip between extreme dry and wet conditions. By accounting for these shifting climatic trends, we can more accurately track global whiplash events and uncover the physical forces driving them. Contrasting stationary and nonstationary frameworks reveals that trend-caused nonstationarity driven by large-scale climatic factors, play a much larger role in triggering these extreme transitions than previously thought. Over the last six decades (1961–2024), the world has seen a sharp rise in both the frequency and intensity of sudden “whiplash” transitions between drought and flood. This escalation is not accidental and is fueled by increasingly erratic atmospheric moisture and shifting circulation patterns. Our data shows that ENSO appears to be consistently associated with these flips, with La Niña phases notably intensifying their impact. As the climate continues to warm, the danger from these rapid hydrological swings will only grow. These results highlights the need for enhanced monitoring systems to better anticipate such abrupt shifts.

title: A realistic spatiotemporally variable rainfall event generator for flood catastrophe modeling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Yuran Li, Jian He, Lun Dai, Yunhong Lv, Yuanen Pang, Limin Zhang
abstract: Catastrophe modeling, which simulates regional hazard scenarios and losses under extreme events, has become an important tool for flood risk management. Observations of extremes are inherently scarce because such events are rare, making it essential to augment the historical record with synthetic rainfall events that are realistic and spatiotemporally variable. Current probabilistic rainfall models primarily focus on either single-station analysis or the spatial dependence of rainfall metrics (e.g., cumulative rainfall). However, these approaches often fail to capture the dynamic spatiotemporal characteristics of short-duration extreme rainfall events, which are the primary drivers of urban flooding. In this study, we propose a novel spatiotemporal stochastic rainfall generator to simulate rainfall sequences at multiple stations while preserving spatial correlation, as well as realistic hourly temporal variability and correlation. The generator is applied to and calibrated in Hong Kong, a densely urbanized and flood-prone coastal city, using hourly in-situ observations from 141 stations during 1984–2017. Despite operating at hourly resolution, the generator reproduces rainfall statistics consistently across accumulation durations of 1–24 h. It reproduces the main statistical characteristics of historical rainfall, with Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency values of 0.836–0.986 for accumulation durations of 4–72 h. It also captures the spatial patterns of extremes, with a Pearson correlation of 0.806. Hydrodynamic simulations further demonstrate that the realistic temporal variability produced by the generator leads to average flood depth differences of 18.1% and 25.8% compared with the simplified exponential and constant hyetograph scenarios, respectively. These results highlight the importance of representing realistic short-term rainfall variability in stochastic rainfall models for reliable catastrophe modeling.

title: Freezing onset of soil pore water under non-stationary conditions: a heterogeneous nucleation framework
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 682 Author(s): Zunyi Wu, Zhaohe Wang, Jiaqi Tian, Dihan Zhao, Mengke Zhou, Shuangyang Li, Yuanming Lai, Chong Wang
