This study developed a site and scenario-based one-dimensional reactive transport and interface flux model for Pb, Cd, and As remobilization from contaminated River Tano sediments under hydrodynamic and redox disturbance. The model coupled advection-diffusion-dispersion transport, sediment diagenesis, redox-sensitive reaction networks, Freundlich sorption/desorption, mineral dissolution-precipitation, and a sediment-water interface formulation that separates diffusive, advective, erosion/resuspension, and reaction enhanced exchange. Calibration and evaluation used porewater profiles, overlying water concentrations, interfacial flux observations, sequential extraction constraints, and an eight-site benthic chamber disturbance dataset. Scenario simulations indicated that stronger shear and turbulence increased sediment-water exchange by thinning the diffusive boundary layer and activating shear dependent particulate export, while redox transitions increased dissolved inventories through Fe/Mn oxide reduction and destabilization of sulfide-associated phases. Sensitivity analysis identified critical shear stress, boundary layer scaling, and Fe/Mn oxide reduction kinetics as the dominant controls on peak dissolved metal flux. Performance was strong for Pb and Cd but weaker for As. Including all validation points, the overall model performance was NSE = 0.919, R2 = 0.937, PBIAS = 4.12%, and 95% predictive coverage = 92.64%; after excluding t = 0 initialization points, overall performance remained good but lower (NSE = 0.910, R2 = 0.931, PBIAS = 4.71%, and coverage = 90.80%). The framework is therefore best interpreted as a mechanistic tool for site-specific scenario analysis and hypothesis testing, not as a fully general management predictor without site calibration.

title: Simulating microplastic dynamics in fluvial networks: A case study of the Irwell–Mersey river system
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Nirman Bhagat, Andrea Marion, Andrea Bottacin-Busolin
abstract: Microplastics are increasingly recognised as persistent contaminants in fluvial sediments, yet the processes governing their storage and redistribution remain poorly constrained. Here, we use a numerical sediment-transport model to investigate the accumulation, mobilisation, and redistribution of microplastics in two contrasting rivers within the Irwell–Mersey catchment in Greater Manchester, United Kingdom. Simulations are initialised with a uniform sedimentary microplastic distribution and exclude ongoing external inputs, allowing the role of internal river processes to be isolated. Despite these simplifying assumptions, the model generates pronounced spatial heterogeneity in bed-sediment contamination and large event-driven reductions following extreme floods, consistent with patterns observed between 2015 and 2016. Model results demonstrate that high-flow events exert primary control on microplastic mobility, driving bed scour, downstream transfer, and reorganisation of particle concentrations. Particle density strongly modulates these responses: low-density microplastics are readily mobilised during moderate floods, whereas higher-density particles require larger discharges for significant entrainment. Differences between the Irwell and Upper Mersey reflect contrasts in hydraulic forcing rather than mean channel slope, with higher peak discharges and shear stresses in the Irwell promoting localised accumulation in mild reaches, and stronger slopes in the Upper Mersey favouring more effective flushing, with accumulation mainly in the lower reach. By explicitly resolving flow, sediment transport, and particle properties, the model provides a process-based explanation for observed spatial and temporal variability in sedimentary microplastic contamination. The results show how event magnitude, particle density, and channel morphology interact to control redistribution and retention, offering a quantitative framework for interpreting monitoring data and for assessing the sensitivity of sedimentary microplastic inventories to hydrological extremes.

title: Removable alginate gel barriers for contaminant source zone isolation in aquifer remediation: A bench-scale study
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Geon Namgung, Heonki Kim
abstract: Non-aqueous phase liquids (NAPLs) in aquifers act as persistent sources of groundwater contamination, while conventional flushing and sparging methods often suffer from inefficient sweep and excessive reagent consumption. This study proposes a novel strategy to hydraulically isolate the contaminant source zone using a temporally constructed alginate gel barrier (AGB) to enhance remediation efficiency. A two-dimensional flow chamber model packed with a sand was used for this bench-scale study. The AGB was formed in the flow chamber by sequential injection of sodium alginate and thickener solutions, followed by Ca2+-induced crosslinking, and subsequently removed using a sodium-rich solution. A series of experiments were conducted to evaluate ozone sparging, surfactant flushing (SDS + n-butanol), and cosolvent flushing (ethanol) within the confined source zone containing either a dissolved contaminant (fluorescein) or NAPL (mixture; PCE/hexane/oil-soluble fluorescence agent). The AGB effectively confined gas and liquid flow to the target region, significantly improving contact between remedial agents and contaminants. Ozone sparging removed >96% of the fluorescence from the oil-soluble fluorescence agent dissolved in the NAPL, surfactant flushing eliminated >90% within 12 h, and ethanol flushing achieved >97% removal within 5 h, with 78% PCE recovery in the effluent. Notably, required reagent volumes were substantially lower than those estimated for full-domain treatment. These results demonstrate that temporary source-zone encapsulation using AGB can markedly reduce chemical usage while enhancing remediation performance in NAPL-contaminated aquifers.

title: Laboratory spectral induced polarization monitoring of phosphogypsum leachate-carbonate interactions in karst aquifer materials
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Rujun Chen, Xunzhe Li, Na Hao, Shaoxiu Xue, Wen Zhang, Jian Yin
abstract: Reactive groundwater systems often involve strongly coupled hydrological, geochemical, and electrochemical processes, complicating the interpretation of hydrogeophysical observations. Karst carbonate aquifers are particularly vulnerable to contamination by acidic, sulfate-and phosphate-rich leachates derived from phosphogypsum landfills. In this study, laboratory column experiments were conducted to investigate spectral induced polarization (SIP) responses during phosphogypsum leachate‑carbonate interactions under static, dissolution-dominated, and dynamic breakthrough conditions representative of karst environments. SIP measurements were performed synchronously with geochemical monitoring of pH, fluid electrical conductivity, and major ion concentrations. Multivariate statistical analyses were applied to explore relationships between SIP parameters and evolving geochemical conditions and to aid interpretation of overlapping electrochemical behavior. Results indicate that the conductivity reflects pore-fluid ionic strength but exhibits weak linear correlations with individual ions due to the superposition of electrolytic conduction and reaction-induced pore structure modifications. In contrast, polarization signals and their frequency dependence are primarily sensitive to interface associated with carbonate dissolution and the formation or removal of secondary sulfate and phosphate-bearing mineral phases. Dual-frequency polarization features suggest the coexistence and temporal evolution of matrix-scale interfacial polarization and smaller-scale polarization associated with secondary mineral particles or surface coatings. Principal component analysis separates the dominant variability associated with bulk geochemical conditions from variations in SIP parameters related to interfacial polarization, while independent component analysis identifies statistically independent patterns that are consistent with dissolution- and precipitation-influenced electrochemical responses under heterogeneous experimental conditions. These results indicate that SIP, when interpreted in a multivariate manner and constrained by geochemical and mineralogical evidence, can provide process-sensitive information beyond bulk conductivity and help distinguish hydrologically and geochemically different reaction regimes in laboratory carbonate systems.

title: From boundary delineation to causal interpretation in wetland mapping: HRU-scale wetland identification and evolution mechanisms from a hydrological connectivity perspective
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Zeyu Wei, Hongfei Hou, Xiaocong Qiu, Nan Gou, Hexiang Zheng, Changfu Tong, Cheng Xu, Zengfeng Zhao
abstract: Wetland degradation and areal loss driven by global change and intensified human activities pose increasing challenges to wetland conservation and restoration. Reliable decision-making requires accurate identification of wetland extent and type, which is currently dominated by remote sensing-based mapping. However, gradual wetland boundaries, high intra-class heterogeneity, and spectral similarity among land-cover types often lead to classification uncertainty. Concealed wetlands are particularly prone to omission because of canopy obstruction, temporary absence of open water, and weak spectral separability. More importantly, remote sensing products alone have limited capacity to explain the hydrological mechanisms governing wetland expansion, contraction, and persistence under varying flow regimes. Hydrological connectivity provides a process-based perspective for linking wetland occurrence and function to runoff generation, lateral flow redistribution, and groundwater–surface water interactions within watersheds. To address these limitations, this study developed a SWAT+-based hydrological connectivity wetland classification system, termed SWAT+ HWC. Driven by physically based simulations at the hydrological response unit (HRU) scale, SWAT+ HWC provides a transferable framework for candidate wetland screening and functional wetland classification. Daily HRU-scale fluxes and state variables were used to derive ten process indicators characterizing dominant hydrological connectivity mechanisms, and candidate wetlands were further classified into three functional units: riparian wetlands, shallow depressional wetlands, and deeply connected wetlands. Classification thresholds were adaptively calibrated in quantile space using a particle swarm optimization–classification and regression tree algorithm combined with a K-out-of-N voting rule, thereby constraining the candidate wetland proportion while improving the spatial transferability of classification rules across watersheds with contrasting hydrogeomorphic settings. Model performance was evaluated through process-consistency analysis, quantitative comparison with the WetlandConnectivity v1.0 dataset, and spatiotemporal validation in the Altamaha River Basin. The identified wetland types showed stable correspondence with their expected dominant hydrological indicators. Quantitative evaluation demonstrated strong discriminatory performance across representative geomorphic units, with most ROC-AUC values ranging from 0.89 to 0.95, and seasonal wetland-area dynamics were highly synchronized with the reference dataset, with correlation coefficients exceeding 0.84. By linking wetland identification to testable hydrological process chains, SWAT+ HWC provides a physically traceable basis for wetland mapping, functional interpretation, and cross-period comparison. The resulting hydrological connectivity-based classification enables wetland mapping to move beyond identifying where wetlands are located toward explaining why wetlands occur and persist in specific landscape positions, thereby improving the interpretability and targeting of wetland conservation, ecological restoration, and watershed water resources management.

title: Integrating macroscopic geometry and fluid-fracture feedback in dissolution analysis beyond isolated factors
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Menghan Chu, Haichun Ma, Chunchao Zhang, Jiazhong Qian, Xian Li, Qiankun Luo, Lei Ma
abstract: The acidic dissolution behavior of calcite is an important process associated with geological environments such as karst-related systems and carbonate weathering. The study investigates the fundamental coupling mechanisms among geometric characteristics, fluid transport, and dissolution kinetics through controlled numerical simulations. The core innovation lies in the systematic quantification of the independent impact of the macroscopic curvature (represented by the aspect ratio Rm) on dissolution kinetics by introducing the parameter “Curvature-Dissolution Rate Coupling Response Coefficient (RC)” for the first time, and in revealing the interplay between two-dimensional fracture structure and fluid dynamics. Two-dimensional geometric models of isolated calcite particles and fractured matrices were established coupled with a dynamic mesh approach. For elliptical particles, the dissolution rate initially decreases and then increases with increasing Rm, a trend consistent with the variation of the specific surface area analogy value (B v ). The variation of RC indicates that the reaction rate is highly sensitive to curvature changes when Rm < 1. Multiple nonlinear regression analysis (Sd = 0.037 V a 0.763 ac 1.822 Rm −0.283 (R2 = 0.972)) further reveals that among the acid injection rate (V a ), acid concentration (ac), and aspect ratio (Rm), ac exerts the most dominant control on the shrinkage degree (Sd). At the fracture scale, acid etching drives the morphology toward channelization and significantly attenuates the nonlinear behavior of fluid flow, clarifying the dynamic feedback mechanism inherent in fluid-fracture interaction.

title: Comparative metabolomics reveals stage-specific hypoxia tolerance during early development of the rare minnow ( Gobiocypris rarus )
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Weihui Huang, Nanyan Weng, Hanxiao Zhang, Jingtian Zhang, Shouliang Huo
abstract: Hypoxia is a common environmental stressor in aquatic organisms. It is well known that juvenile and adult fish possess developed gills and livers to adapt to hypoxia. However, the mechanisms by which early undeveloped fish tolerate hypoxia remain unclear. Here, we selected rare minnow (Gobiocypris rarus) to investigate the hypoxia tolerance thresholds of three early life stages: embryo, larvae, and juvenile. We found that embryos could survive for 24 h under hypoxia at 0.5 mg/L, while juveniles were the most sensitive to hypoxia, with a 24-h LC₅₀ of 1.58 mg/L. To explore the differences in hypoxia tolerance across developmental stages, we investigated the oxygen demand and metabolic changes following exposure to hypoxic conditions (2 mg/L). The oxygen consumption rate increased from the embryo to the juvenile stage, generating more aerobic respiration to support the development of additional organs. Growth was inhibited by hypoxia, particularly in the embryo and larvae, which produced energy to maintain survival by consuming fats and amino acids, respectively. Juveniles showed minimal changes in metabolites before and after hypoxia, with sex hormone and lysophosphatidylcholine synthesis affected. Juveniles responded to hypoxic stress by increasing corticosterone via neuroendocrine control. The limited hypoxia adaptation and metabolic suppression methods explain the low tolerance of juvenile fish to acute hypoxia during a critical growth period with high routine metabolic rates. Our results reveal metabolic differences and hypoxia adaptation strategies across different early life stages, providing basic thresholds and guidance for biodiversity conservation.

title: Physics-informed spatiotemporal graph neural network models for groundwater contaminant prediction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Dai Wan, Ge Ying, Hu Danxin, Xu Ruibing, DengYi, Yi Shuping
abstract: Groundwater contamination prediction is challenging because of the strong concealment, complex spatiotemporal coupling, and high parameter dependence of physical mechanism models. However, traditional data-driven models lack spatial representations. To address these limitations, this study developed and compared three physics-driven spatiotemporal graph neural network (STGNN) architectures for groundwater contamination prediction: a recurrent model (RGNN-ST), a convolutional model (ConvGNN-ST), and an attention-based model (AttentionGNN-ST). A dynamic graph construction strategy was designed to embed hydraulic head and hydraulic conductivity into edge weights, thereby linking data-driven learning to Darcy-flow constraints. Training and testing datasets were generated using coupled MODFLOW-MT3DMS simulations of homogeneous and heterogeneous aquifers. The model performance was evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, computational efficiency, robustness, and interpretability of the results. The results indicate that RGNN-ST provided the most reliable overall performance: under homogeneous conditions, R2 reached 99.95% and NRMSE was 1.68%; under heterogeneous conditions,the average R2 was 99.60%. RGNN-ST also exhibited the strongest stability and the best accuracy-efficiency balance across monitoring configurations. All models exhibited good robustness to monitoring node density, time window length, and aquifer heterogeneity, and accurately captured the spatiotemporal migration patterns of contaminants. Interpretability analysis revealed that RGNN-ST balances multi-source physical features (concentration, hydraulic head, hydraulic conductivity), automatically identifies key monitoring nodes and critical time steps, and its prediction behavior conforms to the physical mechanism of groundwater movement. The proposed physics-informed STGNN framework provides a transferable modeling strategy for groundwater contamination forecasting, risk management, and monitoring-network optimization.

title: Synergistic amplification and threshold vulnerability of coastal aquifer barriers under sea-level rise and freshwater decline
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Rajagopal Sadhasivam, Venkatraman Srinivasan
abstract: Coastal aquifers are increasingly threatened by saltwater intrusion (SWI) driven by climate change-induced sea-level rise (SLR) and anthropogenic freshwater decline (FWD). Although physical barriers such as cutoff walls (COWs) and subsurface dams (SSDs) are widely used to mitigate SWI, their performance under hydrological stresses such as SLR and FWD remains underexplored. In this study, four widely investigated field-scale conceptual aquifers are used to systematically evaluate the resilience and vulnerability of COWs and SSDs to these hydrological stresses under contrasting inland boundary conditions. Numerical simulations with the variable-density SEAWAT model show that inland boundary conditions strongly control barrier performance. Barriers remain largely resilient under flux-controlled (FC) conditions but become vulnerable under head-controlled (HC) conditions. Under HC conditions across a range of stress levels, COWs provide consistent mitigation benefits. However, SSDs exhibit distinct threshold behavior: they remain effective up to a critical stress level, beyond which their performance rapidly deteriorates. Model simulations reveal synergistic amplification under the combined effects of SLR and FWD, wherein SWI magnitudes far exceed the sum of their individual impacts. Furthermore, vulnerability maps are developed to delineate resilient and vulnerable regimes of barrier performance across a range of hydrological stress scenarios. These findings highlight the boundary-condition-dependent, threshold-driven, and synergistic amplification of barrier vulnerability, underscoring the need to explicitly account for combined climatic and anthropogenic stresses in the design of coastal groundwater protection strategies.

title: Migration and retention of polystyrene nanoplastics in porous media regulated by walnut shell biochar
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Yuheng Wu, Hui Li, Ming Wu, Qusheng Li, Yanru Hao, Jianfeng Wu, Jichun Wu, Bill X. Hu
abstract: The extensive accumulation of plastic waste in soil-groundwater poses a significant threat to subsurface environments. This study systematically elucidates the regulatory mechanisms governing the transport of polystyrene nanoplastics (PSNPs) in porous media amended with walnut shell biochar (WBC) through a combination of column experiments, Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) analysis, and two-site kinetic modeling. The results indicate that the incorporation of WBC markedly retards the migration of PSNPs. Owing to the pronounced microscopic surface roughness and well-developed lamellar pore structures of the biochar, the repulsive potential barrier between PSNPs and WBC is consistently lower than that between PSNPs and quartz sand, thereby providing abundant irreversible deposition sites. The modeling confirms that the synergistic effects of roughness-induced physical entrapment and short-range hydrophobic interactions drive the enhanced immobilization of the contaminants. Furthermore, the transport process of PSNPs is highly sensitive to hydrodynamic and hydrochemical variations. Increasing the WBC mass fraction, ionic strength, or acidity significantly compresses or neutralizes the electrical double layer, minimizing electrostatic repulsion and intensifying retention; here, divalent calcium ions exhibit a superior charge-neutralization and bridging capability compared to monovalent sodium ions. Conversely, elevated flow velocities, alkaline conditions, and the presence of humic acid enhance PSNPs mobility due to enhanced hydrodynamic shear, strengthened electrostatic repulsion, or competitive site occupation. These findings clarify the environmental behavior and interfacial mechanisms of nanoplastics under soil amendment practices, providing a scientific baseline for risk mitigation within soil-groundwater regimes.

title: Freshwater inflow, riverine nutrient load and salinity: Unraveling dominant drivers of dissolved inorganic nutrients in a bay-estuary system using Generalized and Neural Additive Models
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Sumon Hossain Rabby, Ebrahim Ahmadisharaf, Megan Lamb, Mark Rains, Jason Garwood
abstract: Nutrient dynamics in bay-estuary systems are shaped by the complex interplay between hydrology, biogeochemistry and hydrodynamics. Riverine nutrient loads are widely recognized as primary drivers of nutrients, yet how these loads translate into internal nutrient dynamics across varying hydrologic and salinity regimes remains poorly resolved. We addressed this gap by investigating long-term (19 years) dynamics of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and dissolved inorganic phosphorus (DIP) loads and their role in governing nutrient variability under varying freshwater inflow and salinity regimes in Apalachicola Bay, Florida. We applied a series of generalized additive models (GAMs) that incrementally accounted for freshwater inflow, nutrient load and estuarine salinity alongside Neural Additive Models (NAMs) with concurvity regularization to account for the correlation among these drivers. Our results showed that riverine nutrient load is the dominant driver of estuarine nutrient dynamics. Although freshwater inflow and riverine nutrient loads are often used interchangeably in past studies, we show that “inflow as a proxy for nutrient load” is an oversimplification, particularly under low-flow conditions. We further showed that estuarine DIN exhibits more predictable, seasonally coupled variability with freshwater inflow and salinity. In contrast, episodic and localized biogeochemical processes make DIP dynamics less predictable and obscure the influence of salinity on DIP at monthly timescales. However, we showed that the dependence of estuarine DIN concentrations on the riverine load is strongly structured by salinity regimes, with fresher conditions favoring this dependence. Increasing variability in sea level and freshwater supply under climate change can make these dynamics less predictable.

title: An explainable machine learning surrogate framework for colloid-facilitated contaminant transport in porous media
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Mayur Mundada, Akhilesh Paswan
abstract: Colloids act as important transport carriers in subsurface environments, facilitating the migration of strongly sorbing contaminants and significantly influencing breakthrough curve (BTC) in porous media. This study develops a machine-learning surrogate model capable of accurately reproducing BTCs generated by an equilibrium colloid-facilitated contaminant transport model over a wide range of transport conditions. The mechanistic model was first validated against the experimental phenanthrene transport data, demonstrating excellent agreement under both colloid-free and colloid-present conditions. The presence of colloids significantly accelerated contaminant transport, reducing the retardation factor from 339.69 to 64.76. Three machine-learning algorithms, namely Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were evaluated for BTC prediction. Among them, RF exhibited the highest predictive accuracy with an R 2 of 0.9982, RMSE of 1.23 × 10 − 2 , and MAE of 5.89 × 10 − 3 . Explainable artificial intelligence analyses based on feature importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) revealed that flow velocity was the dominant controlling parameter, followed by contaminant partitioning coefficients associated with mobile and immobile colloids. Furthermore, the RF surrogate accurately reproduced BTCs across diverse transport scenarios while maintaining excellent generalization capability. The novelty of this study lies in the integration of a physics-based colloid-facilitated contaminant transport model with interpretable machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence to develop a computationally efficient surrogate framework that not only accurately predicts BTCs but also reveals the relative importance of governing transport parameters.

title: Fulvic acid-iron colloid promotes the migration of As(III) in porous media
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Yanhao Li, Youru Yao, Xinyi Wang, Huimin Zhang, Fengman Fang, Yuesheng Lin, Zhiming Zhang, Qing Ji, Jia Yu
abstract: Fulvic acid (FA), a highly reactive and soluble fraction of dissolved organic matter in cultivated soils, facilitates the formation of stable colloids through complexation with iron (Fe), thereby significantly modulating the environmental mobility of arsenic (As). However, the migration behavior of As associated with FA-Fe colloids in porous media remains insufficiently characterized, particularly regarding the integration of coupled migration processes with quantitative modeling. This study investigated colloid-mediated As(III) migration in saturated porous media using column experiments and a time-fractional advection–dispersion equation (fADE). Increasing FA concentration enhanced As mobility, as evidenced by elevated breakthrough ratios and an increase in the fractional order α from 0.475 to 0.881, signifying the attenuation of memory effects and a transition toward Fickian migration. Conversely, elevated Fe concentrations promoted colloidal aggregation and suppressed As migration, with α decreasing to 0.437, capturing non-Fickian behavior associated with particle retention and deposition. Mechanistically, FA stabilizes FA-Fe colloids through electrostatic repulsion and steric hinderance while competing for adsorption sites, whereas Fe induces aggregation and enhances pore-scale interception, leading to As sequestration via inner-sphere complexation with Fe-OH groups. Under alkaline conditions, surface charge effects strengthened electrostatic repulsion and promoted migration, while elevated ionic strength compressed the electrical double layer, facilitated deposition. These results demonstrate that As migration is governed by the coupling between colloidal stability and interfacial interactions, which is effectively quantified by fADE. These findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding As mobility in subsurface environments and offer critical insights for groundwater remediation strategies involving colloid-facilitated migration.

title: New insights into radionuclide sorption on bentonite under variable geochemical conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Rishi Agrawal, Mutaz Jamal Al-khreisat, Manoj I. Patel, B. Jayaprakash, Mohammed Wael Mohammed, Prabhat Kumar Sahu, Vikas Wasson, Mandeep Kaur Chohan, Fereyba Noorzai
abstract: Radionuclide sorption on bentonite governs an important component of the retardation capacity of engineered barriers in geological repositories. This study compared fourteen regression approaches for estimating the logarithm of the radionuclide distribution coefficient, Log (Kd), from ten geochemical and physicochemical variables. The processed dataset comprised 776 observations drawn from a published compilation of 777 sorption measurements. Decision Tree, AdaBoost, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, ensemble learning, convolutional neural network, support vector regression, multilayer perceptron, Extra Trees (ET), linear regression, radial basis function neural network, Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net models were evaluated. Hyperparameters were selected by five-fold cross-validation within the 90% model-development partition, and the remaining 10% was reserved for testing. ET achieved the best test performance (R2 = 0.926; MSE = 0.100), whereas the radial basis function neural network performed least well. Pearson analysis identified pH as the strongest positive linear correlate of Log (Kd) (r = 0.42), followed by the liquid-to-solid ratio (r = 0.26). SHAP analysis of ET predictions identified pH and the liquid-to-solid ratio as the dominant contributors, followed by ionic strength. The results support the use of ET for preliminary sorption estimates within the sampled domain. Broader applicability requires validation across additional radionuclides, bentonites, and geochemical conditions.

title: Numerical simulation of a discrete fracture model for radon diffusion-seepage coupling in fractured rocks
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Chao Pu, Qianran Jia, Guojie Chen, Dong Xie
abstract: Fractures are major pathways for radon transport in rocks; however, their heterogeneous, discontinuous nature complicates predicting radon exhalation. Therefore, fracture-network characteristics must be considered when investigating radon diffusion-seepage in fractured rocks. In this study, a two-dimensional stochastic discrete fracture network (DFN) model was developed to investigate the effects of fracture aperture, roughness, matrix diffusion coefficient, water saturation, and temperature on radon diffusion-seepage transport through coupled diffusion and seepage. The results indicate that fracture aperture and roughness significantly influence radon transport by regulating fracture permeability, with millimeter-scale fracture apertures substantially enhancing convective transport within the fracture network. Increasing the matrix diffusion coefficient intensifies fracture-matrix mass exchange, promoting temporary radon storage in the matrix and delaying the transient outlet response. However, it also facilitates sustained radon release from the matrix later on, increasing the steady-state radon exhalation rate. Higher water saturation suppresses radon migration by reducing gas-phase transport pathways, whereas increasing temperature enhances radon transport by increasing the diffusion coefficient.

title: Natural radioactivity and radiological risk assessment due to naturally occurring radionuclides in common fish species from Lake Manyara, northern Tanzania
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Ayub M. Mokono, Gordian R. Mataba, Nelson Mpumi
abstract: Lake Manyara serves as an important source of water and food for the surrounding population. However, its proximity to the Minjingu phosphate mining area, which is associated with elevated levels of natural radioactivity, has raised concerns about possible environmental contamination. Therefore, this study assessed the radioactivity levels of naturally occurring radionuclides in sediment, water, and selected fish species from Lake Manyara, Tanzania. A total of 54 samples were collected and analyzed using a high-purity germanium (HPGe) detector to assess radiological risks. The mean radioactivity levels in Bq/kg in sediments were 44.58 for 226Ra, 112.59 for 228Th, and 606.78 for 40K, while corresponding values in Bq/L in water were 1.11, 2.97, and 18.25. Fish showed intermediate levels, with Manyara tilapia recording 0.62, 0.58, and 62.33 Bq/kg; Nile tilapia 1.03, 0.86, and 82.35 Bq/kg; and African catfish 0.23, 0.42, and 73.82 Bq/kg for 226Ra, 228Th, and 40K, respectively. Overall, radioactivity levels in sediments and water exceeded UNSCEAR and WHO reference levels, whereas in fish species, the measured radioactivity levels of all radionuclides remained within the IAEA SRS-114 median level and IAEA-414 reference level for freshwater fish activity concentration. The estimated annual committed effective dose (ACED) from fish consumption was 0.035, 0.021, and 0.009 mSv/y for Nile Tilapia, Manyara Tilapia, and African Catfish, respectively, and all below the public dose reference level of about 1 mSv/y. Generally, the results indicate that consumption of the investigated fish species from Lake Manyara does not pose a significant radiological health concern to consumers.

title: Transfer of tritium from tritium-contaminated drinking water and hay to cow and mare milk following single exposure
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Dinara T. Turgaliyeva, Zhanat A. Baigazinov, Medet R. Aktaev, Symbat A. Baigazy, Nurlan Zh Mukhamediarov, Aray E. Temirzhanova, Almagul A. Mukhamediarova, Nazira N. Berikbol, Aray N. Anuarbekova, Sergey N. Lukashenko, Zere A. Mazhit, Arafat M. Mamyrbekov, Csaba Gyöngyösi, Tibor Kovács
abstract: Tritium can enter livestock through contaminated drinking water and forage and may subsequently be transferred to milk. Understanding the short-term response after a single intake is relevant to radioecological assessment. This study characterized the early appearance and subsequent decline of tritium in cow and mare milk following a single intake of tritium-contaminated drinking water or hay. Four lactating animals (two mares and two cows) were studied. One exposure pathway consisted of a single intake of tritium-contaminated drinking water and the other of a single feeding with contaminated hay, followed by uncontaminated feed and water and a 30-day observation period. Tritium was determined in the milk free-water fraction (TFWT). The contaminated drinking water contained 180 ± 20 kBq/L of 3H. The calculated 3H intake was 3330 ± 410 kBq for the cow and 4500 ± 450 kBq for the mare. In the hay pathway, the free-water fraction contained 20 ± 3 kBq/kg and the calculated 3H intake was 24.8 ± 7.6 kBq for the cow and 14 ± 3.2 kBq for the mare. The first milk sample, collected approximately 6 h after exposure, showed the highest measured TFWT concentration. The Fhh values were 3.8 × 10−3 L−1 for cow milk after water exposure, 1.7 × 10−2 L−1 for cow milk after hay exposure and 5.7 × 10−3 L−1 for mare milk after hay exposure. Cow-milk activity decreased by approximately 50% by day 8 after water exposure and around day 13 after hay exposure. A single intake of tritium-contaminated drinking water or hay resulted in rapid appearance of tritium in the milk free-water fraction. The subsequent decline differed between the two exposure media. These findings provide experimental observations of short-term, pathway-specific tritium transfer to milk.

title: Experimental validation and CFD analysis of ventilation-dependent thoron distribution at breathing height in a full-scale mud test house
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Rajat Parkash, Sandeep D. Kanse, Tarun Kumar Agarwal, R.P. Chauhan
abstract: Thoron (220Rn) emitted from thorium-bearing building materials exhibits strong spatial non-uniformity indoors, making exposure assessment highly sensitive to ventilation and airflow patterns. This study investigates the role of ventilation in controlling thoron transport, spatial distribution, and breathing-zone exposure using a validated Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) framework combined with experimental measurements in a full-scale mud test house representative of traditional building construction. Experimentally measured thoron exhalation rates from interior surfaces were applied in the CFD model as surface-flux boundary conditions, and the CFD model was validated against multi-point thoron concentration measurements under ventilation rates ranging from 0.73 to 15 h−1. The results demonstrate persistent near-wall concentration enhancement and rapid decay toward the room interior, with spatial non-uniformity decreasing as ventilation increases. Analysis at breathing height (1 m) reveals a transition in transport behavior: diffusion-dominated decay under low ventilation (≤2.5 ACH) and a two-zone structure at higher ventilation (≥5 ACH), comprising a steep near-wall gradient and a well-mixed interior region driven by advective airflow. A two-region exponential model quantifies this behavior and shows that characteristic decay lengths increase approximately linearly with ventilation. From a building-performance perspective, ventilation primarily attenuates peak breathing-zone concentrations rather than room-average levels, highlighting the importance of ventilation layout, occupant position, and spatial heterogeneity in indoor pollutant exposure assessment.

title: Decomposition of indoor gamma dose rates into wall, floor, and ceiling contributions: A Geant4-based analytical framework
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): F. Gharbi
abstract: Accurate assessment of indoor gamma radiation requires quantifying the contributions of the structural surfaces surrounding the occupied space. This study investigates whether the specific dose rate, SDR, of a reference room can be represented through independently calculated wall, floor, and ceiling contributions. Geant4 simulations were performed for 40K and the 238U and 232 Th day series using a 5 × 4 × 2.8 m 3 concrete room with a centrally located detector. The sum of the independently simulated surface contributions reproduced the complete-room SDR within approximately 1.5%, numerically verifying the consistency of the decomposition, source-normalization, and dose-scoring procedures. For the investigated configuration, walls contributed approximately 50% of the total SDR, while floor and ceiling contributions were each close to 25%. Wall and floor responses over the investigated surface-density range were represented by saturation functions with component-dependent asymptotic values and broadly similar buildup behavior. These quantitative relationships are specific to the reference geometry, detector position, and concrete composition. The proposed component-resolved formulation establishes a necessary methodological foundation for the subsequent development, calibration, and validation of element-resolved models for rooms with independently varying structural properties.

title: Reassessing Arctic 137 Cs deposition history with a 70-year Greenland ice core archive
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Xue Zhao, Mikael Hult, Guillaume Lutter, Krzysztof Pelczar, William Colgan, Jixin Qiao
abstract: Accelerated Arctic warming may remobilize legacy radioactive contaminants preserved in the cryosphere, increasing the need for reliable historical baselines. Here, we report a previously unrecognized systematic bias in environmental radionuclide measurements, and demonstrate its impact through reconstruction of a high-resolution 137Cs record (1947–2015) in an ice core collected at Camp Century, Greenland. Ultra-low-background gamma-ray spectrometry in the underground HADES laboratory enabled robust detection of ultra-low-level post-1975 137Cs signals that are difficult to resolve using conventional aboveground spectrometry. Comparisons between direct measurements and processed meltwater analysis reveal systematic underestimations of 137Cs activity by 25–50% in processed water. Direct measurement of storage bags identifies adsorption onto low-density polyethylene bags as the dominant loss mechanism. This finding highlights the need to account for often-overlooked storage to avoid bias in future environmental 137Cs analysis. Correcting these biases resolves discrepancies with previous monitoring data and yields the first inland 137Cs record for northwest Greenland. Spatial patterns indicate that deposition is controlled by latitudinal transport gradients, precipitation driven scavenging, and enhanced in-cloud removal at high altitude sites, providing a mechanistic basis for future environmental risk assessments under Arctic warming.

title: Comparison of components and processes among river catchment systems using interaction matrices prepared for different climate conditions using Fukushima case as a benchmark
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Keiko Tagami, Mutasem Abu Ghazal, Mahmoud Albooq, Faris Alhawsawi, Mohammed Al Subhi, Matthew Asamoah, Joanne Brown, Abdullah Dirican, Ndeye Fatou Fall, Shoji Hashimoto, Seiji Hayashi, Yasunori Igarashi, Mathew P. Johansen, Lylia Kateb, Masabumi Komatsu, Rena Mikailova, Naoko Murakami-Sugihara, Paulo Nunes, Nils Ole Stabo-Eeg, Hideki Tsuji
abstract: Conducting radiological impact assessments for environmental systems such as river catchments requires the identification of radionuclide mobility and transfer processes across multiple interlinked components. These linkages can be effectively described using Interaction Matrices (IMs), which define key environmental components (e.g., air, soil, water, and biota) and the associated radionuclide transfer processes within the connected system. IMs provide a structured framework for organizing the data and parameters required for the modelling of radionuclide transfer in the environment and the assessment of radiation doses to human and non-human biota. Despite these advantages, IMs have not yet been widely applied in radiological impact assessments, particularly for river catchments, where they are especially needed due to the diversity and large number of components and processes involved. Radionuclide transfer processes following the accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant have been extensively studied for more than a decade. In this study, the Fukushima river catchment system including its transfer pathways and processes is presented as a case study for the development and application of IMs. Building on the ‘Fukushima’ IMs, scientists from countries with a range of climatic and landscape conditions have developed fit-for-purpose IMs to support dose assessments for nuclear facilities and sites worldwide. By comparing these IMs with those developed for the Fukushima river catchment, key components and processes have been identified that need to be considered under different climatic conditions. This work has helped clarify common elements for the modelling and assessment of doses in river catchments which, in turn, supports the development of international best practice. Overall, this study demonstrated the key features and the benefits of applying IMs in radiological impact assessments across diverse global environmental systems.

title: High-fidelity dose calculation for atmospheric dispersion modelling: Revisiting the Suffield Full-Scale RDD Field Trials
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Jens Peter K.W. Frankemölle, Luke S. Lebel
abstract: Atmospheric dispersion models (ADM) are important radiation protection tools for modelling the public consequences of a radiological release. Conventional ADM approaches, like Gaussian plume models, have known limitations, and so much active research goes into improved flow modelling. However, in the radiological and nuclear field it is also important to be able to calculate the external doses. Conventional external dose models often break apart as well in the near range, because of heterogeneity of the plumes and deposition fields. In this work, we present an improved external dose modelling technique for use in ADM based on three-dimensional (3D) finite cloud modelling. For this, we adapted the Atmospheric Dispersion and Dose Equivalent Rates (ADDER) model by (I) including a puff algorithm alongside the existing plume algorithm, (II) implementing the Briggs’ rural dispersion parameterisation and (III) implementing a bespoke RDD puff rise algorithm that builds on previous work by Sharon et al. (2012). We benchmark our model on results from the Suffield Full-Scale Radiological Dispersal Device (FSRDD) Field Trials, which involved the detonation of three explosives labelled with lanthanum-140, and monitoring of their dispersion in the near range. We report the correspondence between deposition, ground shine and cloud shine model predictions and measurements. For the ground shine measurements, we quantitatively compare a direct dose conversion model with our finite ground algorithm. For 2/3 trials, we report FAC2 > 0.5, NAD < 0.5, MG ≤ 1.33 and VG ≤ 2.0 for the ground shine computed with our finite algorithm. While previous studies of the FSRDD Field Trials only looked at time-integrated metrics, here, we also report continuous-in-time model predictions and measurements. We see future potential in coupling our external dose model to a more detailed Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) dispersion model.

title: Long-term validation of gaseous iodine (I 2 ) dry deposition model in a grassland environment
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Oumar Telly Bah, Didier Hébert, Olivier Connan, Bastien Darmau, Philippe Laguionie
abstract: Mechanistic models of iodine dry deposition have been developed to describe the transfer of radioiodine from the atmosphere to vegetation, but their applicability to long-term environmental exposure conditions remains poorly documented. This study evaluates the applicability of a dry deposition model under long-term environmental conditions using 129I measurements collected near the Orano La Hague reprocessing plant (France) between October 2018 and December 2019. Atmospheric gaseous and particulate 129I were monitored, and atmospheric activities were reconstructed at a 30-min time resolution using simultaneously measured 85Kr as a tracer of plant releases. Dry deposition to grass was simulated using mechanistic deposition models for gaseous and particulate iodine and compared with monthly 129I measurements in rain-protected grass. Approximately 90% of atmospheric 129I was present as gaseous I2, which accounted for more than 95% of the modelled deposition to grass. The original deposition model overestimated measured 129I inventories by approximately a factor of three. Introducing an effective post-deposition elimination term with half-lives of 7.7-8.5 days substantially improved the agreement between modelled and measured inventories. These results indicate that initial dry deposition alone is insufficient to describe 129I inventories in vegetation over long-term exposure periods and that post-deposition losses need to be considered when extending mechanistic I2 deposition models to environmental conditions.

title: Post-quasi-equilibrium compartment-level radial and vertical distributions of Fukushima-derived 137 Cs in Japanese cedar ( Cryptomeria japonica ) wood
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Vasyl Yoschenko, Muyiwa Michael Orosun, Toshihiro Wada, Polina Pavlenko, Kenji Nanba
abstract: More than a decade after the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant accident, the internal redistribution of 137Cs within Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica) wood remains an important unresolved question for timber safety and radiological forest management. This study provides the first post-2020, compartment-level, multi-height 137Cs dataset for Japanese cedar at the Yamakiya Experimental Forest (Kawamata Town, Fukushima Prefecture; ∼1000 – 3000 kBq m−2 deposition). In 2024, wood cores were extracted at tree-base (∼0.4 m), breast height (1.3 m), and upper-trunk (10 m) from three model trees using a 12-mm increment borer, divided into the three youngest sapwood annual rings (SW1-3) and consequent 5 annual rings samples of bulk sapwood (SW) and heartwood (HW), and measured for 137Cs activity by a high-purity Ge-detector. A water-leaching fractionation protocol (distilled water, 20:1 water-to-fresh-mass ratio, 24 h orbital shaking) was applied to each sample to resolve 137Cs into a leachable fraction and a residual matrix-bound fraction. The heartwood-to-sapwood (HW/SW) 137Cs concentration ratio averaged approximately 2.0 across the three trees by 2024 confirming continued heartwood enrichment beyond the system-level quasi-equilibrium reached around 2020. Vertical 137Cs distributions were broadly uniform across all three sampling heights, contrasting with the height-dependent gradients of the early post-accident period. The leachable fraction was dominant in both sapwood and heartwood, with total concentrations strongly correlated with leached (R2 = 0.4–0.9) but not matrix-bound concentrations, indicating that 137Cs in cedar wood is predominantly present in a hydrated, water-soluble ionic form. Proportion of the leached 137Cs activity averaged 0.57 ± 0.15 for sapwood and 0.51 ± 0.14 for heartwood. The study significantly contributes to understanding of 137Cs distribution and cycling in Japanese cedar.

title: Biogenic and green-synthesized nanomaterials for radionuclide remediation: promise, radiolytic stability and environmental fate
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Jeyaseelan Aravind, Bhavya Sajeet, Govindharajan Sattanathan, Selvarajan Ramganesh, Srinivasan Venkatesh
abstract: Biogenic and green-synthesised nanomaterials, including microbially produced iron and manganese oxides, metal sulfides and phosphates, and zero-valent iron, metal oxides and hydroxyapatite prepared with plant extracts, are increasingly proposed for removing radionuclides from contaminated water. Most studies report high removal of uranium under laboratory conditions. Three questions that decide whether these materials are fit for field use remain largely unanswered: whether they retain their structure and binding capacity under ionising radiation, what happens to the radionuclides they carry once the particles reach soils and waters, and how the spent material should be managed. This review covers uranium, thorium, caesium, strontium, technetium, iodine and trivalent actinides. Synthesis routes are compared and their “green” credentials examined in practice, and removal performance is assessed under realistic conditions of competing ions, trace concentrations and natural water matrices. The limited evidence on radiolytic stability is evaluated, separating effects on organic capping layers and biopolymer supports from those on inorganic cores. The aggregation, dissolution and redox transformation of radionuclide-loaded nanoparticles are then examined, together with their potential to carry radionuclides through colloid-facilitated transport. Recovery, regeneration and conditioning of spent nanosorbents are considered alongside life-cycle and regulatory constraints. The evidence remains dominated by short laboratory batch tests with uranium in synthetic solutions. Radiation stability and post-use fate are rarely measured, so the advantages claimed over conventional sorbents cannot yet be judged. A minimum testing protocol is proposed, covering irradiation, real-water performance and environmental fate, so that future studies can be compared and translated to field conditions.

title: Sources, accumulation and fate of 36 Cl in terrestrial ecosystems: A review of knowledge
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): P. Ciffroy, L. Benedetti, S. Cornu, D. Sourabie
abstract: 36Cl is a naturally occurring radionuclide produced mainly in the atmosphere. In addition to its natural production, 36Cl has been introduced in significant quantities by humans into the environment because of nuclear bomb tests or nuclear accidents. Natural inputs, together with anthropogenic inputs, contribute to an ambient background activity of 36Cl in the environment. In addition to these inputs, other potential future inputs associated to civil nuclear activities (decommissioning of nuclear power plants, waste disposals) should be anticipated. A good understanding of sources of 36Cl in the environment, including an assessment of their variability, accumulation in soil, and fate in environmental media and at interfaces, is therefore necessary in the context of nuclear activities assessment. Considering this background, we propose here a review of knowledge relating to the sources, exchanges, accumulation, and fate of 36Cl in the environment. It addresses: (i) the identification and quantification of natural and anthropogenic sources and fallout of 36Cl in the environment, and the factors of spatial and temporal variability, including solar cycles and events, latitudinal geomagnetic effect, latitudinal differences in Stratosphere-Troposphere Exchange, distance from the sea, and local precipitation; (ii) the assessment of the exchange processes at the interface between atmosphere and soils, i.e. dry and wet deposition; (iii) the assessment of 36Cl accumulation, fate and speciation in soils and the factors of variability, in particular chlorination/dechlorination processes; (iv) the bioaccumulation processes of 36Cl in plants, i.e. root uptake, foliar absorption and translocation.

title: Microbial biofilm–radionuclide interfaces in contaminated soils and waters: Extracellular polymeric substances, redox transformations and remobilisation risks
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Meivelu Moovendhan
abstract: Microbial biofilms are increasingly recognised as chemically active interfaces that determine whether radionuclides remain dissolved, accumulate in sediments or enter secondary transport pathways. Their extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) supply diverse binding ligands, create steep microenvironmental gradients and retain redox-active cofactors, thereby coupling sorption to metabolic and mineral-mediated transformations. Yet these same properties complicate claims of durable immobilisation: adsorbed radionuclides may desorb, biomass-associated reduced species may be less persistent than crystalline minerals, and detachment can convert a local sink into a mobile carrier. This review critically examines the interaction of microbial biofilms with uranium, technetium, neptunium, plutonium, caesium, strontium and selected redox-sensitive co-contaminants in contaminated soils, groundwater and surface-water sediments. Particular attention is given to molecular EPS composition, coordination chemistry, extracellular electron transfer, U(IV) product identity, Fe–Mn–S coupling, phosphate mineralisation and redox reversal. Recent evidence from contaminated-aquifer biofilms, field bioaugmentation, flow-through reactors and molecular spectroscopy is assessed by distinguishing instantaneous removal, retained inventory, mineralogical persistence and cumulative contaminant export. A mechanistic risk framework is proposed in which long-term performance depends on the evolving relationship among biofilm physiology, aqueous ligands, oxidant fluxes, hydraulic connectivity and particle mobilisation. The central implication is that biofilm-enhanced sequestration should be judged by radionuclide mass balance and post-disturbance stability rather than by short-term decreases in dissolved concentration alone.

title: Four decades of actinide (U, Th, Pu, Am) analysis in environmental samples (1986–2026): evolution of measurement, detection and quantification, with a multivariate bibliometric assessment
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 301 Author(s): Edmundo Escareño-Juarez
abstract: Uranium, thorium, plutonium and americium are determined in soil, sediment, water and air for radiation protection and source attribution, but the change in measurement techniques since Chernobyl has not been quantified. This review combines a critical synthesis of method papers with a bibliometric data set of 32,181 OpenAlex records (1986–2026; 3254 naming a technique), analysed by trend tests, correspondence analysis, principal component analysis and Ward clustering and cross-checked in IAEA INIS, to test three hypotheses. H1, that mass spectrometry has replaced decay counting, was only partly supported: the share of analytical records naming inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) rose from 19% in 1990–99 to 41% in 2016–25 (Mann–Kendall τ = +0.43, p < 0.001) and thermal ionisation mass spectrometry, neutron activation and fission track declined, but alpha spectrometry fell only from 21% to 15%, gamma spectrometry stayed near 29%, and the two families have shared mentions roughly equally since 2011. H2, that technique use is organised by the analytical problem, was supported: the only bootstrap-stable cluster grouped alpha spectrometry with sector-field ICP-MS and accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) as a transuranic ultra-trace group, and correspondence analysis separated transuranic from natural-series methods (47.9% of inertia). H3, that the transition is not an artefact of one index, was supported (Spearman ρ = 0.83 between OpenAlex and INIS). Detection limits for 239Pu range from 10 fg (alpha spectrometry) to 0.2 fg (AMS). Priorities are comparable detection-limit reporting, wider access to AMS and ICP-MS/MS, and monitoring of 241Am ingrowth until the mid-2030s.

title: Guidelines to writing a review paper for the journal of environmental radioactivity
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Sheldon Landsberger
abstract: The art of writing a good, meaningful and well-appreciated review paper for respective audiences is not an easy task to undertake. Often review papers have no hypothesis and are just a rehash of references, data, figures and tables with little inference to what future scientific directions need to be undertaken. On the other hand, some review manuscripts lack figures and tables and make reading cumbersome. There is a plethora of review styles in science, engineering technology, social sciences, business, etc. which can differ depending on the subject matter and journal expectations. This paper is a modest effort to outline guidelines to enhance the review contributions to the Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, (JENVR) while achieving a high standard of submission.

title: Radionuclides accumulation by plants in hydroponics and in soil pots under conditions of hyperarid desert climate
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Jihen Jalali, Olivier Péron, Abdesselam Abdelouas, Thierry Lebeau, Ahmed K. Alkaabi, Yacine Addad, Prasoon Raj, Noor Faraj, Raed Alamoodi, Irené Saayman, Mohamed Bagahizel, Abdulla Alhameli
abstract: Radionuclides (RN) transfer from soil to plants in arid environments is sparsely documented, limiting the availability of baseline data for understanding RN uptake in arid environments. This study investigated the uptake, accumulation, and translocation of radioactive (3H, 14C, 60Co, 137Cs, 238U, 241Am) and stable isotopes (88Sr, 127I) by two plant species: the native grass Cenchrus ciliaris and the crop plant Solanum lycopersicum. Experiments were conducted in hydroponics and with sandy soils simulating hyperarid environments of the United Arab Emirates. After exposure to each multielement mixture, soil-to-plant transfer factors (TF), translocation factors, and accumulation profiles in plants were determined. Plant uptake was generally higher under hydroponic than soil conditions, indicating a strong influence of the growth medium on element availability. C. ciliaris showed substantial root accumulation, with TF values reaching 46 for 14C, 39 for 88Sr, and 28 for 137Cs. In contrast, S. lycopersicum exhibited lower uptake, and showed visible symptoms of plant stress, including chlorosis and necrosis. In sandy soil, lower RN uptake was observed due to reduced mobility, yet C. ciliaris maintained TF > 1 for most of the studied elements. Roots represented the primary site of RN accumulation for both species particularly in soil conditions highlighting its potential for phytostabilisation. Translocation factors values indicated limited translocation to aerial parts for both species, particularly in soil conditions. This study provides new data on RN transfer in hyperarid environments and identifies C. ciliaris as a species of interest for further evaluation in radionuclide monitoring and phytomanagement studies under such conditions. These findings contribute to improving the understanding of radionuclide soil–plant transfer in hyperarid environments and may support future environmental radioactivity assessments in these regions.

title: Particle-size-dependent enrichment of 226 Ra, 232 Th, 40 K and 137 Cs in biomass pellet ash and coal combustion residues: Implications for reuse as secondary raw materials
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Selena Samardžić Cvijanović, Robert Lakatoš, Tomas Nemeš, Jan Hansman, Sofija Forkapić, Dušan Mrđa, Ivana Lončarević, Milica Vučinić Vasić, Kristina Bikit
abstract: Combustion ash is increasingly valued as a secondary raw material in the construction industry, and large quantities of pellet ash are generated in households during the heating season. Activity concentrations of 226Ra, 232Th, 40K and 137Cs were determined in two wood-pellet ash samples with contrasting feedstocks and in five coal combustion residues. Both pellet ashes and two of the coal residues were separated into seven size classes ( 500 μm) to study their redistribution among the fractions. Particle size was characterised by laser diffraction, and radionuclide activities were measured by HPGe gamma spectrometry. In the coal series, enrichment was confined to the process level, peaking in electrostatic precipitator fly ash (EF = 8.7 for 226Ra), with no systematic size dependence. In pellet ash, by contrast, all four radionuclides were progressively concentrated in the finer fractions. This dependence was well described by a surface activity model, A = A0(1 + D0/D[3,2]), with adjusted R2 = 0.909–0.997. In the 137Cs-rich pellet ash, the standard activity concentration index remained below 1 in every size fraction, whereas a recently proposed extended index that includes 137Cs, used here as an exploratory indicator, exceeded 1 in all fractions. The estimated domestic inhalation dose from the finest fraction was small (0.65–0.84 μSv y−1). For 137Cs-bearing biomass ash, these results suggest that both the size distribution of the material actually used and the contribution of 137Cs, which the standard index does not consider, should be taken into account when its reuse is assessed.

title: Deriving reference activity concentrations in Spanish terrestrial ecosystems to protect the public and the environment
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Alicia Escribano, Javier Guillén, Almudena Real
abstract: This study adapts the methodology developed by the OSPAR Convention to protect the marine environment of the North-East Atlantic to Spanish terrestrial ecosystems to derive Reference Activity Concentrations (Cref) ensuring adequate radiological protection of humans and wildlife. For each radionuclide, the activity concentration in air (CDL), corresponding to a dose of 0.1 mSv·y−1 to the representative person (dose-limit criterion accepted by the Spanish Regulatory Body), was calculated using the SRS-19 dispersion models. These CDL values were used to estimate dose rates to reference organisms using the ERICA Tool. The estimated dose rates were compared with the lower bound of the ICRP Derived Consideration Reference Levels (DCRL) for each organism group. When the concentration associated with the human dose results in a biota dose rate exceeding the relevant DCRL, a correction factor was applied to derive the corresponding Cref. These Cref, ensure that radiological impact to humans and wildlife remains negligible at or below these concentrations, while exceedances of monitored or modelled environmental activity concentrations require a more detailed assessment. The integrated Risk Quotient (∑RQ) framework applied to derive Cref values provides a practical, tiered screening approach aligned with international regulatory practice. A ∑RQ < 1 confirms simultaneous compliance with the 0.1 mSv·y−1 dose constraint established by the Spanish Regulatory Body for nuclear power plants and with the ICRP ecological reference levels. These results are intended solely for screening purposes and do not replace a detailed radiological assessment when evaluating total doses in specific scenarios or when considering radionuclides not included in this approach.

title: Decadal decline in exchangeable 137 Cs in a Cryptomeria japonica forest soil estimated from storage-corrected extraction yield
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Masami Kanao Koshikawa, Mirai Watanabe, Akiko Takahashi, Shoko Ito, Tatsuhiro Nishikiori, Shin-ichiro S. Matsuzaki, Seiji Hayashi
abstract: Exchangeable 137Cs is an operationally defined fraction that represents a potentially mobile component of radiocesium in forest soils. Its long-term dynamics are important for understanding radiocesium behavior after nuclear accidents. This study quantified storage-induced changes in 137Cs extractability and estimated decadal changes in exchangeable 137Cs in the forest soil of a Cryptomeria japonica plantation on Mount Tsukuba, Japan, following the Fukushima nuclear accident in 2011. Surface soil samples collected annually from 2012 to 2021 were air-dried and archived until batch extraction in 2024. Exchangeable 137Cs was extracted using an optimized procedure with 1 M NH4NO3 for 48 h. Repeated extraction of aliquots from a single air-dried soil sample over storage durations of 0.2–10.5 years demonstrated decreasing extractability, described by an exponential function. This function was applied to the archived monitoring samples to estimate extraction yields at sampling, assuming the same storage response, although the estimates could not be independently validated against measurements made immediately after collection. The storage- and decay-corrected extraction yields suggest a decrease of approximately half during the decade following the Fukushima nuclear accident, whereas decay-corrected values alone exhibit no clear temporal trend. A similar decline was estimated after excluding samples requiring extrapolation. Despite this decline, the mean storage-corrected extraction yield for samples collected in 2021 was approximately 19%. These results suggest a progressive decline in exchangeable 137Cs in forest soils following the Fukushima nuclear accident and highlight the importance of considering storage effects when estimating long-term trends from archived samples.

title: Tracing sediment sources in small watersheds during an extreme rainstorm using fallout radionuclides in the Wuding River watershed
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Mian Li, Hongzhe Bao, Shengchao Zhao, Qiang Yi, Hai Du, Zhenzhou Shen
abstract: Following the large-scale implementation of the Grain for Green Program across the Loess Plateau, watershed sediment yield has declined substantially. Nevertheless, the potential shifts in sediment source composition remain poorly understood. Characterizing sediment sources at the small-watershed scale is a fundamental scientific basis for watershed management practices. Based on field investigations of sediment trapped by check dams after the extreme rainstorm on July 26, 2017, this study selected fourteen dam-controlled small watersheds without drainage facilities, which are located in the storm center of the Wuding River Watershed in the Yellow River Basin. The activities of 137Cs and 210Pbex (excess 210Pb, refers to the atmospherically derived unsupported fraction of total 210Pb in soils and sediments originating from atmospheric fallout) in topsoil samples from hillslopes, gully sides and dam lands were analyzed, the relative sediment contribution proportions of the two sediment sources (hillslopes and gully sides) were quantified for each individual watershed. The results indicate that the activities of 137Cs and 210Pbex in dam-deposited sediments are markedly lower than those in hillslope topsoils but highly consistent with those in gully side topsoils. During this extreme rainstorm, hillslopes only produced a moderate volume of sediment in most study watersheds. In contrast, gully side sediment contributions exceeded 69% of the total sediment yield across all investigated catchments. Although the spatial variability of fallout radionuclides and the inherent limitations of simple mixing models introduce uncertainties to the estimation results, the findings can still broadly reflect the dominant sediment source characteristics of small watersheds. Compared with the pre-conversion land-use conditions in the Loess Hilly Area, gully side sediment production has shown an increasing trend. Despite the dramatic changes in hillslope land-use patterns induced by ecological restoration, gully sides remain the predominant sediment source during extreme rainstorms. Accordingly, priority should be given to gully side erosion control in future watershed management strategies.

title: Temporal trends and compartment-specific behaviour of 137 Cs across five decades of environmental monitoring in tropical Malaysia
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): M.S.M. Sanusi, K.Y.H. Gin, S. Hashim, H.N. Idris, R.M. Taha
abstract: Long-term environmental surveillance of radiocesium (137Cs) in tropical regions provides important baseline data for assessing radionuclide behaviour under low-background conditions, yet multi-compartment synthesis studies from Southeast Asia remain scarce. This study presents a retrospective analysis of 137Cs activity concentrations across five environmental compartments: seawater (n = 609), soil (n = 483), sediment (n = 474), biota (n = 114), and airborne particulates (n = 20 seasonal records), in Malaysian environments spanning 1972–2024. Censored observations below analytical detection limits were treated using Regression on Order Statistics (ROS), with Limit of Detection (LOD) substitution sensitivity assessed under three scenarios (X i = 0, LOD/2, LOD). A complementary statistical framework combining Mann–Kendall (MK) trend analysis, Pettitt change-point detection, cumulative sum (CUSUM) diagnostics, relative detectability metrics (SNR), and segmented regression was applied to characterise temporal structure and compartment-specific behaviour. A statistically significant monotonic decline was identified in seawater only (τ = −0.547, p = 0.002), however, a candidate change-point at 1995 (p = 0.026) was excluded from primary inference owing to a 9-year sampling gap (1987–1994; Table S3). Soil and biota exhibited declining tendencies (τ = −0.167 and −0.500, respectively) that did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05). Sediment results were excluded from trend inference as the direction of the apparent trend reversed between LOD substitution scenarios, indicating that the result is driven by the high proportion of censored values (74.7%) rather than the quantified data. Airborne observations (85% non-detect) were reported descriptively only. Indicative effective half-lives of 137Cs were estimated across all four compartments under a sensitivity analysis spanning five historically motivated starting years (Table S2). Seawater yields T ½ (eff) = 27.7–30.8 yr across the primary fits, bracketing the physical half-life (30.17 yr), while biota yields T ½ (eff) ≈ 12–19 yr, consistent with biological turnover superimposed on radioactive decay. Soil and sediment estimates are sensitive to starting year and are considered indicative only. Signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) were below 1 for soil (0.455), sediment (0.060), and biota (0.260); seawater showed marginal detectability (SNR = 1.35, consistent across all LOD substitution scenarios), reflecting the long-term declining trend rather than a post-2011 enrichment signal. Statistical inference is subject to inherent limitations of the analytical framework: the MK test has reduced power for episodic signals and censored-data-rich series; the Pettitt test assumes a single dominant change-point; and CUSUM results are treated as exploratory given irregular sampling intervals and high censoring rates in several compartments. The results document baseline temporal trajectories of 137Cs in a tropical low-background environment and highlight compartment-specific differences in temporal sensitivity, data sufficiency, and inferential reliability as central challenges for long-term radionuclide surveillance in tropical radioecology.

title: Radon emanation coefficients of coal fly ash and soil: Measurement, wall flux geometry correction, and indoor dose implications
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): M. Swarnkar, S.K. Sahu, T.D. Rathod, M. Tiwari, R.C. Bhangare, P.Y. Ajmal, V. Pulhani
abstract: Radon (222Rn) is a radioactive noble gas released from terrestrial materials via the alpha recoil of its parent radium-226 (226Ra), and is the second leading cause of lung cancer worldwide. The fraction of radon atoms that escape from the solid grain matrix into connected pore spaces — the emanation coefficient (η) — governs the radon source term and is essential for indoor radiological hazard assessment. This study estimates η for one coal fly ash and one agricultural soil using γ-spectrometry for 226Ra quantification and an expanded 16-can sealed-can method with LR-115 type II solid-state nuclear track detectors (SSNTDs). The approximately 2.3-fold difference in η (fly ash: 0.0056 ± 0.0015; soil: 0.0127 ± 0.0035, expanded uncertainty k = 2), despite the higher 226Ra activity of fly ash (102.4 vs. 77.6 Bq kg−1), is consistent with the hypothesis that radium is less accessible for recoil release in the glassy aluminosilicate matrix of fly ash; no microstructural measurements were made to test this. The emanation data are combined with the semi-empirical Sahoo et al. wall exhalation model, using estimated diffusion lengths and assumed block and wall geometries, to assess the 3-D to 1-D diffusion geometry transition from sample to constructed wall. The resulting model-derived wall-to-sample flux enhancement factors are 2.35 (fly ash) and 4.1 (soil). Under the assumptions of this first-order model, the estimated dose for the investigated fly ash sample remains below the EU reference level of 1 mSv y−1; this has not been validated by direct wall-flux measurements and should not be generalized to fly ash as a material class. The results indicate that geometry correction may be important when extrapolating laboratory-scale exhalation measurements to building-scale exposure.

title: Assessment of radionuclide transport and containment performance for a proposed borehole disposal system at the GAEC site using AMBER
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Paul Essel, Eric T. Glover, Abdallah M.A. Dawood, Gustav Gbeddy, Yaw Adjei-Kyereme, Emmanuel Atule Aberikae, Evans Mawuli Ameho
abstract: This study presents the application of the compartmental modelling software AMBER to assess radionuclide transport and the containment performance of a proposed Borehole Disposal System (BDS) at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission (GAEC) site. The analysis supports post-closure safety assessments by simulating the long-term migration of radionuclides from disposed disused sealed radioactive sources (DSRS) under a range of geosphere and biosphere conditions. The model integrates site-specific geological, hydrogeological, and geochemical data to evaluate the time-dependent behavior of potential contaminants and their migration pathways. The assessment indicates that, under the scenarios considered, the proposed BDS provides effective containment and isolation of radionuclides, with calculated doses remaining below the regulatory constraint over the assessment period.

title: Experimental study on the radon barrier performance of cover materials under frozen and unfrozen isothermal conditions
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yongjun Ye, Ao Huang, Ting Yu, Shiyu Mou
abstract: Seasonal temperature variations, particularly frozen and unfrozen conditions, exert a considerable influence on radon exhalation from the surfaces of uranium tailings impoundments.
