To evaluate the radon barrier performance of cover materials under frozen and unfrozen isothermal conditions, three indoor-cured materials—pure laterite, a laterite-bentonite mixture (1:1 mass ratio), and a laterite-zeolite powder mixture (1:1 mass ratio)—were tested across five temperature setpoints (−20 °C, −10 °C, 0 °C, 10 °C, and 20 °C) in a temperature-controlled test chamber, using bare uranium tailings as a control. The results indicate that: (1) At a cover thickness of 15 cm, the radon barrier efficiencies of pure laterite, the laterite-zeolite powder mixture, and the laterite-bentonite mixture ranged from 89.07% to ∼100%, 81.99% to ∼100%, and 98.59% to ∼100%, respectively, with barrier efficiency gradually increasing as temperature decreased. (2) For all materials, the rate of change in radon barrier efficiency with temperature was lower above 0 °C than below 0 °C. The temperature sensitivity followed the order: laterite-zeolite powder mixture > pure laterite > laterite-bentonite mixture, demonstrating that the laterite-bentonite mixture maintained the most stable performance across thermal fluctuations. Additionally, preliminary empirical piecewise equations were established to describe the relationship between barrier efficiency and temperature across frozen and unfrozen regimes. Overall, this study demonstrates that radon exhalation barrier by cover materials depends not only on their intrinsic physical properties and ambient temperature, but also exhibits distinct behavioral shifts between frozen and unfrozen states.

title: Machine learning for atmospheric radioxenon source discrimination based on isotopic activity concentrations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Xiangrui Jiang, Ruiqin Zhang, Yungang Zhao, Qilong Guo, Shaohang An, Yazhou Niu, Yuhao Qin, Qi Li, Yuanqing Fan, Xinjun Zhang, Huaimao Jia, Shujiang Liu, Shilian Wang
abstract: Monitoring the activities of radioxenon isotopes (131mXe, 133Xe, 133mXe, 135Xe) in the atmosphere is a key task of the International Monitoring System (IMS) under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). Discriminating the source of radioxenon detected at monitoring stations is crucial and highly challenging. This paper investigates the performance of machine learning for radioxenon source discrimination. Based on simulated and measured data, a synthetic dataset of radioxenon isotopic activity concentrations was generated, comprising samples from nuclear explosion, reactor, and hybrid sources. This dataset was then used as training data for machine learning models. The performance of the trained models was evaluated on a series of randomly generated test datasets. Under an idealized low-MDC scenario, the radioxenon source discrimination accuracy reaches 88.6%, and the probability of correctly identifying nuclear explosion signals is as high as 94.2%, corresponding to a false negative rate of 5.8% and a false positive rate of 14.9%. A sensitivity analysis using more realistic MDC settings shows that the discrimination performance decreases substantially as the MDC increases.

title: Enrichment of uranium-resistant microbial flora for U(VI) removal and mechanism analysis
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Taotao Zeng, Zhiyu Xiong, Yi Xiao, Jiayao Liu, Guohua Wang, Mingjuan Zhang, Shiyou Li
abstract: A community of uranium-tolerant microorganisms was isolated from a soil sample collected from the vicinity of a uranium tailing mine in South China to investigate the efficiency and mechanism of uranium removal. The maximum uranium (U(VI)) removal efficiency for microbes reached up to 90.9% at pH 6 and 35°C. Uranium can cause membrane lipid peroxidation to produce malondialdehyde, and activity levels of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase and catalase, changed accordingly. Fourier transform infrared spectrometry (FT-IR) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) showed that oxygen-containing functional groups and amide groups were the main functional groups involved, and that H2(UO2)2(PO4)2·8H2O and HPUO6·4H2O were formed. The isolated uranium-resistant bacterial flora included Aeromonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, Unclassified f-Enterobacteriaceae, Shewanella and Pseudomonas. Microbial functional gene prediction revealed an increased abundance of genes associated with intracellular transport, lipid transport and metabolism, inorganic ion transport and metabolism. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis showed that mainly genes related to the tricarboxylic acid cycle and quorum-sensing-related enzymes in resistance to uranium toxicity. This comprehensive analysis of the mechanisms of uranium resistant by microbial communities offers novel perspectives on the defensive responses of microorganisms under such stress.

title: A spatiotemporally corrected radiological contamination mapping platform for multi-scenario nuclear and radiological emergencies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Hyunsung Kim, Myeongsik Shin, Ku Kang
abstract: Rapid, quantitative assessment of the environmental consequences of radioactive contamination (and protection of responders operating within it) requires reconstructing continuous contamination fields from heterogeneous reconnaissance measurements. We present an automated platform that converts geo-referenced dose-rate data from ground and airborne assets into hazard-consequence maps. This study presents the platform architecture and quantitatively validates its spatial-reconstruction and decision-support modules; the altitude-correction and temporal-normalization modules are formalized as architecture components whose empirical validation is identified as future work. Airborne measurements are first converted to ground-equivalent dose rates through an altitude-dependent air-to-ground correction factor (AGCF) modeled as a segmented broken power-law (SBPL), then normalized to a common reference time using radionuclide half-life decay for radiological accidents or the Kaufmann power law for nuclear detonations. Normalized data are reconstructed into continuous 2-D fields by interpolation. Five methods, namely inverse distance weighting (IDW), ordinary kriging (OK), universal kriging (UK), anisotropic OK, and thin-plate spline (TPS), were evaluated in two scenarios: a 2000 kT nuclear surface burst (HotSpot 3.1.2) and the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant accident (JAEA airborne surveys, 2011–2025). Performance was strongly scenario-dependent: for the detonation, TPS and anisotropic OK far outperformed isotropic OK ( R 2 = 0.866 and 0.849 vs. 0.256), a gap robust across resampling (95% CIs non-overlapping), whereas all methods converged in the Fukushima field (mean R 2 = 0.938 –0.957) under random hold-out; under spatially-independent block cross-validation this convergence is weaker and accuracy is lower ( R 2 ≈ 0.70 –0.75), yet the anisotropy-aware advantage in the detonation field is reinforced. No single method is universally optimal; scenario-adaptive selection is essential for consequence estimation, exclusion-zone delineation, and minimum-dose routing in operational platforms.

title: Nonlinear dynamics and predictability limits of indoor radon under temperature and humidity variability
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Dragutin T. Mihailović, Mounir Aït-Ziane
abstract: Indoor radon variability is shaped by coupled physical processes that limit short-term predictability and challenge conventional statistical modeling. We analyzed high-resolution 10-min indoor radon measurements (4842 samples, October–November 2023) at the Centre de Recherche Nucléaire d’Alger, alongside simultaneous indoor temperature and relative humidity records. Nonlinear time-series metrics, including Kolmogorov complexity (KC), the Kolmogorov complexity spectrum (KCS), and the largest Lyapunov exponent (LLE), were applied to characterize dynamical structure. The KC spectrum indicates that radon exhibits non-zero algorithmic complexity over a broader range of normalized amplitude thresholds than temperature or humidity, reflecting enhanced multiscale structural heterogeneity. Radon also shows a larger LLE (λ = 0.0826 per 10-min interval; 95% CI: 0.0728–0.0924), corresponding to a characteristic Lyapunov divergence timescale ∼ 2 h. Because the observations were obtained from a single indoor location over approximately one month, this estimated predictability timescale should not be generalized to indoor radon dynamics beyond the analyzed conditions. By comparison, temperature and humidity display lower dynamical instability and longer predictability horizons. These findings demonstrate that indoor radon has stronger short-term instability and reduced deterministic predictability relative to microclimatic variables. The results provide a quantitative framework for assessing structural complexity and intrinsic forecast limits in radon time series, offering practical insights for predictive modeling and ventilation-based mitigation strategies.

title: Fukushima-derived radiocesium in the subarctic and transition areas of the North Pacific in 2017
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yuichiro Kumamoto, Yasunori Hamajima, Mutsuo Inoue
abstract: The East-Japan Earthquake and the subsequent tsunami on 11 March 2011 damaged the Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant (FNPP1). As a result, radioactive cesium isotopes (134Cs and 137Cs) and other radionuclides were released into the North Pacific Ocean. Over the past decade, previous studies have examined the transport processes and total inventory of the FNPP1-derived radiocesium in the North Pacific. In this study, we measured vertical profiles of dissolved radiocesium at stations along nominal 47°N zonal and 145°W meridional lines during the summer of 2017. With these data, we delineated the three-dimensional distribution of the FNPP1-derived radiocesium in the subarctic and transition areas of the North Pacific and discussed its transport process by 2017. Additionally, we estimated the total inventory of the FNPP1-derived radiocesium in this area in 2017 to be approximately 6 PBq. This inventory in 2017 was approximately half of that estimated in 2014 (12 PBq). The missing inventory of approximately 6 PBq had been partially transported northward into the Bering Sea (0.3−1.3 PBq). In contrast, the expected southward transport from the subarctic/transition to the subtropical areas has not yet been observed. We proposed that one of the possible export paths is subduction in the eastern subarctic/transition area, followed by southward transport through the subsurface layer to the eastern subtropical and then the tropical areas.

title: Particle-tracking assessment of potential groundwater pathways for radionuclide transport across the Futaba Fault, coastal Fukushima, Japan
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Fengrui Zhang, Shinji Takeuchi
abstract: Radiocesium deposited after the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant accident remains a long-term environmental concern, but its groundwater pathways toward inhabited coastal lowlands are poorly constrained. This study evaluates conservative groundwater pathways potentially relevant to radionuclide transport near the Futaba Fault in coastal Fukushima by coupling a steady-state MODFLOW-2005 model with MODPATH 7. One thousand realizations varied hydraulic conductivity and the porosity components used to derive effective porosity for the fault zone, granitic basement, mudstone, and three sandstone units using bounded PERT and log-PERT distributions. Fixed particles were released separately on each side of the fault. Of 2,000,000 western endpoint records, 93.24% terminated west of the fault, 6.33% reached eastern non-ocean cells, and 0.43% reached the ocean boundary. Western paths were concentrated in local circulation cells and valley-directed discharge zones. Eastern non-ocean outcomes originated from 465 of 2000 western release locations and were spatially clustered rather than controlled by fault distance alone. Of 6,000,000 eastern endpoint records, 89.02% remained within the eastern sedimentary domain and 10.98% reached the ocean boundary; none returned to the western block. Within the adopted barrier-dominated conceptual model and specified hydraulic-property distributions, endpoint maps, travel-time-distance densities, ensemble cross sections, and representative-realization visualizations show that the limited west-to-east pathways remain spatially restricted. Because sorption and decay were omitted, the results represent a conservative, retardation-free pathway assessment rather than a concentration forecast. Even under this formulation, west-derived pathways into the eastern lowland were spatially restricted, indicating limited potential for widespread groundwater-mediated radionuclide transport under the modeled conditions.

title: National intercomparison of environmental gamma radiation dose rate in China based on ice surface cosmic ray response measurements
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Meiqun Xiao, Tao Wang, Xun Ding, Jun Xiao, Jianfeng Lu, Zhonggang Cao, Liang Wang
abstract: This study reports the first national intercomparison of environmental gamma radiation dose rate in China where each device’s response to the ubiquitous cosmic rays was measured on top of a frozen lake ice surface. A total of 78 ambient gamma dose rate instruments from 38 institutions were tested at four typical sites, including a low-terrestrial-background site on the ice surface of the Bosten Lake to measure the detector-specific cosmic ray responses, and wilderness, road, indoor sites nearby. The measured dose rates on the ice surface show significant variations for different detector types but exhibit good consistency within the same model. The cosmic ray responses were then subtracted from the measured dose rates at the other three environmental sites, and the corrected terrestrial gamma radiation dose rates are generally very similar for all instruments. A robust Z-score analysis was applied to evaluate proficiency and identify outliers. This work demonstrates the feasibility of ice-based measurement of the detector-specific apparent cosmic-ray response, and offers a practical technical reference for future intercomparison activities and quality assurance in environmental gamma radiation measurements.

title: Evaluation of gamma-irradiated Barbula indica moss bags for monitoring geogenic dust and norm deposition in bauxite mining areas
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Sang Nguyen Thi Minh, Khiem Le Hong, Son Nguyen An
abstract: This study investigates a biomonitoring approach using gamma-irradiated Barbula indica moss bags to evaluate atmospheric elemental deposition at the Tan Rai bauxite mining complex in Lam Dong, Vietnam. Moss samples were pre-treated with a 14 Gy dose to modify the matrix before a three-month dry-season deployment across four industrial nodes (P1–P4). Elemental quantification was performed using Total Reflection X-ray Fluorescence (TXRF). The results demonstrate a systematic increase in elemental concentrations for the irradiated matrix, with values rising by 12.4% to 28.1% compared to non-irradiated controls. Specifically, the relative difference in sequestration for Thorium (25.9%) and Uranium (28.1%) reached a peak at the industrial hotspot (P3), suggesting that radiation-induced surface modification may enhance the affinity for these elements. Comparative analysis indicates that while geogenic markers (Fe, Al, Ti) align with reported data from global bauxite-impacted regions, the elevated Thorium levels (mean 1.31 mg/kg) signify a distinct geochemical signature in the study area. These findings suggest that 14 Gy irradiated moss can serve as a stable passive sampler, providing a potential framework for environmental forensic monitoring in mining regions.

title: Effects of initial water content and Na 2 SO 4 on pore structure and radon exhalation of dried remolded loess
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yuxin Zhang, Qiang Sun, Yuzhen Han, Zetang Wang, Hui Liu, Liangfu Xie, Houen Li
abstract: The pore structure of loess directly governs the storage and migration of radon. In this study, remolded loess specimens were prepared at four initial water contents (8%, 10%, 12%, and 14%) and five Na2SO4 contents (0%, 0.4%, 0.8%, 1.2%, and 1.6%). Low-temperature nitrogen adsorption, Frenkel–Halsey–Hill (FHH) fractal analysis, and radon exhalation tests were conducted to investigate the pore-structure evolution and radon-release characteristics of loess under coupled water–salt effects. The results showed that the pore system was dominated by micropores and mesopores, and all specimens exhibited typical type IV adsorption isotherms with H3 hysteresis loops. With increasing initial water content, the pore structure evolved nonlinearly with increasing water content, with enhanced micropore–mesopore development at intermediate water contents, while the fractal dimension D2 first increased and then decreased, reaching its maximum at approximately 12% water content. The radon exhalation rate followed a similar trend, increasing initially and subsequently decreasing, with relatively high values observed near 12% water content. By comparison, Na2SO4 had only a limited influence on the fundamental pore type but likely modified pore connectivity through salt migration and crystallization. These findings indicate that initial water content is the dominant factor controlling pore-structure evolution and radon release in loess, whereas salt primarily modifies the connectivity of the pore network. Radon release from loess is jointly governed by pore-size composition, pore connectivity, and pore-structure complexity. This study elucidates the intrinsic relationship between pore-structure evolution and radon release under coupled water–salt conditions and provides a theoretical basis for evaluating radon migration and environmental radiation risk in saline loess regions.

title: Bioaccumulation, food web transfer, and tissue distribution of polonium-210 and lead-210 in Canadian freshwater ecosystems
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Stephanie Walsh, Hailly Degagne, Jamie Carr, D.J. Rowan, J.M. Blais, M.J. Bond
abstract: Understanding the bioaccumulation and trophic transfer of naturally occurring radionuclides is essential for assessing ecological risk in freshwater systems. This study provides a large-scale assessment of polonium-210 (210Po) and lead-210 (210Pb) bioaccumulation, trophic transfer and tissue-specific biodistribution in freshwater food webs across Canada. Activity concentrations were measured in water and biota samples collected from multiple ecozones and land-use settings. Bioaccumulation factors were calculated to evaluate water-to-food web transfer, while trophic position patterns and 210Po:210Pb activity concentration ratios were used to assess trophic transfer and preferential radionuclide uptake and retention. Results showed the bioaccumulation of 210Po in freshwater biota relative to surface water, while 210Pb was generally less enriched in biota and showed lower relative retention across organisms. Relationships with trophic position indicated that 210Po transfer was not well described by a linear trophic magnification factor, showing enrichment from primary producers to primary consumers, followed by substantial variability among higher trophic positions. The 210Po:210Pb activity concentration ratio was generally elevated in consumer organisms, indicating preferential biological uptake and retention of 210Po relative to 210Pb. Tissue-specific analyses indicated that 210Po was concentrated primarily in viscera and internal organs, whereas muscle contributed a smaller proportion of whole-fish 210Po burden. Together, these findings demonstrate that 210Po bioaccumulates, but its biological uptake and retention vary nonlinearly with trophic position, and that 210Po:210Pb activity concentration ratios provide a consistent and integrative metric of trophic enrichment.

title: Selecting a spectrometric detector for drinking water monitoring in the case of nuclear and radiological emergencies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Jonathan Sundström, Charlotta Nilsson, Mats Isaksson, Christopher Rääf
abstract: Rapid and reliable radionuclide-specific monitoring of drinking water may be required following a radiological or nuclear (RN) emergency. In this study, ten gamma-detector configurations were evaluated for continuous drinking-water monitoring using Monte Carlo simulations combined with measured detector backgrounds. Two source terms were investigated, representing fallout from a nuclear weapon detonation and a nuclear power plant accident, each at 48 h and 7 d after release. Two measurement geometries were simulated: a 4 L Marinelli beaker and a shielded detector positioned directly against a water pipe. A conservative scenario was assumed in which the complete source-term radionuclide composition was transferred to the drinking water. Minimum Detectable Activity (MDA) and Minimum Quantifiable Activity (MQA) were calculated for 131I and 137Cs, including contributions from other radionuclides within the respective regions of interest. Larger detectors generally provided lower MDA and MQA values, with the lowest values mainly obtained for HPGe. Despite substantially lower volume-normalised full-energy peak efficiency for the Pipe geometry, its concentration-based MDA and MQA values were relatively similar to those of the Marinelli geometry because of the much larger sampled water volume. Energy resolution strongly affected radionuclide-specific quantification. For 131I, 7 d after a nuclear weapon detonation in a Marinelli geometry, non-target radionuclides contributed approximately 79% of the NaI(Tl) ROI counts, compared with approximately 29% for HPGe. The results show that both detection efficiency and energy resolution must be considered when selecting detector systems for radionuclide-specific drinking-water monitoring following an RN emergency.

title: Metabolic and oxidative stress biomarker responses to enhanced levels of natural radioactivity in three edible bivalve species
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): D. Hunt, M.G.L. Assunção, T. Davis, C. Martin, L. Pearson, N. Willey, F.L.G. Dal Molin
abstract: Despite the known contribution of industrially derived natural radioactivity, also known as Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material (NORM), to animal and human radiation dose via seafood consumption, its ecotoxicological effects on marine organisms remain poorly understood. In particular, the physiological responses of bivalve molluscs to enhanced natural radioactivity have not been studied under controlled conditions. We conducted laboratory exposure experiments on three edible bivalve species, Cresstoderma edule, Mytilus edulis and Magallana gigas, selected for their ecological relevance and economic importance, with the aim to evaluate metabolic and oxidative stress responses to enhanced levels of natural radioactivity. Cellular energy allocation (CEA) and glutathione S-transferase (GST) assays were used as indicators of physiological stress. These assays commonly provide insight into energy budgeting and detoxification processes and are widely used in ecotoxicological studies. Results revealed significant metabolic and oxidative stress effects in all exposed groups with evidence of 210Po and 210Pb bioaccumulation from the surrounding water. These findings suggest that bivalves under radiological stress may experience compromised physiological function, with potential implications for population health and welfare. Importantly, this study represents the first experimental investigation linking biomarker responses to natural radioactivity in edible bivalves, offering a novel approach for assessing the ecological risks associated with the presence of NORM in coastal environments.

title: Decadal downward migration of 137 Cs in forest soils after the Fukushima nuclear accident revealed by migration center analysis
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Mirai Watanabe, Masami K. Koshikawa, Tatsuhiro Nishikiori, Akiko Takahashi, Takuya Manaka, Naohiro Imamura, Junko Takahashi, Shin-ichiro S. Matsuzaki, Seiji Hayashi
abstract: Forest soils became the primary reservoir of 137Cs following the Fukushima nuclear accident in March 2011; however, site-specific observations of its vertical migration with annual resolution encompassing the first decade post-deposition remain limited. This study analyzed one of the few such long-term records of 137Cs depth profiles in forest soils to quantify decadal downward migration dynamics. The migration center, calculated in this study as the inventory-weighted mean depth from the litter surface, was used as a site-comparable indicator. Soil-core measurements collected repeatedly between 2011 and 2021 at cedar plantation (Ce) and deciduous broadleaved forest (DB) plots on Mount Tsukuba were analyzed. The observed mean migration center increased from 3.5 cm to 6.8 cm in Ce and from 3.8 cm to 7.5 cm in DB over the ten years. The three-parameter exponential model, including an asymptotic value, captured the decadal trends better than linear or simple exponential models, indicating that downward migration persisted through the first decade but became increasingly limited over time. The model predicted asymptotic migration-center depths of approximately 9 cm, suggesting a tendency toward long-term stabilization. In addition, this dataset was combined with published datasets from forest sites in Fukushima Prefecture. Across seven cedar plantation plots, the migration center showed a relatively consistent downward shift of approximately 4 cm, reaching nearly 8 cm below the litter surface during the first decade. The migration-center approach provides a common depth-based framework for comparing long-term radiocesium migration among forest sites and may facilitate interpretation by researchers and forest managers.

title: High-resolution comparison of coupled atmospheric dispersion systems for a hypothetical I-131 release
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Cillian Joy, Damien Martin, Colin O'Dowd
abstract: High-resolution atmospheric transport and dispersion predictions may diverge when different meteorological and dispersion models are coupled. We compared two coupled meteorological-dispersion systems, HYSPLIT–HARMONIE and FLEXPART–WRF, for a hypothetical 24 h I-131 release from Heysham nuclear power station. Four paired simulations combined April and October 2015 meteorological cases with gaseous and particulate I-131. Source timing, activity, release profile, radioactive decay, output grid, vertical output layers, and fixed dry-deposition velocities were aligned. Spatial agreement was evaluated using area-weighted figure of merit in space (FMS) for ground-level and total-plume threshold-exceedance areas at a study-defined 250 Bq m−3 threshold, with sensitivity analyses at 50 and 1000 Bq m−3. At 20 h, ground-level FMS was 14.39–19.49%, and total-plume FMS was 27.09–33.55%. October ambient activities differed by 1.96–2.81% despite ground-level FMS below 15.00%. At 20 h in April, the systems had similar within-domain sums of ambient and deposited activity, but the separate components and predicted plume locations differed. The comparison shows why plume location should be reported alongside integrated activity when multiple modelling systems inform emergency monitoring.

title: Using 210 Pb and related proxies to decode event-driven sedimentation in shelf environments: The Laptev Sea case study
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): J.M. Abril-Hernández
abstract: The reliability of 210Pb dating relies on the assumption of continuous sediment accumulation, which may not hold in dynamic environments. This study assesses its applicability in sediment cores from the Laptev Sea shelf and compares the results with cores from the East/Japan Sea under more stable conditions, using literature data. Laptev Sea cores exhibit irregular unsupported 210Pb profiles, with plateaus and uniform and/or anomalous values of independent proxies (sand content, bulk density, 226Ra and 137Cs). These features indicate short-term sedimentation events, frequently accompanied by abrupt changes in sediment provenance. Such episodes are here collectively termed event-driven sedimentation (EDS). In contrast, East/Japan Sea cores display profiles consistent with continuous accretion. The application of the TERESA model in its basic formulation, with the truncation of the 210Pbexc profiles to remove homogenites, and with its multimodal (multi-transect) version, proves useful for full and semi-quantitative analyses in these complex sedimentary scenarios. The major sedimentary events in the Laptev Sea were dated in the 1990s, consistent with the intensification of global warming. In EDS environments, consistency across multiple proxies is required to constrain physically plausible interpretations, and 210Pb data are better suited to infer sedimentary processes than for establishing precise chronologies.

title: Natural and artificial radionuclides in wood pellets and derived ashes
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Ioannis Kaissas, Konstantinos Bitos
abstract: This study presents a radiological assessment of wood pellets and their combustion ashes, with a focus on the activity concentrations of caesium-137 (Cs-137) and potassium-40 (K-40). A total of 23 commercial pellet samples and 16 corresponding ash samples from domestic appliances in Greece were analyzed using high-resolution gamma-ray spectrometry. The results reveal that K-40 activity concentrations in pellets (10–80 Bq/kg) are consistent with values typically reported for wood biomass. In contrast, Cs-137 levels show strong geographical dependence, ranging up to 60 Bq/kg in pellets from Eastern Europe, particularly Ukraine and Romania, reflecting the heterogeneous Chernobyl fallout distribution. Combustion resulted in an increased radionuclide concentration in the ash, with arithmetic mean activities of 2751 ± 40 Bq/kg for K-40 and 281 ± 5 Bq/kg for Cs-137, corresponding to average enrichment factors of 76 and 33, respectively. These values indicate radiological concerns for densely populated areas that burn pellets for heating and align with enrichment ranges reported in comparable European studies. From a regulatory perspective, this concentration effect is of particular significance. Although none of the analyzed pellet samples exceeded the exemption limit of 100 Bq/kg for Cs-137, several ash samples surpassed this threshold due to combustion-induced enrichment. This finding indicates that fuels considered radiologically safe at the point of use may produce ashes that warrant further regulatory consideration and scenario-specific assessment. Spatial mapping of Cs-137 activity, measured in pellets and the corresponding ash from different countries, is consistent with Chernobyl deposition models, underscoring the long-term persistence of radiocaesium in forest ecosystems.

title: Uptake and internal transfer of dietary 137 Cs in rainbow trout ( Oncorhynchus mykiss ) assessed by a two-compartment model
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Takashi Akutsu, Yugo Kinoshita, Shun Watanabe, Yumi Yuasa, Hajime Arai, Toshihiro Kuge, Kentaro Akasaki, Masanobu Mori, Yukiko Okada, Yuko Hatano, Kyuma Suzuki
abstract: We quantified the dynamics of dietary 137Cs uptake, internal transfer, and elimination in rainbow trout by using a two-compartment model that separated the viscera and the muscle. During the contaminated feeding period, 137Cs accumulated rapidly in the viscera and was subsequently transferred to the muscle with a distinct time lag, whereas model estimates suggested relatively limited back-transfer from the muscle to the viscera. Model estimates indicated that approximately 34% of dietary 137Cs was incorporated into the two-compartment system (viscera and muscle), whereas the remainder was attributed to pathways outside the modeled system, including incomplete absorption and fecal loss as well as possible redistribution to other tissues. During the depuration period, 137Cs declined rapidly in the viscera but persisted in the muscle, reflecting strong retention. By analyzing the absolute activity (Bq) rather than the concentration (Bq kg−1), the biological half-life of 137Cs in the muscle was estimated independently of growth dilution. These findings provide quantitative parameters describing radiocesium kinetics in freshwater fish and improve our understanding of contamination persistence and recovery.

title: Model-based assessment of geogenic radon exposure in Chaco Canyon and adjacent Ancestral Puebloan residential settings
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Reynold E. Silber, Elizabeth A. Silber, Carman Melendrez, Robert E. Silber
abstract: Naturally occurring radon-222 and its short-lived alpha-emitting progeny are important sources of environmental radioactivity in enclosed, earth-contact spaces, yet their potential relevance to archaeological built environments has rarely been quantified. Here we evaluate chronic radon exposure in Chaco Canyon, where Ancestral Pueblo people occupied earth-contact and semi-subterranean rooms associated with Pueblo Bonito and other great houses during AD 850–1150. We developed a Chaco-specific source-to-risk model using an ensemble of uranium-miner radon risk functions to link uranium- and radium-bearing geology, soil-gas radon production, diffusion- and advection-driven indoor entry, ventilation, dust/smoke-enhanced progeny exposure, floor-level occupancy, premodern survival, and radon-associated lung-cancer mortality. The model converts indoor radon scenarios to working-level-month exposure and propagates risk through reconstructed birth cohorts and competing mortality. Under the reference population trajectory, modeled exposure produced notable conditional lifetime lung-cancer risk among long-lived residents and an age-structured mortality burden during AD 850–1150. Because survival into older adulthood was limited, realized population-level burden remained demographically constrained even where conditional individual risk was elevated. We do not propose radon as a primary cause of Chacoan depopulation, Pueblo Bonito decline, or regional abandonment. Rather, the results indicate that elevated radon in selected earth-contact microenvironments could have imposed a chronic, elder-concentrated health burden within an already stressed social and ecological system, making geogenic radioactivity a testable contributor to cumulative vulnerability.

title: Chemical forms of inorganic 129 I originating from the spent nuclear fuel reprocessing plant observed off Rokkasho, Aomori Prefecture
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Shinichi Gasa, Natsuko Akihama, Hisaki Kofuji
abstract: This study analyzed the chemical speciation and characteristics of inorganic 129I and 127I in seawater collected off the coast of Rokkasho, Aomori Prefecture, Japan. The atomic ratios for each species were as follows: (129I− + 129IO3 −)/(127I− + 127IO3 −), 6.1–13.1 × 10−11; 129I−/127I−, 11.0–74.1 × 10−11; and 129IO3 −/127IO3 −, 3.3–5.9 × 10−11. At several stations, elevated values were detected from the surface to a depth of 20 m, which likely reflected the influence of the effluent. 129I discharged from the nuclear fuel reprocessing plant was primarily present as dissolved 129I−, and no significant oxidation of 129I− to 129IO3 − was observed 13 days after discharge. Furthermore, 129I supplied by riverine inputs was also present predominantly as dissolved 129I−.

title: Rn-222 gas-phase release from shallow Ra-226 sources under representative Taiwan climate conditions: A HYDRUS-1D study
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Neng-Chuan Tien
abstract: Naturally occurring Ra-226 is routinely detected in scrap metal entering Taiwan's steel recycling industry; of the 69 radiation anomaly cases reported during 2022–2023, 38 involved Ra-226, motivating the contamination case examined here. However, the potential for Ra-226 to migrate into the underlying vadose zone through rainfall infiltration during interim outdoor storage, and the consequent Rn-222 gas-phase release has not been systematically evaluated. This study employs numerical simulation with HYDRUS-1D to model Rn-222 transport through unsaturated soil columns under an idealized, hypothetical case, using site-realistic climate forcing derived from five-year (2021–2025) meteorological records at three stations spanning northern, central, and southern Taiwan. Twenty-six cases were constructed, encompassing three co-located soil–climate pairings (clay loam, loam, sandy loam), a source-depth series, sustained-rainfall and drought perturbations, a water-table series, and a soil–climate factorial that separates the soil and climate contributions. Because the site-specific Ra-226 inventory is unknown, fluxes are reported per unit source term (in cm−2 day−1 for an unspecified solute-mass unit), and comparisons across cases are interpreted on a relative basis. Results show that soil texture is the dominant control: sandy loam produces roughly twice the annual mean surface flux of clay loam with minimal seasonal variation, while clay loam exhibits nearly sixfold seasonal modulation. Adding 10 cm of overburden reduces flux by approximately 37% in clay loam but only marginally in sandy loam. A pronounced climate asymmetry emerges: drought increases summer flux substantially, whereas the sustained-rainfall-induced suppression, though substantial in fine-textured soil, is smaller than the drought enhancement. Across the fifteen baseline and perturbation cases, surface flux spans less than half an order of magnitude, governed primarily by the inherent soil–climate combination at the source location rather than engineering measures or extreme weather.

title: A mesh type model for a Chinese indigenous dog applied to radiation dosimetry in uranium mining areas
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yuchen Yin, Shaofei Cao, Bing Lian, Wenjing Gong, Liye Liu
abstract: The International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) Reference Animals and Plants (RAPs) framework employs highly simplified geometries and limited size categories, introducing uncertainties in dose assessments for medium-sized terrestrial mammals in complex environments. To address this gap, a high-fidelity mesh type model of an adult male Chinese indigenous dog (15 kg) was developed based on contrast-enhanced CT imaging. The model comprises 18 major organs and tissues and was implemented in the PHITS Monte Carlo code for direct tetrahedral mesh transport. Absorbed fractions (AFs) and specific absorbed fractions (SAFs) for monoenergetic photons (0.01–4 MeV) and electrons (0.015–4 MeV) were calculated for all organs under internal irradiation—including both self-irradiation and cross-irradiation. External dose coefficients (DCs) were derived for key uranium-series radionuclides (226Ra, 214Pb, 214Bi, and 214Po) along with the naturally occurring radionuclide 40K under three representative exposure scenarios in uranium mining areas: ground surface contamination with the animal in standing and prone postures, and lateral irradiation from a vertical mine wall. Results demonstrated significant influences of organ geometry, body posture, and source configuration on organ-level doses. Prone posture increased DCs for high-energy gamma emitters by up to ∼4% compared to standing, while lateral irradiation revealed strong position-dependent dose distributions—organs facing the source received doses comparable to or higher than those under ground contamination, whereas contralateral organs were substantially shielded. Organ-level doses varied considerably with posture and source geometry: superficial and small organs received higher DCs under ground contamination, while cephalic organs facing the source received the highest DCs under lateral wall irradiation. This anatomically realistic dog model fills a critical size gap in the ICRP RAPs and provides robust tools for site-specific radiation risk assessment of free-ranging canids (Canidae, e.g., dogs, wolves, foxes, and jackals) in contaminated uranium mining environments. The developed datasets support more accurate ecological protection under heterogeneous exposure conditions.

title: Temporal variation of indoor 222 Rn concentrations under contrasting room-opening conditions: A case study in Da Lat, Vietnam
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Nguyen Ngoc Huynh, Nguyen Ngoc Anh, Phan Bao Quoc Hieu, Nguyen Minh Dao, Nguyen Xuan Hai
abstract: Indoor exposure to 222Rn depends not only on the mean concentration but also on temporal concentration variation in relation to room occupancy. Therefore, hourly radon data, when combined with space-use information, can provide a basis for occupancy-weighted exposure assessment. This study analysed hourly 222Rn concentration time series in two residential rooms in Da Lat: an upper-floor room without direct ground contact and with a direct opening to outdoors, and a lower-level, basement-like room with ground contact and indirect air exchange through an adjacent space. During the sequential monitoring segments, the enhanced natural air-exchange state had a lower mean 222Rn concentration than the closed state in both the basement-like room (154.6 versus 433.1 Bq m−3; 64.3% lower) and the upper-floor room (50.8 versus 89.3 Bq m−3; 43.1% lower). An exploratory one-zone mass-balance analysis yielded higher fitted effective removal parameters, aeff, under enhanced exchange (0.499 versus 0.315 h−1 and 0.338 versus 0.213 h−1, respectively), consistent with faster apparent radon removal. In the basement-like room, the effective source-related term, Eeff, was also lower under enhanced exchange (2348 versus 4945 Bq h−1); however, this parameter represents a model-inferred source–removal balance rather than an independently measured source strength. These findings support systematic, long-term investigations, prioritising lower-level, ground-contact and poorly ventilated rooms.

title: Low-methoxyl pectin–Ca 2＋ gelation as a sample solidification protocol for marine radioactivity monitoring by HPGe gamma spectrometry
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yejin Lee, Hyunsung Kim, Myeongsik Shin, Gyoung Jun Choi, Jun Yoo, Ku Kang
abstract: Marine radioactivity monitoring requires rapid, reliable sample preparation methods that remain functional aboard ships and other mobile platforms. Liquid seawater samples, however, are prone to geometric instability and spillage during vessel motion, which degrade HPGe gamma spectrometry measurement quality. We developed a solidification procedure based on low-methoxyl (LM) pectin and controlled Ca 2 + supplementation, which converts seawater into a mechanically stable, leak-resistant gel through egg-box cross-linking. Under the optimised condition (1.4 g LM-pectin per 28.26 g seawater, 300 rpm, 120 min), the gel formed a mechanically stable cylindrical counting geometry (diameter 60 mm, fill height 10 mm) under the selected preparation condition. Paired activity retention, calculated from measurements of the same sample before and after solidification of Korea Institute of Nuclear Safety (KINS) proficiency-test samples, was 100.2 ± 6.1 % for 137 Cs ( n = 8 ), 95.5 ± 6.6 % for 134 Cs ( n = 7 ), 97.0 ± 4.9 % for 241 Am ( n = 8 ), and 97.2 ± 2.4 % for 60 Co ( n = 3 ) across a gamma-energy span of 59.5–1332.5 keV. All 26 paired determinations remained within the 80–120% screening range, and 24 of 26 were consistent with complete retention within their expanded uncertainty ( k = 2 ). The procedure uses food-grade reagents, requires no pre-evaporation or specialised equipment, and completes gelation within two hours. With minimum detectable activities of a few Bq kg − 1 for a 28.26 g sample counted for 30,000 s, the protocol is intended for rapid shipboard screening of elevated-activity samples in emergency situations rather than for routine low-level monitoring. These results support further shipboard validation of gel-based sample preparation for environmental radioactivity surveys.

title: T-Rex: the transportable radon-222 explorer for environmental or public health studies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Raghav Hariharan, Cynthia Leung, Alan D. Griffiths, Ot Sisoutham, Scott D. Chambers
abstract: We describe the development and testing of a “suitcase sized” 100 L two-filter dual flow-loop radon monitor, weighing ∼18 kg, flow rate ∼5 L min−1, Rn-222 sensitivity ∼0.02 s−1∙(Bq∙m−3)−1, temporal resolution 30-min, and operational range ∼0.3 – 30,000 Bq∙m−3. Its portability and sensitivity make it an ideal “crossover instrument” between the needs of the Public Health and Environmental research communities. Pending traceable calibration in a controlled climate chamber, here its performance was compared with a 200 L two-filter monitor (1.65 m tall, ∼80 kg), sampling outdoor air over 3 weeks during which radon varied between 0.14 Bq∙m−3 and 9.1 Bq∙m−3. The distribution (10th/50th/90th percentile) of absolute hourly bias was 0.03/0.19/0.54 Bq∙m−3. A separate comparison was made with an AlphaGUARD PQ2000 Pro and DF2000 over 8 days during which radon ranged from 0.6 Bq·m−3 to 9.9 Bq·m−3. The reported 8-day average radon was 3.5 ± 1.97 Bq·m−3 (100 L monitor), 4.01 ± 2.92 Bq·m−3 (PQ2000 Pro) and 4.24 ± 2.65 Bq·m−3 (DF 2000). Daily mean absolute bias reached 1.7 Bq·m−3, and absolute bias of 6-hourly means reached 3.2 Bq·m−3. For the PQ2000 and DF 2000, hourly counting uncertainty reached 30 % at 6 Bq·m−3 and 4.5 Bq·m−3, respectively (c.f. manufacturers reported detection limit of 2 Bq·m−3). The 100 L monitor reached 30 % counting uncertainty at 0.3 Bq·m−3. While this does not meet the measurement criteria for Global Atmosphere Watch “baseline” monitoring (detection limit ≤0.05 Bq∙m−3), the monitor would be well suited for many environmental monitoring purposes and portable enough for indoor use.

title: Calibration of the NDUSRM series and further measurements of 236 U/ 238 U isotopic ratios in the Ewing collection
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Thomas L. Bailey, David Lund, Griffin Mulcahy, Alistaer Zhou, Noah Cabanas, John P. McDonaugh, Ruchi Rathod, William Von Seeger, Philippe Collon
abstract: 236U is one of the rarest isotopes of uranium, occurring in ores with an abundance below 1 × 10−9. Due to a wide variety of geological factors, the 236U content in a given uranium ore body is considered to be a unique “fingerprint” like signature, with applications in nuclear forensics and geophysics. Its low abundance though is only detectable via Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS), capable of measuring 236U/238U ratios below 1 × 10−11. Improvements to the AMS setup at the University of Notre Dame’s Nuclear Science Laboratory, have greatly improved its detection limit, enabling measurements across the entire 236U/238U ratio range found in natural ores. A description of the improvements is presented. A survey of the 236U/238U ratio of various ores from North American and African mines was conducted with the improved setup, using in house reference standards to quantify the measurements. A new detection limit of 1 × 1 0 − 12 was established.

title: Regional exposure to ageing nuclear infrastructure in Europe: Examining plume trajectories and dispersion for the 45-year old Almaraz Nuclear Power Plant under present and future climates
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Angelo Alves, Diogo Costa, Vanda Salgueiro
abstract: Severe accidents at nuclear power plants may release radionuclides whose atmospheric dispersion transcends national borders. Many of Europe’s reactors were commissioned between the late 1970s and the mid-1980s and now operate well beyond their original design life, often under licences extended into the 2030s–2040s. Taking the Almaraz Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) in western Spain – one of at least 17 ageing European reactor sites aged 40–57 years – as a representative case, this study assesses the European-scale atmospheric exposure to a hypothetical severe release of Fukushima-analogue magnitude under current and projected climate conditions. The Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) model was used to compute 48 h forward trajectories and three-dimensional 137Cs dispersion plumes, driven by ERA5 reanalysis (2014–2024) and by 19 CMIP6 SSP5-8.5 simulations bias-corrected with the MBCn multivariate procedure for 2041–2070, using the 137Cs emission inventory of Source Term 5 (JAEA-Katata-6h). Under historical forcing, the dispersion is organised into three recurrent transport modes – westward or near-source (towards Portugal and the eastern Atlantic), eastward (towards the Iberian interior and the western Mediterranean) and northward to north-eastward (towards France) – with opposite seasonal cycles: the westward mode dominates autumn and winter, whereas the continental modes peak in summer. The westward and near-source clusters are also the slowest and shallowest, favouring boundary-layer transport and near-source deposition, so the highest concentrations occur in compact, slow-moving plumes, whereas the fast long-range clusters produce the broadest and most dilute ones. Under SSP5-8.5 the three modes persist, but the winter transport loses its long-range Atlantic reach and concentrates over Portugal and the western Iberian Peninsula, while the summer transport re-orients towards the western Mediterranean as the eastward mode strengthens and the northward mode weakens. Future peak concentrations increase in winter and autumn, decrease in spring and diverge in summer, with higher peaks systematically paired with more compact, near-source plumes. These seasonally and quantile-dependent shifts indicate that historically-informed emergency-preparedness planning may misjudge future transboundary exposure at Almaraz, warranting periodic re-assessment under updated climate projections. The seasonal patterns themselves are site-specific, but the assessment framework is directly transferable to the other long-operating European reactors that will remain in service for decades.

title: Radioecological dynamics in high-altitude ecosystems: Sources, processes, risk, and early-warning systems in mount Aragats
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Nona Movsisyan
abstract: This review presents an integrated conceptual framework describing radionuclide behavior in mountainous environments by synthesizing previously fragmented studies from Mount Aragats into a unified radioecological monitoring framework. Using Mount Aragats as a representative high-altitude ecosystem, the review integrates radionuclide sources, environmental processes, monitoring strategies, spatial modeling, and radiological assessment within a common perspective. Mountain regions function as dynamic orographic traps, where altitude-dependent atmospheric processes, complex topography, and heterogeneous geology govern radionuclide deposition, redistribution, and long-term retention across multiple environmental compartments, including atmospheric particulate matter, snow, soils, mosses, and river sediments. Methodological approaches adapted for complex terrain-including altitude-based sampling, baseline and background definition, geochemical indicators, regression modeling, Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, and ecological risk assessment – are synthesized into a unified framework. These approaches improve the interpretation of spatial variability, identify the principal environmental drivers, distinguish natural background from anthropogenic inputs, and support more robust environmental assessment. The synthesis of long-term investigations from Mount Aragats demonstrates that reliable baseline establishment, combined with a process-based understanding of radionuclide behavior, is fundamental for environmental monitoring in mountainous regions. This review provides a transferable methodological approach for mountain radioecology supports environmental surveillance, baseline reassessment, anomaly detection, nuclear emergency preparedness, and early-warning systems in mountainous regions influenced by both natural and anthropogenic radiation sources.

title: Transport of 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant accident-derived 137 Cs to the tropical North Pacific
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Mutsuo Inoue, Daichi Koshiishi, Yuichiro Kumamoto
abstract: The impact and transport patterns of the 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant (FDNPP) accident-derived radiocesium in the tropical North Pacific remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the latitudinal and vertical distributions of the concentrations (activities) of 137Cs, 226Ra, and 228Ra in this tropical area (8°–10°N) in April–May 2025. We observed low 228Ra concentrations in surface and mixed layers (< 0.5 mBq/L), indicating that the influence of seawater from the coastal area was not dominant, even near the eastern coast of the Philippines. 137Cs concentrations at the surface in the tropical area exhibited moderate variations (1.0–1.2 mBq/L) with the highest concentrations observed at a depth of 200 m (1.7–2.3 mBq/L). Additionally, the surface and 200 m depth fractions of FDNPP accident-derived 137Cs were 0.25–0.4 and 0.35–0.6, respectively. By 2025, FDNPP accident-derived 137Cs was partially transported across the tropical North Pacific by westward currents (e.g., the North Equatorial Current). These findings can be used to elucidate current radionuclide dynamics in tropical areas.

title: Validation of the ray-tracing Monte-Carlo code tRAYcy for geometry and coincidence-summing corrections in environmental gamma-ray spectrometry
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Felix Diel, Marc Breidenbach, Spencer Behling, Herwig Marschelke, Marcus Neuer
abstract: Accurate determination of radionuclide activities in environmental samples requires the detector response to be known for the specific detector–sample geometry, and requires correction for the matrix and density differences between calibration and sample as well as for true coincidence summing (TCS). We demonstrate the scientific validity and practical applicability of the ray-tracing Monte-Carlo code tRAYcy for these tasks by analysing two international proficiency-test materials with assigned reference activities: a soil matrix ( ρ = 1.70 g cm −3 ) and a ground green-tea matrix ( ρ = 0.62 g cm −3 ), both measured in 1l Marinelli geometry on a 40% relative-efficiency N-type HPGe detector calibrated with an aqueous mixed- γ source. Activities were evaluated under successive correction strategies — no correction, geometry (efficiency-transfer) correction, TCS correction, and the two combined — and, additionally, using a sourceless mathematical calibration in which the full-energy-peak efficiency was simulated directly for the sample geometry rather than transferred from the measured source. Uncorrected analyses showed systematic deviations of both signs, with absolute deviations reaching approximately 11%. Fully corrected results agree with the assigned reference values within 4% for 40K, 60Co, 133Ba, 134Cs, and 137Cs. Larger deviations were observed for 241Am in the soil sample (6.6%) and 210Pb in the green-tea sample (-7.7%). The mathematically calibrated activities reproduce the assigned reference values, showing that a physically modelled efficiency can replace a matched calibration source. Finally, complete synthetic spectra generated for both samples in single simulations reproduce the principal measured spectral structures across the investigated energy range, including nuclide-specific contributions, summing features, escape structures, and the Compton continua. Localised discrepancies remain in the low-energy X-ray region and below prominent high-energy peaks. The results show that physically motivated Monte-Carlo modelling delivers accuracy consistent with the assigned reference values for real environmental matrices.

title: A Life-course screening-factor framework for radionuclides in drinking water: identifying when adult-based screening is conservative, representative, or non-conservative
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Alaaddin Alnajjar, Majd Hawwari
abstract: Adult-based drinking-water screening is practical for routine radiological assessment, but it reduces life-course exposure to a single adult reference condition. This simplification cannot determine whether the adult factor represents chronic lifetime-average exposure or whether the limiting annual dose occurs during infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, or late life. A life-course screening-factor framework was developed for 17 radionuclides, with published reference results for Ra-226 and Ra-228 incorporated for comparative context. Chronic ingestion at 1 Bq L−1 was modeled over 70 years using age-specific intake rates and age-dependent ingestion dose coefficients; screening performance was evaluated using Rpeak = Fpeak/Fadult and Rlife = Flife/Fadult. Adult-based screening was neither uniformly conservative nor uniformly non-conservative. Lifetime-average underestimation (Rlife > 1) occurred for Ra-224, Pb-210, Po-210, I-131, Sr-90, and Th-228 among the newly analyzed radionuclides; the published Ra-228 reference case showed the most pronounced bias overall (Rlife ≈ 2.04). Uranium isotopes, Am-241, Cs-134, Cs-137, Pu-239, Th-230, and Th-232 were conservative for lifetime-average exposure, while C-14 and tritiated water were approximately adult-representative. Peak-dose blind spots were identified for Ra-224 (severe infant peak; Rpeak ≈ 15.8), Th-228, Po-210, I-131 (young-child thyroid peak), and Sr-90 (two-peak skeletal-growth pattern). Uranium isotopes and Am-241 showed mixed behavior: conservative for lifetime average but with missed infant dose maxima. Pb-210 and Ra-228, despite identical adult-based screening factors, produced substantially different cumulative lifetime doses (44.4 mSv versus 71.4 mSv at 1 Bq L−1), demonstrating that adult-based equivalence does not guarantee equivalent chronic exposure. These findings demonstrate that adult-based drinking-water screening performance is radionuclide-specific and metric-specific. True lifetime-average underestimation occurs when Flife exceeds Fadult, whereas Fpeak identifies age-specific exposure windows hidden by adult-only screening. The proposed Flife and Fpeak factors provide a practical life-course extension to adult-based screening for drinking-water radiological protection.

title: Indoor radon exposure and ventilation-driven mitigation in a high-rise residential unit using source-term-informed monitored-zone assessment
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Min-Jun Kim, Chang-Hyeon Kim, Won-Jun Jang, Jae-Oh Shim
abstract: Increasing airtightness in high-rise residential buildings can enhance indoor radon accumulation when persistent indoor source terms are combined with limited air exchange. This study evaluated indoor radon accumulation and ventilation-driven reduction in four monitored zones of one newly constructed high-rise residential unit using multi-point detector measurements during actual energy-recovery ventilator (ERV) operation at nominal settings of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7 h−1, complemented by chamber-derived surface-associated radon source information and zone-specific air volumes. Paired pre-ERV concentrations ranged from 496 to 1010 Bq m−3. The combined mean detector-level reductions were 79.2%, 81.5%, and 84.0% at the three nominal settings, respectively. Relative to the 0.3 h−1 tests, the 0.5 h−1 tests had higher mean reductions and fewer residual detector locations above 148 Bq m−3, whereas the 0.7 h−1 tests had the highest combined mean reduction and shortest average response time. Multi-point measurements showed an 18.6% corner-to-center difference under closed-door conditions, indicating spatial non-uniformity within the monitored unit. The first-order mass-balance calculation was retained only as a descriptive setting-level consistency check (combined-mean RMSE 4.37 percentage points; MAE 3.11 percentage points). Effective in situ ACH was not independently verified, and each room-level condition was tested once; therefore, between-setting differences are interpreted within the tested campaign rather than as isolated causal effects of ventilation rate.

title: A rapid atmospheric radionuclide dispersion prediction and dose assessment method based on the physics-aware spatio-temporal neural operator
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Zihui Yang, Boang Ge, Xiao Wang, Jue Wang, Ziwen Mo, Yuchen Li, Yihang Sun, Bin Zhang
abstract: Rapid prediction of atmospheric radionuclide dispersion is essential for emergency decision-making and radiation protection in nuclear accidents. Although computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods provide high accuracy, their limited efficiency makes it difficult to meet timeliness requirements. To address this limitation, this study proposed a method for rapid atmospheric radionuclide dispersion prediction and radiation dose assessment based on a physics-aware spatio-temporal neural operator (PA-STNO). Within the proposed model-based method, condition encoding represents variations in meteorological and release conditions, spatio-temporal attention enhances plume-evolution and spatial-structure features, the Fourier Neural Operator backbone models long-range transport dependencies, and a physics-aware composite loss improves the representation of high-concentration regions, plume boundaries, and overall concentration-mass consistency. Multi-condition tritium dispersion data generated with OpenFOAM were used for model training and evaluation. On the primary test set, PA-STNO achieved a Relative L2 of 0.21, an FAC2 of 0.92, and a Plume IoU of 0.82, while substantially improving prediction speed. The model also outperformed the baseline models, and a supplementary comparison with a conventional Lagrangian dispersion model showed reasonable agreement, with a mean absolute relative deviation of 8.36%. The predicted fields were further used for radiation dose assessment, linking rapid concentration prediction with dose calculation and supporting the preliminary assessment of dispersion consequences and radiological impacts.

title: Equilibrium in segments of natural decay series in NORM samples from the Czech Republic: 238 U – 234 U – 230 Th and 232 Th – 228 Ra – 228 Th
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Tereza Doksanská, Alena Kelnarová, Mahulena Kořistková
abstract: Industrial processing of mineral resources can lead to the redistribution and concentration of naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM). In the Czech Republic, hazards associated with the release of NORM from industrial facilities, its handling, and long-term exposure are assessed by comparing activity concentrations of 10 long-living radionuclides with the associated clearance levels. Six radionuclides are determined by gamma-ray spectrometry: 238U, 226Ra, 210Pb, 228Ra, 228Th, and 40K. Activity concentrations of four radionuclides – 234U, 230Th, 210Po, and 232Th – are derived using a set of estimative equations. These equations frequently lead to overestimation of 230Th and 232Th, and underestimation of 234U. The aim of this work was to study the equilibrium in the first segments of the uranium (238U −234U – 230Th) and thorium (232Th – 228Ra – 228Th) decay series, and to propose an updated set of estimative equations for 234U, 230Th, and 232Th for materials that satisfy the equilibrium condition in the given segments. Importantly, materials originating from different industrial processes were assessed individually, and all materials included in this study were released from workplaces in the Czech Republic. In total, 48 samples from 7 workplace types were split into 8 material categories. For each sample, gamma-ray spectrometry was used to determine 228Ra, and 228Th, and alpha spectrometry to determine 238U, 234U, 230Th, and 232Th. Activity ratios for each radionuclide pair within the given decay segment were assessed using orthogonal distance regression and/or by evaluating the activity ratios. Material categories exhibiting radioactive equilibrium in both decay segments were ashes and slag from coal combustion plants, samples utilized in cement manufacturing, old building materials, drilling muds, and waste from zircon and zirconia processing. In contrast, sludges, sinters and filter materials from water treatment facilities, along with waste from oil and gas transportation and processing, were identified as materials with disturbed equilibrium in the 238U −234U – 230Th and 232Th – 228Ra – 228Th decay segments.

title: Contact dose rate as an operational screening parameter for NORM oily sludge segregation on offshore oil and gas platforms
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Marcelo Macedo Valinhas, Marco Aurélio dos Santos, Francisco Cesar Augusto da Silva
abstract: On offshore oil and gas platforms, limited space, time and logistics create significant challenges for the characterization and segregation of NORM waste. This raises a practical question: can routine contact dose rate measurements, already incorporated into offshore radiological protection practices, provide sufficient information to support safe waste segregation decisions before oily-sludge drums leave the platform? This study evaluates the use of contact dose rate (CDR) measurements as an operational parameter for NORM oily-sludge drum segregation and risk-informed waste-management decisions. A historical dataset comprising 22,782 drum records from Brazilian offshore production was analyzed, including 8304 drums with offshore CDR measurements subsequently reassessed onshore and characterized by in situ gamma spectrometry. Offshore and onshore dose rates showed a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.827; R 2 = 0.684; p < 0.001). A multiple regression model without an intercept, based on 226Ra and 228Ra activity concentrations, showed a strong fit (R 2 = 0.8353). For drums with CDR ≤ 0.5 μSv·h−1, the statistical assessment quantified the probability of exceeding radionuclide-specific activity concentration criteria, providing a basis for evaluating uncertainties associated with dose-rate-based segregation and exemption decisions. The findings support the use of CDR as an operational waste-management parameter that may also support exemption from regulatory control under the applicable regulatory conditions, reducing reliance on systematic gamma spectrometric characterization. The study provides quantitative evidence that may contribute to discussions on the refinement of risk-informed regulatory approaches for NORM waste management in the oil and gas industry.

title: Review on algae-derived biopolymers to remove radionuclides from aquatic systems: sorption mechanisms, kinetics and stability
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Govindharajan Sattanathan, Selvarajan Ramganesh, Jeyaseelan Aravind, Srinivasan Venkatesh
abstract: The carboxyl, sulfate, phosphate and hydroxyl groups on algal biomass and its polysaccharides bind uranium, caesium, strontium and radium. The reported uranium capacities for brown macroalgae vary greatly depending on pH and pretreatment, ranging from roughly 150 to 560 mg/g. Green macroalgae and immobilized microalgae report much smaller uranium capacities, typically in the range of 75-290 mg/g. Certain microalgae remove 88-95% of dissolved 137Cs within 48 h. However, these values mostly stem from acidic, single-solute batch experiments. When the same material is used to test actual effluents, removal rates drop, often dramatically. This review evaluates algae as a feedstock for functional polymers, combines capture mechanisms with the aqueous chemistry that governs them, and re-evaluates how isotherm, kinetic, and thermodynamic models are interpreted. The review then compares the quantitative and qualitative data regarding engineered hydrogels and composites, including their stability, regeneration, and response to competition from other ions. Finally, the loaded sorbent is viewed as secondary radioactive waste, and column operation, life-cycle burden, and traditional alternative options are placed within this context. Maximum capacity is less important than selectivity in real water and safe end-of-life management as critical evaluation criteria.

title: Natural and technologically enhanced radioactivity (NORM/TENORM) in soils, mining residues and waters of mining areas worldwide: a systematic review and multivariate synthesis of the 1976–2026 literature
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Edmundo Escareño-Juarez
abstract: Mining and mineral processing redistribute naturally occurring radionuclides and can generate technologically enhanced naturally occurring radioactive material (TENORM). A PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review of the 1976–2026 literature was combined with a quantitative, multivariate synthesis of activity concentrations reported in abstracts. Of 60,242 records from seven bibliographic sources, including the IAEA INIS database, and citation searching, 16,689 were eligible and 1308 studies from 103 countries provided 4532 values (4276 study-level records). In mining-impacted soils, geometric means of 226Ra(238U), 232Th and 40K were 56.7, 38.1 and 306 Bq kg−1; medians exceeded the UNSCEAR world medians by 11% and 26% for 226Ra(238U) and 232Th, whereas 40K was 18% lower. Uranium mining showed the highest soil 226Ra(238U) (geometric mean 324 Bq kg−1) and tin/rare-earth/mineral-sand operations the highest 232Th (78.9 Bq kg−1). The 232Th/226Ra(238U) ratio was lowest in phosphate and uranium operations (medians 0.30 and 0.56) and 0.7–1.4 in the other industries. After adjustment for industry, region and publication year, tailings and residues contained 6.6 times more 226Ra(238U) than soils, and 31% of tailings records exceeded 1 Bq g−1. Uranium exceeded the WHO drinking-water guideline (30 μg L−1; a yardstick for mine waters) in 45% of groundwater and 83% of mine-water records, and 53% of mine-water records exceeded 1 Bq L−1 of 226Ra. The median outdoor effective dose from soils was 0.072 mSv y−1. In this abstract-level dataset, the largest enhancements and guideline exceedances occurred in residues and mine waters and differed among industries; harmonised reporting would enable full-text meta-analysis.

title: Measurement intensity and regulatory effectiveness in radon governance: A comparative analysis of the United States and Europe
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Robert Bobkier, Peter Bossew, Petros Koutrakis, Ewa Katarzyna Czech, Konstantin Kovler
abstract: Measurement intensity, understood as the capacity of a regulatory system to generate exposure-relevant data at scale, is a revealing indicator of how legal frameworks translate scientific knowledge into protective action. Radon is a leading environmental carcinogen, yet the U.S. and Euratom Community legal systems have responded to the same body of scientific evidence through structurally different regulatory architectures. These architectures have produced deep asymmetrical levels of measurement intensity, thereby substantively shaping the foundations upon which mitigation, optimization, and enforcement rest. The present study examines the development of radon governance in the U.S. and Europe through a combined doctrinal, empirical, and regulatory lens. Drawing on U.S. national radon datasets, European Indoor Radon Maps and an analysis of epistemic capacity, it demonstrates that regulatory effectiveness is not strictly correlated with legal stringency. The U.S. federal-state-market architecture, combining non-binding federal guidance with state disclosure rules, transaction-driven testing, and private-market incentives, has generated reported measurement volumes more than one order of magnitude above the currently documented European map-based dataset, together with substantially greater reported mitigation activity. These gross outputs do not, by themselves, establish a net reduction in the number of high-radon dwellings or in population risk, but they demonstrate a markedly greater capacity to generate exposure-relevant information and activate remedial pathways. The Euratom Community has developed a codified framework under Directive, 2013/59, but exhibits structurally lower testing rates, largely because mandatory workplace duties are concentrated within Radon Priority Areas and because comparable mechanisms for embedding household testing in ordinary social and economic routines remain limited. The article concludes that measurement intensity can function as a structural diagnostic of epistemic and remedial capacity, revealing how divergent normative designs generate distinct pathways for converting scientific insight into concrete public-health protection.

title: 210 Pb ex in lacustrine sediments: A half-century global synthesis (1977-2024)
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Renaldo Gastineau, Floriane Guillevic, Palak Aggarwal, Anthony Foucher, Olivier Evrard, Christine Alewell, Robert Sabatier, Pierre Sabatier
abstract: Unsupported 210Pb (210Pbex) is a naturally occurring radionuclide widely used to establish sediment chronologies spanning the past ∼150 years, thereby providing high-resolution temporal frameworks for palaeolimnological reconstructions. Since the late 1970s, numerous hypotheses have been advanced to explain the environmental and climatic controls on 210Pbex deposition in lakes, yet no comprehensive synthesis of the accumulated empirical evidence is available. Here, we compile a global database of 210Pb measurements from 670 lacustrine sediment cores from studies published between 1977 and 2024 CE, encompassing 530 lakes across 61 countries and all continents except Antarctica. Before 2000 CE, approximately 85% of the sediment cores studied were located in the Northern Hemisphere. This proportion declined to 45% after 2000, reflecting a geographic expansion of 210Pb-based chronologies use toward the Southern Hemisphere. Using this dataset, we first assess the bivariate relationships between the 210Pbex surface activities, depositional fluxes, inventories, and individual environmental covariates, such as mean annual precipitation, land/ocean ratio, latitude and elevation. We then apply ordinary least squares multiple linear regression (OLS) and random forest (RF) models to rank the drivers of spatial variability in 210Pbex deposition at the global scale. The RF models outperform the OLS; the surface activity, flux and inventory models have low to high explanatory power for interpretation (R2 = 0.21, 0.35 and 0.66, respectively). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) indicate that elevation is the dominant predictor of both fluxes and inventories, followed by latitude and mean annual precipitation. These findings demonstrate that large-scale atmospheric processes primarily govern global patterns of lacustrine 210Pbex deposition. This study provides the first quantitative, data-driven global assessment of the environmental controls on lacustrine 210Pb deposition, enhancing the robustness and comparability of 210Pb-based chronologies worldwide.

title: Reshaping millennial-scale human–water relationships: A multi-disciplinary synthesis of the Yellow River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qiting Zuo, Lu Liu, Junxia Ma
abstract: Study region Yellow River Basin, China, a large sediment-laden river system shaped by millennia of human activities, environmental changes, and river management. Study focus Recent reviews have documented Yellow River flood history and anthropogenic disturbances in considerable detail, yet their relevance to long-term socio-hydrological governance remains insufficiently synthesized. This review integrates historical, archaeological, paleoenvironmental, ecological, hydrological, geomorphological, and governance evidence to re-examine the millennial-scale evolution of human–water relationships in the basin. New hydrological insights for the region The synthesis identifies four broad stages: adaptive coexistence (ca. 2070 BCE–581 CE), agricultural expansion and landscape transformation (581–1368 CE), sediment-driven vulnerability and hydraulic dependence (1368–1949 CE), and engineering regulation and ecological restoration (since 1949 CE). Across these stages, increasing human pressure and changing ecological buffering capacity altered erosion, sediment accumulation, and river-system responses, while increasing hydraulic dependence during periods of heightened vulnerability.
