Conversely, slope boundaries required longer lags of 24–48 h. Upslope areas exhibited extended lags due to delayed infiltration and macropore flow, while downslope areas reflected prolonged saturation and direct interactions with the riparian water table. Ultimately, these data driven AI structures successfully capture complex, localized subsurface flow mechanisms and threshold behaviors on mountain hillslopes.

title: Modelling climate change impacts on river temperatures in two Norwegian catchments
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Lennart Schönfelder, Knut Tore Alfredsen, Johan Strömqvist, Tor Haakon Bakken
abstract: Study region: Gaula and Nausta are two Norwegian river catchments that differ in size, hydrological setting, and degree of hydropower regulation. Gaula includes regulated tributary sections affected by diversions and reservoir operation, whereas Nausta represents a smaller, largely unregulated western Norwegian catchment. Together, the catchments provide contrasting test cases for assessing climate-change impacts on river discharge and water temperature at management-relevant spatial scales. Study focus: This study applies the HYPE model to simulate daily discharge and water temperature at river-segment scale. The model was calibrated and validated against observed discharge and river water temperature, with satisfactory performance for both variables. Future hydroclimatic conditions were assessed using an ensemble of regional climate projections under RCP4.5 and SSP3-7.0. New hydrological insights for the region: The simulations indicate substantial changes in seasonal discharge regimes, including reduced spring flood magnitude and increased winter discharge. Simulated river water temperatures increased across both catchments and all future periods, with long-term warming at river mouths reaching approximately 0.20 °C/decade under RCP4.5 and 0.30 °C/decade under SSP3-7.0. Warming generally intensified downstream and towards the late 21st century. In regulated parts of the Gaula system, bypass reaches downstream of hydropower diversions showed thermal differences to unregulated conditions, suggesting reduced thermal buffering under low-flow conditions. These results indicate that environmental flow design in regulated rivers should consider thermal conditions alongside discharge.

title: Generation-associated high-frequency oscillations in reservoir water levels and implications for inflow data quality: A case study of Chuncheon Dam, Korea
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Dong Hyun Kim, Seung Oh Lee, Hongjoon Shin, Jeonghwan Ahn
abstract: Study region This study focuses on Chuncheon Dam in the Bukhangang River basin, South Korea, a cascade reservoir system where precise real-time inflow estimation is critical for integrated water resources management and flood control. Study focus This study quantifies how millimetre-scale, generation-associated water-level oscillations propagate into 1-min inflow estimates. A targeted band-stop correction, applied to every month of 2023 whose stage record can resolve the oscillation, reduces the standard deviation of 1-min inflow by 21.7% over the record (40.8% in June 2023) while conserving cumulative inflow volume to within 0.02%. The negative-inflow count, widely used as a quality indicator, is also shown to be strongly affected by the 0.7 mm quantisation step of the stage sensor rather than directly reflecting estimation quality. New hydrological insights for the region Oscillation amplitude is not primarily controlled by absolute water level or mean power output; it correlates strongly with power-output variability and ramp rate, while elevated RMS amplitudes recur within specific operating water-level ranges. These results identify generation-associated oscillations as a manageable source of non-physical variability in short-interval inflow estimates. An operation-aware diagnostic procedure can reduce this variability when the monitoring record resolves the oscillation and satisfies both relative and absolute detection criteria. The procedure is transferable, whereas the target frequency band and amplitude threshold require site-specific identification.

title: Cumulative impacts of climate change, permafrost thaw and wildfire drive increasing streamflow in a discontinuous permafrost watershed
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Abigail R. Baran, Élise G. Devoie, Stephanie N. Wright
abstract: Study region La Martre River watershed, in the Mackenzie River Basin, is a discontinuous permafrost watershed in the Northwest Territories, Canada. Accelerated climate warming in northern Canada is driving significant changes in temperature patterns, precipitation, permafrost, and wildfire frequency and severity. These changes have individually been linked to observed increases in annual and winter streamflow, though the underlying drivers and cumulative effects remain complex and poorly understood. Study focus This study investigated the relative and cumulative contributions of climate change, permafrost thaw, and wildfire to streamflow variability using a semi-distributed hydrological model. New hydrological insights Hydrological changes were investigated across three periods: past (1976–2000), present (2001–2025), and future (2026–2050) under a high-emissions scenario (CMIP6 SSP5–8.5). The model represented climate- and disturbance-derived permafrost thaw, including expanded perennially unfrozen ground, increased subsurface transmissivity, and land cover change. Precipitation increase was found to be the dominant driver (5.3%, 15.2%, 33.9% percent increase in annual discharge from the base case in the past, present, and future periods, respectively), while permafrost thaw also enhanced discharge (1%, 10.2%, 18.3%). Wildfire, while having a small individual impact (-0.6%, −0.6%, 3.3%), accelerated permafrost thaw, amplifying streamflow. The combined effect of precipitation increase and permafrost thaw resulted in greater discharge increases than any individual factor (7.4%, 31.7%, 55.7%). These findings highlight the vulnerability of northern watersheds to the interaction of climate, permafrost thaw, and disturbance in (sub-)Arctic regions.

title: Assessment of agricultural groundwater-irrigation demand in the Mississippi Delta
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Mohsen Nekooei, Prem Parajuli, Joel O. Paz, Mary Love Tagert
abstract: Study region The Mississippi Delta, a lenticular alluvial plain of approximately 19,000 km² in northwestern Mississippi, USA, encompassing 19 counties wholly or in part and underlain by the Mississippi River Valley Alluvial Aquifer (MRVAA), the principal source of irrigation water in the region. Study focus Groundwater management in the Mississippi Delta is constrained by the scarcity of metered groundwater withdrawal records, because flowmeter installation is voluntary and reporting is aggregated at coarse temporal scales. This study (i) characterized daily growing-season groundwater-level (GWL) dynamics using continuous records from 11 USGS observation wells for the 2016–2021 growing seasons, and (ii) developed a spatially distributed framework to estimate agricultural groundwater-irrigation demand — used here as a proxy for groundwater withdrawal — at seasonal, monthly, and daily time steps. The daily values represent monthly-average daily irrigation-demand rather than day-to-day pumping. Estimates were derived from annual USDA-NASS Cropland Data Layer maps of corn, cotton, rice, soybean, and aquaculture, combined with crop-specific seasonal application depths and monthly distribution coefficients, and were allocated to 1921 proxy well locations. The estimates are not independently measured withdrawals; they were evaluated against groundwater withdrawals reported for the MRVAA by the U.S. Geological Survey to assess plausibility. New hydrological insights for the region Growing-season GWL declines were spatially centered in the central Delta, where a well in Sunflower County showed an average decline of 3.15 m across the 2016–2021 growing seasons. Estimated irrigation demand averaged 21.04 million m³ per day across the growing season, peaking in July and August, with soybean and rice accounting for the majority of demand. Bolivar, Sunflower, Washington, and Leflore counties consistently showed the highest demand, reflecting crop composition and cultivated extent. After adjustment for crop-specific irrigated fractions, the estimated 2016 crop irrigation demand agreed with the independently reported value for the aquifer to within 28%. Because the framework resolves demand in both space and time, it provides transient pumping inputs for regional groundwater-flow models and a transferable approach for other irrigated alluvial aquifer systems where metered withdrawal data are sparse.

title: Zone-specific selection of CMIP6 models using relative importance metrics for projecting precipitation extremes in South Kivu, eastern DRC
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Luc Cimusa Kulimushi, Jean M. Mondo, Katcho Karume, Aimé HK. Bisimwa, Alphonse Z. Balezi, Jackson-Gilbert M. Majaliwa, Janvier B. Bashagaluke
abstract: The intensification of precipitation extremes threatens hydro-ecological stability in topographically complex regions such as the Albertine Rift, yet global climate model (GCM) projections there are limited by structural uncertainties. We present a multi-stage framework to evaluate historical and future extreme precipitation (ten ETCCDI indices) across six agroecological zones (AEZs) of South Kivu, eastern DRC. From eight CMIP6 GCMs, we isolated regime-specialist models using Relative Importance Metrics (RIM), the Compromise Programming Index (CPI), and Jenks Optimized Classification (JOC), then apply Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM) and Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) under SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5. Model fidelity is zone- and index-specific: MPI-ESM1–2-HR excelled for orographic intensity in high-altitude zones, while MRI-ESM2–0 in lowland and rain-shadowed zones. Several AEZs showed significant historical declines (1983–2014) in precipitation indices (e.g., decline of −4.5 mm yr−1 for PRCPTOT in the EHAZ), which reverse under high-emission pathways by the late 21st century, with PRCPTOT trends up to + 18.1 mm yr−1 and R95Ptot trends up to + 7.1 mm yr−1. The THMAZ evolved into a hotspot of hydro-climatic whiplash combining longer dry spells with intensified convective extremes. The Time of Emergence (ToE) for SDII was as early as 2024 in the EMAZ and THMAZ, and that of RX1day was ~ 2027–2029 in the EHAZ. In contrast, most intensity and volume indices showed no emergence in the high-variability lowland and transitional zones. Provincial-scale averaging masks this sub-regional vulnerabilities: the THMAZ R95pTOT trend (+7.06 mm yr⁻¹) is more than twice the provincial mean (+3.2 mm yr⁻¹). These results provide a physical baseline for infrastructure and early-warning systems in this climate-exposed region.

title: Vegetation loss and response to hydrological drought on the islands of the Congo River
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Janae Steadman, Mark A. Trigg, Greta C. Dargie, Mark W. Smith, Raphael Tshimanga, Paul O’Hanlon, Andrew B. Carr, Gode Bola
abstract: Study Region The study focuses on floodplain islands along a ~400 km reach of the middle Congo River between Mbandaka and Mpouya in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The study area contains approximately 800 geomorphologically stable river islands covering roughly 1040 km² and supporting vegetation ranging from early successional grasses and shrubs to mature forests, alongside small-scale fishing and agriculture. Study Focus This study investigates vegetation responses to the 2024 hydrological drought across Congo River islands and examines how hydroclimatic conditions propagated through the river-floodplain system. Hydrometeorological conditions were characterised using CHIRPS precipitation data, ERA5-Land temperature and evaporation, and HydroWeb altimetry river stage records. Drought severity was assessed using SPEI-3, consecutive dry days, and warm day frequency. Vegetation change was evaluated using spectral indices and supervised land-cover classification derived from cloud-free Sentinel-2 Level-2A imagery. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The 2024 event was characterised by persistent precipitation deficits and elevated temperatures, followed by below-average river levels consistent with reduced upstream discharge and the development of hydrological drought. Vegetation decline closely coincided with lower river stage, suggesting that reduced river–floodplain connectivity contributed to drought impacts on floodplain vegetation. Vegetation loss was greatest in shorter vegetation, suggesting that vegetation structure influences ecosystem sensitivity to water limitation.

title: Importance of glacier shrinkage for sustaining runoff in Panj River of Pamir, Central Asia
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yun Bai, Min Xu, Shichang Kang, Guanghui Wei, Safarov Mustafo, Xingdong Li
abstract: Study region The study area is the Panj River basin, situated in the upper reaches of the Amu Darya basin. Study focus Glacier and snowmelt runoff are vital for sustaining streamflow in the Panj River Basin, a key cryospheric water source region in Central Asia. However, the impacts of glacier retreat, snow changes, and precipitation variability on long-term runoff remain unclear under global warming. This study applied the Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) model to quantify runoff components, including rainfall, snowmelt, and glacier runoff, and integrated the Budyko framework, scenario simulations, and glacier retreat experiments to assess runoff drivers and the hydrological response to glacier loss. New hydrological insights The results showed that total runoff, rainfall runoff, and snowmelt runoff exhibited significant decreasing trends during 1982–2020, whereas glacier runoff increased, reflecting a temporary compensation effect from enhanced glacier melt under climate warming. Meltwater runoff accounted for 67.9% of total runoff and played an important role in regulating streamflow, particularly during dry years. Attribution analysis revealed that runoff changes were mainly controlled by climatic factors (122.5%), with precipitation being the dominant driver, while human activities (−22.5%) partially offset the decline in runoff. Glacier retreat scenarios indicated that continued glacier loss would reduce summer meltwater supply and may alter the seasonal distribution of runoff, with potential implications for the stability of downstream water supply. The impacts of glacier change on mountain runoff processes and regional water resources provide a basis for understanding potential changes in downstream water availability in Central Asia.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution of sediment supply in the Yangtze River Basin from 2006 to 2024: A hydrologically constrained diagnostic framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zhixiong Chen, Mingmin Xu, Fei Zhang, Chi Yung Jim, Saied Pirasteh, Brian Alan Johnson, Nan Xu, Yuanfang Chai, Hongtao Xu, Shuke Tang, Sichen Xiong, Sha Zhu, Zhuoling Zheng, Ziwen Tang
abstract: Study Region: The Yangtze River Basin (YRB) exhibits heterogeneous hydrology and sediment transport, but basin-wide suspended sediment concentration (SSC) changes and responses to contrasting flow conditions remain unclear. Study Focus: We analysed 63,996 Landsat 5/7/8 images and SSC–discharge observations from 30 stations across eight sub-basins (2006–2024), integrating optical water type (OWT)-specific machine learning, long-term trend analysis, and station-specific SSC–discharge relationships. Two representative OWTs were retained, with optimal models achieving R² values of 0.56 and 0.73 and RMSE values of 62 and 44 g m⁻³ , respectively. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: SSC declined significantly across all seasons, most rapidly in autumn (−1.09 g m⁻³ yr⁻¹), with sensitivity tests confirming robust basin-wide declines under varying temporal data availability. Hydrologically normalised SSC anomalies showed that Normal Transport remained dominant under diagnostic thresholds of ±0.2, ±0.3, and ±0.4. Constrained responses strengthened particularly in the Main Stem, Jinsha River, and Poyang Lake. During floods, six sub-basins exhibited negative median sediment-response anomalies, whereas seven showed positive anomalies during droughts. This spatially heterogeneous flood–drought asymmetry reveals shifts in runoff–sediment coupling relative to local hydrological baselines rather than sediment responses simply proportional to runoff magnitude.

title: Uncertainties in water availability estimates derived from multiple precipitation and evapotranspiration datasets and fusion methods for semi-arid and arid regions
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jinghong Liu, Zhipin Ai, Yonghui Yang, Yanmin Yang, Hasi Bagan, Bayarsaikhan Uudus
abstract: Study region: Mongolia, an arid and semi-arid region. Study focus: Water availability (WA), calculated as precipitation minus actual evapotranspiration (AET), is difficult to estimate in drylands because the small residual can be sensitive to differences between input products. We evaluated 37 WA estimates, comprising 35 combinations of seven precipitation and five AET products and two estimates based on arithmetic average (AA) and Bayesian three-cornered hat (BTCH) fusion. We compared their temporal and spatial characteristics and evaluated their performance with observed and gridded runoff. New hydrological insights: Across the 37 estimates, the mean long-term annual WA was 39.5 ± 63.5 mm yr⁻¹ (mean ± SD), and trend slopes averaged −0.5 ± 0.8 mm yr⁻². The CV of long-term means was 160.8%, and the relative slope spread was 158.7%. Most estimates showed higher WA in northern Mongolia, although some displayed the opposite spatial gradient. Runoff agreement was weaker in southern arid basins and varied among individual combinations. ERA5_ERA5 showed comparatively strong runoff agreement, while AA and BTCH exhibited relatively consistent, intermediate performance across basins and significant correlations with gridded runoff over relatively large areas of Mongolia. Precipitation-product selection accounted for 74.5% of the combined normalized main-effect variation associated with precipitation and AET selection among the 35 individual combinations. These findings support careful input selection and regional evaluation of fusion-based WA estimates.

title: Water balance dynamics in adjacent glaciated and unglaciated high arctic catchments (SW Spitsbergen, Svalbard)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Nicole Hanselmann, Marzena Osuch, Abhishek Bamby Alphonse
abstract: Study region Hornsund, SW Spitsbergen, Svalbard – area representing the Atlantic sector of High Arctic Study focus Rapid climate warming across Svalbard is fundamentally altering high-latitude terrestrial cryospheric systems and hydrological processes. To investigate these transitions, a seasonal moving-parameter HBV modeling framework was implemented to evaluate and compare the long-term water balance dynamics of two adjacent catchments underlain by continuous permafrost: the unglaciated Fuglebekken catchment (monitored 2014–2024) and the glaciated Ariebekken catchment (monitored 2007–2024). New hydrological insights The findings suggest a structural divergence in the runoff regimes of these neighboring watersheds. While the unglaciated Fuglebekken regime is driven by seasonal snowmelt and rainfall events, the glaciated Ariebekken system benefits from a substantial glacial meltwater buffer that sustains high, steady baseflow late into the summer. Crucially, Fuglebekken shows a significant positive multi-annual storage gain over the study period (+325 mm), challenging the traditional baseline assumption of negligible annual storage changes (ΔS = 0) in continuous permafrost catchments. This net water accumulation could be consistent with localized active layer thickening and talik development. Methodologically, the integration of intra-annually shifting parameter sets allows the model to represent the non-stationary hydrogeological features of permafrost soils. Additionally, updating the model via an area-scaling glacier module accurately represents the retreat of the Ariebreen glacier, providing a physically plausible meltwater input and highlighting the transient nature of current high-discharge volumes in the deglaciating catchment.

title: The water use paradox in China: Phenomenon, driving factors, and policy implications
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Wenqing Li, Guohua He, Hanlin Zhu, Yong Zhao, Fan He
abstract: Study region China. Study focus Although China’s water use (WU) has declined since 2013, national water demand diverges when accounting for virtual water (VW) embodied in international trade. This study defines real water consumption (RWC) as WU plus VW in imports minus VW in exports, quantifying China’s RWC from 1990 to 2021. We construct time-varying water-use coefficients rather than fixed coefficients and integrate them into a multiregional input–output model spanning 189 economies. We examine the divergence between RWC and WU, decompose the drivers of RWC, and assess how trade reshapes China’s water stress. New hydrological insights for the region China’s RWC increased continuously, exceeding WU by 44.30 billion m3 in 2021; thus, WU has decoupled from economic growth solely on the production side. Around 2014, China became a net VW importer, drawing increasingly on agricultural imports from developing economies. By 2021, agriculture constituted 55.53% of total VW imports, and net imports supplied 6.96% of national water demand, mitigating water stress. The increase in RWC was driven primarily by consumption scale, which contributed 252.72% to the total change, whereas demographic growth played a secondary role and efficiency gains failed to offset consumption expansion. Consequently, China’s water security cannot be evaluated solely from withdrawals; it is increasingly tied to external agricultural suppliers, necessitating demand-side governance, supply-chain trade resilience, and efficiency enhancements.

title: Quantifying non-additive synergy in Blue–Green–grey Infrastructure for adaptive urban water resilience: A case study of Zixing City, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yifan Liu, Qiulin Liao, Yueyuan Hang, Yi Tang, Yuchi Cao, Jiaao Chen, Peng Xiao, Yurou Li, Xiaoru Liu, Xi Yu, Shouyun Shen, Jingpeng Liao
abstract: Study region This study was conducted in the central urban area and northern ecological zone of Zixing City, Hunan Province, China. This medium-sized mountainous urban catchment is affected by rapid urbanization, wetland degradation, impervious surface expansion, and fragmented hydrological connectivity, leading to reduced stormwater regulation capacity and increased water-quality risks. Study focus This study examined whether integrated Blue-Green-Grey Infrastructure (BGGI) can generate non-additive synergistic effects under different rainfall conditions and clarified the underlying mechanisms. A coupled SWMM-based hydrological and water-quality simulation and graph-theoretic network analysis framework was used to evaluate constructed wetlands (CWs), low-impact development (LID), and hydrological connectivity enhancement (HYCE). Eight scenarios, including baseline, single-measure, dual-measure, and fully integrated configurations, were compared under three 120-min design rainfall events. Rather than treating integrated performance as a general combination effect, this study quantified non-additive synergy against a multiplicative expectation derived from independent single-measure effects. Dummy variable regression, two-way ANOVA, graph-theoretic analysis, and sensitivity tests were used to identify rainfall-dependent functional roles, assess the mediating role of structural connectivity, and test robustness. New hydrological insights for the region The fully integrated scenario outperformed all single- and dual-measure scenarios in both runoff regulation and pollutant reduction. Compared with the theoretical combined expectation, integrated BGGI showed positive non-additive synergistic effects across all rainfall scenarios and indicators, with absolute synergistic gains of 8.41–56.16 %age points and relative synergistic gains of 16.73 %–183.71 %. Peak-flow reduction showed stable synergistic gains across rainfall intensities, whereas TN and TP achieved higher relative gains under low-intensity rainfall. These results indicate that integrated BGGI performance is not a simple additive outcome of individual measures, but arises from functional complementarity among LID-based source control, HYCE-mediated runoff routing and hydraulic redistribution, and CW-based downstream retention and purification. Sensitivity tests confirmed that the main conclusions were not dominated by any single scenario parameter. This study provides a mechanism-oriented framework for distinguishing non-additive synergy from general combination effects and supports rainfall-adaptive, network-coordinated BGGI planning.

title: Asymmetric impacts of climate warming and vegetation restoration on streamflow in the Ji-shaped bend of the Yellow River: Evidence for threshold effects
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xuan Zhang, Yixuan Wang, Tingxi Liu, Long Ma, Xiaomin Liu, Jianguo Ji, Wenbo Song, Shiyu Zhang
abstract: Study region Six representative basins within the Ji-shaped bend of the Yellow River. Study focus This study aims to investigate the nonstationary responses of streamflow to climate warming and vegetation restoration. A Comprehensive Ecological Index (CEI) was developed, and a time-varying moments model was improved to better characterize periodic variations in distribution parameters. By integrating enhanced nonstationary statistical modeling with explainable machine learning, we systematically evaluated streamflow variation characteristics and quantified the marginal contributions and threshold effects of key driving factors. New hydrological insights for the region (1) Streamflow variations exhibit pronounced spatial heterogeneity: annual streamflow in the drier northern basins showed a significant declining trend (up to 6.82 mm/10 years), whereas in the wetter southern basins, variations were dominated by periodic patterns. (2) The marginal contribution of precipitation to annual streamflow variation was 31.6–61.0%, showing a positive effect above its long-term mean. Temperature contributed 18.5–39.4%, with low temperature promoting streamflow and high temperature suppressing it in drier basins, whereas the opposite pattern was observed in wetter basins. The CEI accounted for 7.9–38.4% of the variation. (3) In the drier northern basins, the effect of vegetation restoration on streamflow shifted from promotion to suppression when CEI exceeded a threshold of approximately 0.25. These asymmetric impacts and threshold behaviors provide important insights for water resource management and ecological restoration in semi-arid regions.

title: A dual branch deep learning framework with trend gating for nonstationary monthly runoff prediction
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haijiang Ma, Xiaodan Zhang, Yongkun Zhang, Tong Zhao, Yuanchen Huang
abstract: Study region: The Source Region of the Yangtze River in the Three-River Headwaters of the Tibetan Plateau, with three representative stations: Tuotuo River, Zhimenda, and Xinzhai. Study focus: This study addresses monthly runoff prediction in alpine basins with pronounced nonstationarity and multi-scale variability. A variational mode decomposition (VMD)-based trend guided dual branch gated collaborative network (VCLT-Net) is proposed. VMD decomposes runoff into a slowly varying trend component statistically dominated by baseflow-like variability and a high-frequency fluctuation component containing rapid response signals, with no unique mapping to physical processes. An LSTM simulates the trend, multi-scale convolutional Transformers extract high-frequency features, and a trend-driven gated interaction network (TDGN) adaptively fuses both branches in a data-driven manner. Hyperparameters are optimized by a heuristic optimization algorithm (HOA); SHAP quantifies driver attribution. VCLT-Net is benchmarked against multiple models using seven metrics. New hydrological insights: VCLT-Net robustly outperforms benchmarks at all three stations. At Zhimenda, it increases Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) by 16.21%, reduces root mean square error (RMSE) by 152.47 m3/s, improves Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) by 13.37%, and lowers mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) by 6% over standalone LSTM; both NSE and KGE exceed 0.95. The consistent outperformance demonstrates the model’s ability to capture complex nonstationary runoff dynamics, suggesting that integrating decomposition, dual-branch feature extraction, and trend-driven interaction improves the representation of long-term and short-term variability in monthly runoff.

title: Enhancing event-based flood forecast stability and physical interpretability via Reg-TCN-LSTM coupled deep learning with discharge regularization constraints
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qiqi Guo, Qingyuan Luo, Shentang Dou, Yalin Zhang, Caihong Hu, Chengshuai Liu, Lina Liu, Tianning Xie, Gan Miao
abstract: Study region The Anyang River Basin, Henan Province. It’s a representative data-scarce, flash-flood-prone small-medium basin with mixed urban-plain flooding. Study focus To address limitations of deep learning in capturing local dynamics, long-term dependencies, error accumulation, and weak physical constraints at longer lead times, we propose a lightweight discharge-regularized coupled model, Reg-TCN-LSTM, combining TCN's local feature extraction with LSTM's long-term memory. A flow-magnitude regularization term softly constrains predicted discharge amplitudes, enhancing stability and physical consistency without added complexity. Using 20 flood events split 7:3 into training and test sets, we evaluated its 1–12 h forecasting performance against TCN, LSTM, and TCN-LSTM benchmarks with metrics including NSE, RMSE, RE, andΔt. New hydrological insights for the regions Reg-TCN-LSTM achieved the best overall performance across all lead times (NSE: 0.574–0.969; RMSE: 7.06–26.25 m³/s), improving NSE by up to 14.34% over TCN, LSTM, and TCN-LSTM, while reducing peak and timing errors. It better preserved flood hydrographs and showed enhanced stability at 9–12 h lead times. Gradient-based attribution reveals that TCN dominates short-lead forecasts by capturing local dynamics, whereas LSTM gains importance at longer lead times via antecedent hydrological memory. The flow-magnitude regularization term was particularly effective during flood peaks. Overall, Reg-TCN-LSTM offers improved accuracy, stability, and interpretability with low complexity, providing a practical solution for real-time forecasting in data-scarce small-to medium-sized basins.

title: Evapotranspiration trend detection in Austria: A comparison of global remote sensing and reanalysis products with water-balance estimates
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Viera Rattayová, Juraj Parajka, Doris Duethmann, Kamila Hlavčová, Milan Onderka
abstract: Study region The study investigates 130 watersheds across Austria spanning four major hydro-climatic regions to assess long-term changes in evapotranspiration (ET). Study focus Previous studies have reported increasing water-balance ET across Austrian catchments during recent decades; however, it remains unclear whether widely used global ET products can reproduce these trends. This study evaluates whether five remote-sensing and reanalysis ET datasets (ERA5, MERRA-2, GLEAM, GLDAS, and MODIS) reproduce water-balance ET trends for two periods: 1981–2020 and 2001–2020. New hydrological insights for the region Water-balance ET (ETWB) increased in Austria over 1981–2020 (field-mean slope +14 mm yr⁻¹ decade⁻¹, 95% interval +3 to +26); 37 of 130 catchments showed significant trends, 34 of them increasing. In 20-year windows ending after 2010, the median slope turned negative, from +45 (1981–2000) to −15 mm yr⁻¹ decade⁻¹ (2001–2020). This decline is indicative only: the 2001–2020 field-mean slope of −18 mm yr⁻¹ decade⁻¹ has an interval reaching zero (−38 to +2), and the six significant trends equal what chance would give (6.5 of 130). The global ET products do not follow the decline: ERA5 and GLEAM keep positive median slopes in all windows, MERRA-2 only drops to about zero, and product slopes correlate weakly with ETWB slopes (|r| ≤ 0.26). Global ET products should therefore be used with caution when assessing ET trends in Central European catchments.

title: Linking rainfall-driven accumulation to staged warnings: A rapid flood forecasting framework for the Sangabeol underpass, South Korea
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jinhyeok Kim, Hwandon Jun, Soon Ho Kwon
abstract: Study region The Sangabeol underpass in Gwacheon, South Korea, receives road network runoff at a single low point, examined using a local rainfall record and two additional records from Taean and Naju. Study focus A process-based module couples runoff, routing, effective drainage, and storage-depth conversion with 5-min warning updates, using an effective drainage parameter (η = 0.85) fitted to one approximate depth–time observation and absorbing multiple uncertainties. Rolling forecasts and full-record reference simulations separate accumulation dynamics from rainfall-coverage and warning-rule effects; a hydraulic diagnostic estimates approach-flow depth and velocity from simulated discharge. New hydrological insights for the region Early shallow accumulation alone did not determine subsequent depth-rise rates. Simulated 10–15 cm and 15–20 cm transitions had 60-min/31-min (Gwacheon), 14-min/13-min (Taean), and 23-min/11-min (Naju) durations. The Taean–Naju ranking reversal links evolving rainfall and routed inflow to changing accumulation rates, so an initially slower rise need not imply more time at higher depths. Approach-flow velocities (0.33–0.89 m/s) reversed similarly between the two intervals, indicating discharge contrasts originating upstream of the low point. Predicted remaining times at first Danger were 26–27 min, reflecting the 30-min decision window and 5-min update cycle; limited future rainfall caused 21-, 2-, and 2-min delays in first-Alert 20-cm crossings relative to the full-record reference. These results support interpreting depth, velocity, crossing-time updates, and rainfall coverage for this configuration and retrospective inputs.

title: Dynamic hydro-geomechanical modeling reveals coal mining-induced lake function inversion and intensified water scarcity in arid regions: A case study in the Nalinxili Coalfield, Yellow River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fu Yicheng, Li Haixue, Liu Zhidong, Feng Jian, Zhang Jian, Huang Xiao
abstract: Study region The Nalinxili Coalfield, situated in the ecologically fragile and water-stressed Yellow River Basin, experiences intensifying conflicts between underground coal extraction and groundwater-dependent lacustrine ecosystems, particularly Hadatu Naor Lake. Study focus This study develops and applies a dynamically coupled SWAT-MODFLOW-Mine framework to quantify the spatiotemporal evolution of mining-induced surface subsidence, hydraulic fracture zone (HFZ) permeability, and surface water-groundwater interactions, aiming to evaluate hydrological alterations, ecological thresholds, and adaptive management pathways. New hydrological insights Mining operations trigger a mechanistic hydrological reversal wherein Hadatu Naor Lake transitions from a groundwater-receiving system to a terminal discharge sink, driven by the upward propagation of the HFZ (28.71–116.35 m) that establishes a new deep seepage pathway (Q) of 5000–50,000 m³ /year. Concurrently, regional groundwater drawdown reduces lateral lake recharge by 24.6%, while subsidence (2.24–3.92 m) increases lake storage capacity by 4.5 million m³ , fundamentally altering bathymetry, thermal stratification, and littoral habitat connectivity. Despite an overall volumetric loss of < 1%, the system crosses a critical ecological threshold as the hydraulic gradient inversion disrupts natural groundwater-driven flushing mechanisms, amplifying shoreline capillary salinization and reducing drought resilience. These process-based dynamics demonstrate that hydrological pathway integrity, rather than absolute water volume, governs ecological stability in arid mining landscapes, providing a quantitative, threshold-driven basis for lake conservation and adaptive water governance.mine

title: A soil moisture estimation model based on Stacking of decision trees and its evaluation over China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sha Sha, Die Hu, Yang Yang, Lijuan Wang, Xiaoyu Jiang, Jianshun Wang, Teng Ma
abstract: Study region This study focuses on mainland China, spanning arid, semi-arid, semi-humid, and humid climatic zones. Study focus A Stacking ensemble model integrating CLDAS land data assimilation product, AMSR2 microwave soil moisture, GPM precipitation, and static environmental variables is developed to estimate pentad-scale relative soil moisture (RSM) at a 0.1° (~10 km) resolution. The model uses Cubist, Random Forest, and Bagging as base learners. The contributions of dynamic and static features are quantified via SHAP analysis. New hydrological insights for the region The estimations reveal pronounced spatial variations and systematic bias patterns across China's climatic gradients. In semi-arid regions, the model systematically underestimates moisture (BIAS = −3.35%), whereas humid regions exhibit overestimation (+1.81%). The semi-humid transitional zone shows negligible bias (−0.31%) but the highest random error (RMSE = 18.62%), driven by localized spatial heterogeneity. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of moisture is closely associated with static environmental features, particularly topography and soil texture, through their interactions. Under severe drought (RSM < 30%), the model substantially overestimates soil moisture (BIAS = +17.48%), posing a critical limitation for operational drought warning. These findings provide quantitative insights into the varying dominant controls on soil moisture across diverse climatic gradients.

title: Urbanization-driven simplification of deltaic channel networks: Landsat super-resolution reveals the hidden loss of small channels
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Junjie Chen, Junshi Lin, Weilun Gao, William Nardin, Li Huang, Zhihao Xu, Zhenchang Zhu, Zhifeng Yang
abstract: Study region Dongjiang Delta, China, where rapid urbanization since the 1980s has significantly altered deltaic channel networks and hydrological connectivity. Study focus The topology of channel networks controls drainage efficiency and hydrological connectivity in river deltas. However, existing studies have predominantly focused on main distributaries and overlooked the widespread small channels. As such, we quantitatively examined how urbanization has altered the channel network and hydrological connectivity of the Dongjiang Delta, using a super-resolution technique to reconstruct high-resolution historical channel networks. New hydrological insights for the region Our results reveal a hidden pathway of hydrological degradation, i.e., the selective loss of small channels can substantially reduce the complexity and connectivity of the channel network even when main distributaries remain. Specifically, the loss of small channels caused decreases in the geometric and structural fractal dimensions of the channel network, indicating reduced space-filling capacity and weakened topological connectivity. Furthermore, we found a significant increase in the mean connectivity distance, signifying a reduction in river–floodplain connectivity of the Dongjiang Delta. Spatial analysis confirmed a positive relationship between urban expansion and the loss of river–floodplain connectivity, driven by both local direct effects and regional spillover effects. Our findings show that small channels are more susceptible to urbanization while playing crucial hydrological roles. Therefore, protecting and restoring small channels should be integrated into regional monitoring and coastal flood management.

title: Translating snowmelt and freeze–thaw legacies into irrigation–drainage zoning of water–salt constraints in seasonally frozen oasis croplands
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Mingyue Sun, Ping Gong, Pengfei Li, Yingsheng Dang, Hongguang Liu
abstract: Study region The Manas River Basin in northwestern China is a snowmelt-fed, seasonally frozen oasis that depends strongly on mountain snowmelt for irrigation. High evaporative demand, shallow groundwater, drainage heterogeneity, and water-saving irrigation create spatially variable salinity, sodicity, and water-status constraints, making it suitable for examining associations between antecedent cold-season hydroclimatic conditions and late-season soil water–salt management. Study focus We asked whether a management-oriented water–salt constraint index (WSCI) can integrate moisture, salinity, alkalinity, sodicity, carbonate status, and texture to identify dominant constraints; whether snow, snowmelt, and freeze–thaw covariates add predictive information beyond surface, terrain, groundwater, and climate conditions; and whether the resulting maps support irrigation–drainage zoning. We constructed weighted-average (WSCI_WA) and dominant-constraint-sensitive (WSCI_DE) formulations from 1250 topsoil samples and predicted them using multisource covariates under 10-fold spatial block cross-validation. Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) best predicted WSCI_DE: coefficient of determination (R²) = 0.761, root mean square error (RMSE) = 0.108, mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.086, and residual prediction deviation (RPD) = 2.05. New hydrological insights for the region Removing snow, snowmelt, and freeze–thaw predictors reduced R² to 0.707 and RPD to 1.85, indicating non-redundant statistical information for 2024 late-season topsoil WSCI prediction. Moderate, high, and very high relative constraints covered 38.7%, 19.6%, and 3.2% of cropland, respectively. Salinity was dominant, while sodicity, carbonate alkalinity, water-status imbalance, and texture created distinct management needs. The framework translates cold-season signals into relative priorities for leaching, drainage, sodicity mitigation, irrigation adjustment, and compound remediation.

title: Cost-effective aquifer protection: Verifying the combination of vulnerability mapping with wellhead protection area delineation methods in the Cape Flats, South Africa
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Brynn Hunink, Thomas Wöhling, Moritz Kraft, Reynold Chow
abstract: Aquifer vulnerability assessments are essential for identifying areas at risk of groundwater contamination and for guiding land use management to prevent aquifer degradation. In this study, we propose a cost-effective approach to characterize aquifer vulnerability by combining and simplifying existing methods. Our focus is the Cape Flats Aquifer (CFA) in the Western Cape, South Africa, where groundwater quality has declined over the past decade due to urbanization and agricultural activities. We assessed vulnerability using the DRASTIC-L method and delineated wellhead protection areas (WPAs) through a calibrated (root mean squared error = 5.6 m, mean absolute error = 4.4 m, and R = 98%) steady-state MODFLOW model with reverse particle tracking (MODPATH). Given the subjectivity of DRASTIC-L and the resource intensity of numerical modelling, we developed a simplified alternative by removing redundant parameters through sensitivity analyses (DRASTL) and integrating it with an analytical WPA delineation method. The resulting hybrid method, DRASTL-WPA, offers a faster and more accessible approach to aquifer vulnerability mapping. Our findings show high vulnerability across the CFA, with lower values in higher elevation zones. The DRASTL method yields more conservative results, though with less precision in identifying hotspots. The analytical WPA method aligned closely with MODPATH outputs when wells were more than 12 km from complex boundaries, indicating its suitability in simpler hydrogeologic settings. Overall, the combined method provides a practical framework for groundwater protection in data- or resource-limited regions, though refinement is needed for complex terrains.

title: Vegetation greening and soil drying in Central Asia: Evidence for bidirectional vegetation-soil moisture feedback
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Huili He, Peng Cai, Rafiq Hamdi, Geping Luo, Suwei Huang, Chongrong Jiang, Jiao Lu
abstract: In arid Central Asia (CA), variations in soil moisture (SM) strongly influence vegetation dynamics, while vegetation can affect SM through evapotranspiration. Although SM variation and its influence on vegetation dynamics have been widely documented, the bidirectional feedback between vegetation and SM remains inadequately explored. This study examined trends in Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and four SM layers (SM1~SM4, from shallow to deep) across CA for 1982–2022, using correlation analysis and Granger causality test to characterize their associations and bidirectional Granger-predictive feedbacks. Results indicated that: (1) significant NDVI greening occurred in eastern CA and browning in the west, while SM generally declined across much of the region; (2) NDVI was predominantly positively correlated with shallow-to-intermediate SM, but the proportion of negatively correlated areas increased with soil depth; (3) Bidirectional Granger-predictive feedback occurred across 88.4%, 79.8% and 72.2% of pixels for SM1, SM2, and SM3, respectively, the influence of SM4→NDVI dominated the deep-layer significant causality relationship; (4) coupling-trend included concurrent NDVI and SM decreases in western CA and increasing NDVI alongside declining SM in eastern. These findings demonstrated that both vegetation–soil moisture trends and relationships vary with influence of human activities and climatic conditions in such water-limited region, providing a scientific basis for climate adaptation, ecological restoration and water-source management.

title: IAH’s position paper for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference: Why groundwater is core to sustainable development across all interactive dialogues
abstract: The 2026 United Nations Water Conference (UNWC), to be held in Abu Dhabi (United Arab Emirates) in December 2026, represents a unique opportunity to set global water priorities. It is essential that groundwater is fully recognized throughout this agenda. The International Association of Hydrogeologists (IAH) is committed to raising the visibility of groundwater and is actively contributing to the conference preparations, notably through the drafting of an IAH position paper. This essay presents this position paper and describes its development.

title: Pore-throat geometry influences microplastic transport in gravel sediments
abstract: Microplastic (MP) transport in rivers and aquifers has received attention, yet MP infiltration through saturated gravel under high hydraulic gradients in natural sediments remains unclear. This study investigated MP infiltration in saturated gravel sediments using column experiments combined with micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) for pore-throat characterization. MP with minimum Feret diameters (d F,min, 0.24–3 mm), densities of 1.03–1.42 g⋅cm −3 and shapes (spherical, fibrous, fragment, flake and flat disk) were tested in unimodal and bimodal gravels (d 50 = 1.5–11 mm). Experiments were conducted at a relatively high flow condition that may be relevant to local high-gradient flow paths through filter gravel packs around injection wells. Micro-CT and image analysis revealed a close association between pore-throat geometry and MP infiltration patterns. Infiltration depth was closely related to the particle-to-pore size ratio defined using minimum Feret diameter and characteristic pore size (d F,min /d pore,85). Lower ratios were associated with deeper penetration. Size effects were most pronounced for spherical MP, while density had limited impact within the tested range. For non-spherical MP particles, the relevance of d F,min to infiltration depended on MP morphology. MP fibers showed infiltration patterns consistent with d F,min, whereas flat disks showed strong near-surface retention despite their very small d F,min. The findings indicate that MP fibers may infiltrate more deeply into gravel packs, while flat or flaky MPs are more likely to be retained in pore spaces and with potential for clogging. Pore-resolved approaches are needed to improve predictions of MP mobility in aquifers.

title: Bayesian hierarchical uncertainty quantification of a helical-path tortuosity predictor for modeling hydraulic conductivity in sandstone aquifers
abstract: Hydraulic conductivity and effective diffusivity in saturated sandstone aquifers depend on the square of tortuosity, so using a point estimate of tortuosity leaves its contribution to uncertainty unquantified in groundwater-flow and contaminant-transport models. A Bayesian hierarchical framework quantifies uncertainty in a published helical-path tortuosity predictor using a dataset of 51 sandstone samples spanning three formation classes: Tight German sandstones, clean Fontainebleau-analogous sandstones, and unconsolidated high-connectivity sandstones. The framework propagates uncertainty to hydrogeological quantities using the existing model and published data. Posterior predictions of tortuosity agree with the observations, with a mean absolute percentage error of approximately 3.3% and conservatively calibrated predictive intervals. Convergence was assessed using rank-normalized split $$\widehat{R}$$ R ^, effective sample sizes, and autocorrelation times, and out-of-sample performance was assessed using Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out and five-fold cross-validation (held-out mean absolute percentage error near 5.1%). Fixing the class critical porosities at their published values and inferring them yield statistically indistinguishable predictions, with information-criterion differences within two paired standard errors; the comparison is a robustness check, and the published thresholds remain within the credible intervals under widened and flat priors, although the data constrain them mainly from above. The tortuosity posterior is then propagated into the formation factor, the effective diffusivity and a multiplicative hydraulic-conductivity uncertainty factor, and an ensemble of one-dimensional transport simulations converts these into 90% envelopes on contaminant plume extent and on diffusive breakthrough time through a low-permeability layer, providing uncertainty bounds for models of the sandstone classes studied.

title: Groundwater flow heterogeneity and residence time in a Ryukyu Limestone aquifer (Okinawa Island, Japan) impounded by an underground dam: joint inverse modeling with hydraulic heads and borehole-dilution velocities
A conceptual model of groundwater flow and geothermal resource formation in a semi-arid region of Inner Mongolia, China: Insights from hydrochemistry and multi-isotope analysis
An implicit double-medium approach for simulating saltwater intrusion in fractured aquifers
Analytical calculations and analysis of seepage fields in hydraulic tunnels considering the effect of composite support
Experimental Investigation of deformation evolution in cover-collapse sinkholes under groundwater drawdown: An underground excavation site in SW China
Groundwater evolution modeling using multiple dating methods in the Pacific coastal area of Shimokita Peninsula, Japan
abstract: Groundwater age is a key constraint for understanding long-term groundwater flow and evaluating the safety of the geological disposal of radioactive waste. This study reassessed groundwater ages and reconstructed groundwater evolution in the coastal sedimentary sequence of the Rokkasho area, Shimokita Peninsula, northeastern Japan, using multiple environmental tracers. Groundwater samples were analyzed for major dissolved constituents, stable isotopes, 3 H, 14 C, 36 Cl/Cl, and dissolved noble gases. Corrected 14 C ages of fresh groundwater were evaluated using hydrogen isotope ratios and noble-gas recharge temperatures, whereas the residence time of deep saline groundwater was assessed using the 36 Cl/Cl method. Fresh groundwater occurs from the shallow subsurface to approximately 180 m below sea level. Corrected 14 C ages range from modern to about 35 ka and are consistent with paleoclimatic variations inferred from δ 2 H values and noble-gas recharge temperatures, supporting the reliability of the age correction. Deep saline groundwater exhibits 36 Cl/Cl ratios close to secular equilibrium, indicating residence times of at least 400 ka. In the upper part of the low-permeability formation, groundwater chemistry indicates mixing among freshwater, fossil seawater, and relatively younger seawater. These results suggest that seawater infiltrated into the shallow formations during marine transgression, whereas older fossil seawater was preserved in deeper, low-permeability strata. Subsequent uplift and sea-level regression promoted freshwater flushing of the shallow aquifer while preserving mixed saline groundwater at intermediate depths. The combined use of multiple groundwater-dating techniques provides a robust reconstruction of long-term groundwater evolution at the Rokkasho site.

title: Influence of tile-drainage water on groundwater nitrate concentrations within a saturated riparian buffer zone
abstract: Saturated riparian buffers (SRBs) are edge-of-field conservation practices that divert tile drainage into riparian soils to reduce nitrate delivery to streams, but the long-term response of saturated-zone groundwater to repeated tile-water inputs remains uncertain. This study evaluated 6 years of tile-flow, nitrate-nitrogen (NO 3 -N), and chloride data from an SRB in central Illinois to determine whether tile diversion altered groundwater NO 3 -N concentrations or caused multi-year nitrate accumulation. Groundwater samples from upgradient wells, representing background conditions, were compared with downgradient wells influenced by SRB distribution tiles. Mixed-effects models showed no significant relationship between daily tile-flow volume and groundwater NO 3 -N concentration and no significant difference between upgradient and downgradient groundwater. A 5-week lag analysis also showed no NO 3 -N response to prior tile flow. In contrast, chloride, used as a conservative tracer, increased with prior tile-flow volume, indicating hydraulic connectivity between diverted tile water and downgradient groundwater. The decoupling of chloride and NO 3 -N responses suggests that nitrate was attenuated within the SRB rather than simply diluted while transported to the monitored wells. During September and November no-flow periods, downgradient NO 3 -N concentrations remained low and did not increase progressively across years. These results indicate that the SRB sustained nitrate attenuation over multiple years without measurable dissolved NO 3 -N accumulation in the monitored shallow groundwater.

title: Sedimentary organic carbon contents control the nitrate reduction potential in a Holocene aquifer: Evidence from batch incubations
abstract: Groundwater quality is increasingly threatened by nitrate (NO 3 −) contamination from agricultural activities. In many aquifers, NO 3 − is attenuated through microbially mediated reduction coupled to the oxidation of reduced constituents in the aquifer matrix. However, predicting NO 3 − turnover at the aquifer scale remains difficult because electron donors such as organic carbon and reduced sulfur species are heterogeneously distributed and reliable proxies for NO 3 − reduction potential are lacking. To address this challenge, batch experiments were conducted using eight facies types from a previously characterized tufaceous Holocene aquifer in southwestern Germany. The facies exhibited a wide range of solid-phase organic carbon contents (SOC 0.5–40.1 wt.%). NO 3 − reduction in batches was assessed by monitoring temporal changes in NO 3 −, sulfate (SO 4 2−), and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations. NO 3 − reduction followed a two-phase pattern: An initial rapid, nonlinear decrease likely driven by readily bioavailable DOC, followed by a linear decline consistent with zero-order kinetics. Long-term NO 3 − reduction rates showed a strong positive relationship with solid phase organic carbon (SOC) (R 2 = 0.69) across all microcosms (n = 40) and facies (n = 8). Experimental reduction rates were combined with facies-specific horizontal groundwater flow velocities to estimate NO 3 − turnover distances and times for an initial concentration of 50 mg L −1 NO 3 −. The results demonstrate that NO 3 − attenuation is controlled by both biogeochemical and hydraulic factors. The study highlights SOC as a key proxy long-term NO 3 − reduction potential and demonstrates the value of facies-based approaches combined with reaction-kinetic modeling for assessing groundwater quality at the aquifer scale.

title: Estimating groundwater levels and their associated uncertainty through spatiotemporal kriging of groundwater-level data
abstract: Sustainable groundwater management requires, among other factors, reliable monitoring of groundwater levels (GWLs) and their spatiotemporal evolution in an aquifer with meaningfully quantified uncertainty. Geostatistical methods can estimate GWL surfaces directly from available groundwater monitoring data. This contrasts with groundwater flow modeling, which requires much more detailed data. This study estimates spatiotemporal GWL maps and quantifies associated uncertainties by spatiotemporal kriging, which combines spatial interpolation with temporal gap filling and noise filtering. The central hypothesis is that including hydrogeological information in kriging improves GWL predictions. To test this hypothesis, spatiotemporal trends and soft information inspired by hydrological understanding are included. These include digital elevation models, river exchange components, and the confinement status of aquifers. To test the necessity of full statistical involvement through Bayesian hyperparameter inference, universal kriging is operated in a fully Bayesian framework and then compared to simpler approaches like non-Bayesian and residual space–time kriging. The approach is demonstrated for the Wairau Plain aquifer, New Zealand, where the spatiotemporal GWL estimates can be compared with transient simulation results from a numerical groundwater flow model. The results indicate that space–time kriging is a valuable tool to estimate transient GWL maps, where auxiliary hydrogeological information is highly useful, that the fully Bayesian treatment of universal kriging is worth the effort, but that a posterior (Bayesian) uncertainty of geostatistical hyperparameters is close to irrelevant.

title: Groundwater sustainability in hyper-arid regions: Integrated groundwater modeling of Qatar’s aquifers under climate change and management scenarios
Hydrochemical characteristics and mixing processes of the multi-aquifer system in a coal mining district, northern Anhui Province, China
Temporal variability of stable isotopes in groundwater: A multi-year seasonal analysis and comparison with groundwater levels in the Piedmont Po Plain (NW Italy)
Assessing the worthwhileness of efficiency enhancement methods mitigating buoyancy flow in high-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage
abstract: High-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) presents a promising approach for achieving a temporally and spatially balanced, continuous energy supply. A key challenge in HT-ATES systems is the density-driven buoyancy flow, which can result in considerable heat losses and reduced energy efficiency, or thermal recovery efficiency. This study explores two strategies for mitigating the effects of buoyancy flow: adjusting the working fluid’s salinity and modifying the production well screen length, under varying intensities of buoyancy flow. Numerical simulations are employed to evaluate the recovery efficiency and pumping energy requirements across a range of fluid salinities and screen lengths over multiple HT-ATES operational cycles. Under conditions of high intensity of buoyancy flow, the impact of different fluid salinities on thermal front evolution and associated hydrodynamic processes is analyzed. Recovery efficiency exhibits a nonmonotonic response to fluid salinity, with the maximum improvement reaching 36.5% at an increase in salinity of 6%. At a moderate intensity of buoyancy flow, altering fluid salinity proves ineffective due to the formation of a buffering layer, where cooled saline water separates the injected fluid from the surrounding groundwater. Comparatively, modifying fluid salinity is found to be more effective than adjusting the production well screen length. For both strategies, the additional pumping energy required is negligible relative to the gain in recovered heat. The number of operational cycles has minimal influence on the heat plume’s location and morphology. Furthermore, owing to the additional preferred pathways and irregular-shape fronts, the recovery efficiency enhancement methods are found more effective in heterogeneous aquifers.

title: Unraveling the interactions between shallow and deep aquifers through analysis of groundwater chemical trends: insights from the Piedmont Po Plain (NW Italy)
abstract: Deep aquifers are essential groundwater resources for human activities, and their exploitation has intensified in recent years, as shallow aquifers generally exhibit a higher occurrence of contaminants compared to deep aquifers. The aim of the study is to examine the interactions between shallow and deep aquifers using hydrochemical approaches, considering the spatiotemporal distribution and trends of physicochemical parameters, major ions, heavy metals, pesticides and specific hydrochemical indices in deep aquifers over the 2000–2021 period in Piedmont (NW Italy). In the Piedmont Po Plain, a shallow phreatic aquifer hosted in fluvial deposits overlies deep confined and semiconfined aquifers, hosted in transitional and marine complexes. Results highlight (1) an increase in physicochemical parameter values and major ion concentrations; (2) enhanced introduction of pollutants, such as pesticides; (3) increased CO 2 levels, leading to increased concentrations of some major ions and decreased concentrations of Fe 2+ and the calcite saturation index (SI calcite ); and (4) intensified ion exchange processes. In conclusion, the increasing trends in physicochemical parameter values and major ion concentrations confirm an increase in the recharge of deep aquifers from overlying shallow aquifers, likely driven by the intensified exploitation of deep groundwater resources. This work represents one of the first regional studies of deep aquifers in the Piedmont Po Plain to analyze both physicochemical parameter and major ion trends and the significant role of interactions with shallow aquifers, providing valuable insights for local authorities, particularly as deep aquifers are expected to be increasingly exploited in the future for agricultural and drinking-water purposes.

title: Groundwater evaporation in an Andean salt flat: A new methodological approach in a brine mining context
Anomalously high wellhead temperatures relative to natural springs in the Niujie Geothermal Field, Yunnan (China): Hydrochemical and structural controls
Re-evaluating coastal salinization in the Mitidja Plain, northern Algeria, using vintage VES data: Statistical clustering and 3D inversion
Correction: How does rewetting propagate through restored peatlands? An integrated surface–subsurface modelling analysis of water–table dynamics
The beginning of groundwater use by hominins and its key to migrations by Homo erectus out of Africa
abstract: Despite growing acceptance of the importance of groundwater use by hominins, there has been little hydrogeological investigation into the controls on groundwater availability as relevant to their evolution and geographic dispersal. This study integrates available fossil and stone tool data with hydrogeological landscape reconstruction and conceptualisation to develop understanding and constraints on the earliest use of groundwater by hominins and early migrations between Africa and Eurasia. It is proposed that the first bipedal human ancestors, appearing in the fossil record in Central and East Africa between 6 and 7 Ma, learned from other mammals how to find and access shallow groundwater in ephemeral streambeds. The first evidence of hominin associations with groundwater discharge from springs is from around 2–4.5 Ma in the East African Rift System (EARS), these locations likely being critically stable hydro-refugia within the driest parts of precession-dominated climatic cycles. The first migrating hominin species appears to have been Homo erectus, with those in the EARS leaving in waves as small bands from around 1.9 Ma at the end of a humid period in the Arabian Peninsula. It is proposed that the most hydrologically plausible routes linking the EARS to Eurasia are via Red Sea crossings and then through the Arabian Peninsula moving along the strike of regional aquifers which would have provided perennial groundwater even over long climatically arid periods. The paper demonstrates the fundamental importance of groundwater for early hominin communities during a critical period in the evolution of human physiology and consciousness.

title: A two-stage clustering algorithm for generating digital cores for grouting in highly fractured rock foundations
Resolving 3-D aquifer architecture through assimilated lithological and geophysical data: Insights from multilayered alluvial systems of the Ganga–Mahananda floodplain, eastern India
Hydrochemical characteristics, origins, and health risk assessment of fluoride in groundwater in the Biliu River Basin, Liaodong Peninsula, China
Effect of bioturbation–induced riverbed morphological changes on groundwater/surface-water exchange in mountain rivers
Characterization of subsurface groundwater pathways from treated wastewater effluent infiltration along the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA
abstract: Recharge of treated wastewater to the environment is increasingly becoming a component of water resources management, especially in water-limited areas such as the Grand Canyon. Treated wastewater from the Grand Canyon South Rim Wastewater Treatment Plant has been discharged to a dry wash located along the surface expression of a fault for decades, but the fate of the wastewater is unclear. Previous research suggested possible connections between the treated wastewater discharge sites and springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon, particularly Monument spring. Additional investigations presented in this report add further evidence to the connection between the wastewater and Monument spring, utilizing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, artificial sweeteners, and stable isotopes of water. A dye trace established the first direct connection between wastewater and Monument spring where the dye added to treated wastewater took about 4–6 months to move through the subsurface and was detectable for 5 months. The persistence of wastewater tracers over time and the timing of dye movement suggests a fast subsurface flow pathway. On the basis of geologic observations of faults and jointing, groundwater flow follows a possible combination of karst and other structural pathways. The dye and wastewater tracers were monitored at other springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon and the combination of repeated dye detections and multiple wastewater tracers were only found at Monument spring. Multiple lines of evidence provide a robust tracer suite to support evidence of structural/karst controls on preferential flowpaths; faults alone are unlikely to explain the flow pathway.

title: Numerical simulation of the impact of tunnel drainage on matrix–conduit water exchange in the karst aquifers of Panzhou City, China
Quantifying water origin of a Mediterranean urban karst aquifer using storm event typology and high-frequency physicochemical signatures
Estimating multi-decadal groundwater levels using incomplete well records in confined and unconfined aquifers of the southern San Joaquin Valley, California (USA)
Hydrochemistry of confined aquifers in Friuli Venezia Giulia, Italy: Regional patterns, trends, and drivers
abstract: Confined aquifers are considered to be protected from surface contamination, yet intensive abstraction and long-term land-use pressures may alter their quality, especially in coastal areas. This study characterises the hydrochemistry of the multilayered confined aquifer system of the lower Friulian Plain (NE Italy), where groundwater is extensively exploited and locally affected by anthropogenic stressors. The study combines hydrochemical data from 1996 to 2025 from the monitoring activity of Regional Environmental Protection Agency of Friuli Venezia Giulia (ARPA FVG) and new samples collected in 2024–2025, compiling 1210 samples from 103 wells. The aim is to determine how recharge sources, residence time, and human activities control groundwater quality. Hydrochemical families were identified using major ions, redox-sensitive species, organic micropollutants, stable oxygen isotopes, and multivariate statistics. Three groundwater families were recognised: submodern waters, with hypoxic conditions, low to absent contaminant load and likely associated with recharge dating back to the late Würmian glacial period; modern-pristine waters, which are characterised by oxidising conditions, are SO 4 2− -rich, and show low to absent NO 3 − and pesticide concentrations; and modern-impacted waters, which are similar to the latter but display elevated NO 3 − concentrations, lower pH values, and detectable anthropogenic contaminants. Long-term trends indicate that although NO 3 − concentrations are overall stable or slightly decreasing in shallow aquifers, slowly increasing trends occur in deeper wells and near the margins of the NO 3 − plume, suggesting downward and lateral migration of impacted modern groundwater. Cl − concentrations show no increasing trends in coastal wells, indicating no evidence of active seawater intrusion.

title: Validating a numerical model for calco-carbonic reactive transport in a laboratory-scale fracture analog
abstract: Calco-carbonic reactive transport controls the dissolution of limestone by carbonic acid, a key process shaping the hydraulic and geochemical evolution of carbonate aquifers. Quantitative understanding of the coupling between flow, transport, and chemical reactions is essential for predicting karstification under variable hydraulic gradients, $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 partial pressures, and pH. To support model validation, laboratory experiments were conducted in a 1 m $$^2$$ 2 vertical karst-fracture analog with variable aperture, representing a simplified hydrogeologic fracture domain. Numerical simulations reproduced these experiments under controlled discharge, $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 concentration, and acidity. The coupled reactive transport models capture feedbacks between forced convection, diffusion, and density variations, linking reactive interface dynamics with evolving flow fields. Simulated and measured calcium and carbonate ion concentrations showed good agreement, indicating that diffusive transport at the water–limestone interface primarily limited dissolution. Insights from the combined modeling and experimental framework refine laboratory-scale design, improve interpretation of dissolution kinetics, and strengthen the basis for upscaling to field-scale carbonate aquifers. The results enhance prediction of permeability evolution, flow-path development, and $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 - $$\text {H}_{2}\text {O}$$ H 2 O -rock interactions in karst systems.

title: Mechanical and chemical rehabilitation of groundwater abstraction wells clogged by iron and manganese precipitates in Finland
abstract: Résumé Le colmatage des puits de captage d'eau souterraine survient généralement lorsque le fer et le manganèse dissous dans l'eau précipitent sur les éléments du puits, entraînant une baisse du débit. En Finlande, ce phénomène est marqué car les sols sont riches en fer et en manganèse, et les aquifères sédimentaires quaternaires recouverts d'argile présentent généralement une carence en oxygène. Une nouvelle approche de réhabilitation des puits, combinant traitements mécaniques et chimiques, a été appliquée à quatre puits de captage d'eau souterraine situés dans des dépôts sédimentaires quaternaires postglaciaires non confinés en Finlande. D'après les analyses par fluorescence X (XRF), les précipités responsables du colmatage étaient composés de Fe₂O₃, SiO₂, MnO et P₂O₅. Les réhabilitations mécaniques et chimiques ont toutes deux permis d'augmenter considérablement les débits (de 68 à 6 692 %) ; même les puits totalement colmatés ont affiché une nette amélioration de leur débit après l'intervention. À l'issue de la réhabilitation mécanique, les crépines des puits présentaient un niveau de propreté modéré. La réhabilitation chimique a permis un nettoyage supplémentaire des crépines, libérant totalement les fentes et réduisant la turbidité. Le traitement chimique a entraîné une augmentation de la conductivité électrique, de la teneur en sulfates ainsi que des concentrations en fer et en manganèse (dissous et totaux) dans l'eau, en raison des réactifs utilisés et de la dissolution du fer et du manganèse contenus dans les précipités. Toutefois, la qualité de l'eau est revenue à ses niveaux initiaux après une journée de pompage suivant le traitement. Cette méthode de réhabilitation est applicable aux puits de captage situés dans des dépôts sédimentaires quaternaires postglaciaires non confinés, au sein d'aquifères constitués de sable et de gravier à forte conductivité hydraulique. Néanmoins, des études complémentaires sont nécessaires pour mieux comprendre le processus de colmatage ainsi que l'applicabilité de ces méthodes de réhabilitation dans des contextes hydrogéologiques et des environnements redox variés.

title: Sustainable groundwater management in coastal areas: Modelling saltwater intrusion dynamics in Muravera, Italy
abstract: The coastal alluvial aquifer of Muravera, in south-eastern Sardinia (Italy), is affected by intense saltwater intrusion that seriously threatens freshwater supply. As groundwater overexploitation is often the main process controlling saltwater intrusion dynamics, it can strongly exacerbate salinization, making sustainable groundwater management essential to safeguard these resources. Reliable hydrogeological models based on robust datasets are powerful tools to support decision-making. This work develops a variable-density groundwater flow and solute transport model to analyse saltwater intrusion into the coastal aquifer of Muravera. Four simulation scenarios were implemented. The first reconstructs the historical evolution of salinization over the period of 1999–2023, whereas the other three extend the simulations to 2050 to quantify the various effects of different groundwater abstraction practices and to test a mitigation scenario. Two modelling codes were coupled to support the analysis. Groundwater recharge was computed using the Soil–Water-Balance (SWB) code and subsequently used as input to the iMOD-WQ code, which simulates variable-density flow and salt transport using SEAWAT. This coupling explicitly captures temporal and spatial recharge variability, which is often oversimplified in other approaches. The results indicate that groundwater abstractions for rice-field irrigation exerts a stronger influence on salinization dynamics than drinking-water abstractions. The mitigation scenario attenuates groundwater salinization in the plain, providing useful insights for future groundwater-management strategies.

title: Groundwater modeling to evaluate saltwater intrusion and freshening processes identified from hydrochemistry in a coastal groundwater system in Vietnam
Correction: Socio-hydrogeology: The past, present, and future of a people-centred and place-based approach to groundwater science
Advancing hydraulic conductivity estimation in the Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group using borehole NMR logging
abstract: The Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group is an important aquifer in the United Kingdom (UK) for groundwater and geothermal energy applications. Hydraulic conductivity (K) is essential for understanding groundwater movement, contaminant and heat transport in aquifers. Pumping test and borehole nuclear magnetic resonance logging (BNMR) were conducted in three boreholes drilled into the Sherwood Sandstone to determine K. BNMR provides information on the water-filled porosity and pore space geometry, and compared to conventional methods, it is an effective way to estimate K at a high vertical resolution. Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) and Timur-Coates (T-C) were used to estimate K using the standard empirical constants initially developed for petroleum reservoir applications. K SDR and K T-C were upscaled to the larger volume represented by K pumping for comparison.
