Both the standard SDR and T-C equations underestimated K by at least two orders of magnitude because of the limited transferability of their empirical constants to shallow groundwater systems, as they were derived for petroleum reservoir rocks rather than near-surface materials. The fits between the K SDR, K T-C and K pumping were optimised using a semi-constrained least-squares approach to obtain a set of site-specific parameters for the Sherwood Sandstone Group. The new K SDR and K T-C estimates, based on site-specific parameters, are within an order of magnitude of the K pumping. This study presents the first reported SDR and T-C constants for the Sherwood Sandstone Group, which may be used to estimate a more reliable NMR-derived high-resolution hydraulic conductivity in other locations where this formation is present.

title: Isotopic assessment of the origin of fresh and saline groundwater in the highly exploited, predominantly fossil Mekong Delta aquifer in Ca Mau, Vietnam
Estimating specific yield from GRACE-based storage change and groundwater levels across India
Mining-induced overburden fracture development and its control on preferential groundwater flow
Hydrochemical differences and origins of karst waters around the Jinan Pluton, North China
abstract: The periphery of the Jinan Pluton, North China, contains abundant cold-water and geothermal karst resources, constituting a natural observatory for investigating karst water origins and hydrogeochemical evolution. To advance the understanding of the occurrence pattern and origins of karst waters around the Jinan Pluton, a total of 36 samples of karst groundwater were collected and analyzed for hydrochemical constituents via ion chromatography (IC) and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), and isotopic composition. The results are as follows: (1) Along the south-to-north regional groundwater flow path, cold-water and geothermal karst groundwaters around the Jinan Pluton exhibit significantly distinct hydrochemical types. From shallow cold-water karst (spring water) to deep geothermal karst systems, the hydrochemical types become progressively more complex, accompanied by a continuous increase in the extent of water–rock interaction. (2) Within the geothermal field north of the Yellow River, the observed gradual increase in total dissolved solids (TDS) of geothermal karst water from west to east can be attributed to two main factors. First, the geothermal karst water in the western segment of the geothermal field receives significant recharge from the Yellow River. Second, the karst water level in the eastern segment of Jinan is the lowest across the study area, making it the convergence center of regional karst groundwater flow, which results in a relatively isolated hydrogeological environment with respect to the surface. This study reveals karst water hydrochemical evolution near the Jinan Pluton to guide water resource utilization and protection.

title: Leveraging machine learning tools to minimize uncertainties of physically based regional-scale groundwater models: A case study on precision modeling of groundwater levels in the Bist-Doab region, India
Hydraulic stimulation geometry governs information efficiency and parameter identifiability in hydraulic tomography: A comparison of dipole and sequential pumping tests

Old water, rapid responses: Process-based hydrogeological domains reveal hydraulic–age decoupling and implications for recharge assessment in a complex aquifer system of the Heuningnes Catchment, South Africa
abstract: Groundwater-level fluctuations are commonly used as recharge indicators because groundwater-level rises are often assumed to represent additions of recently recharged water to aquifer storage. In heterogeneous, multilayer aquifer systems, this assumption remains uncertain because groundwater-level variations may also reflect hydraulic connectivity, pressure transmission, storage redistribution, and groundwater mixing. Misinterpretation of groundwater-level behavior may consequently bias recharge estimates and groundwater-resource assessments. This study evaluated relationships among groundwater-level behavior, groundwater residence times, and hydrogeological process domains within the Heuningnes Catchment, South Africa. Groundwater hydrographs, tritium-derived groundwater ages, and a domain-based conceptual framework were integrated to investigate spatial variability in groundwater flow and recharge processes. Piston-flow (PF) apparent ages ranged from 0 to 60 years, whereas exponential–piston flow model (EPM)-derived mean transit times (MTTs) ranged from 2 to 80–100 years across hydrogeological domains. Recharge-dominated systems showed strong seasonal groundwater-level responses despite the coexistence of young and broad groundwater-age distributions and highly variable hydrograph responses, reflecting mixed recharge and storage influences. Structurally controlled systems showed rapid hydraulic responses despite prolonged groundwater residence times, suggesting pressure transmission independent of groundwater transport times. Residence-time-dominated systems were characterized by older groundwater and subdued hydrograph responses associated with prolonged storage. Groundwater-level response rate showed a weak and statistically non-significant relationship with MTT (Pearson's r = − 0.307, p = 0.460), demonstrating hydraulic–age decoupling and indicating that recharge assessments based solely on groundwater-level fluctuations may substantially misrepresent groundwater recharge processes in structurally complex multilayer aquifer systems.

title: Evaluating the long-term efficacy of subsurface cutoff walls as a barrier against seawater intrusion in unconfined island aquifers under various climatic-stress scenarios
Seasonal fluctuation of spring outflows in contrasting lithological and geomorphological environments of the western mid-hill region, Nepal
Groundwater potential zoning in the Grande River Basin: A semi-arid region of Northeast Brazil
abstract: Seasonal water scarcity in western Bahia, Brazil, has led to increased dependence on groundwater resources; however, basin-scale hydrogeological measurements remain insufficient for preliminary assessments. This study presents a geographic information system-based groundwater potential map for the Grande River Hydrographic Basin (GRHB), where groundwater potential is defined as a relative index reflecting conditions favorable for recharge and subsurface storage, rather than a direct measure of aquifer productivity. Ten hydrogeological and terrain proxy layers, derived from existing datasets and remote sensing, were standardized and integrated using an analytic hierarchy process weighting scheme and a weighted linear combination. The resulting index was classified into five groundwater potential categories. The very high- and high-potential classes account for 48.08 and 25.41% of the basin, respectively, while the moderate class accounts for 19.90%, and the low- and very low-potential classes together comprise 6.59%. Spatial association with available well locations was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis and the area under the curve, which yielded a value of 0.821, indicating that wells are more frequently located in areas with higher index values. Additionally, a groundwater abstraction-pressure proxy, derived from wells with reported daily abstraction volumes, was used to identify potential stress areas where high favorability coincides with concentrated abstraction activities. These outputs serve as a first-order screening tool to guide field verification, monitoring, and targeted data acquisition across the basin.

title: Macroscopic and mesoscopic characteristics of non-Fickian solute transport in rough fractures

Steady-state semi-analytical solutions for assessing the shape of the freshwater–seawater interface induced by a finite-sized underground physical barrier and a pumping well in a sloping coastal aquifer

Application of the new preconsolidation head and safe pumping buffer concepts to groundwater management for preventing land-subsidence recurrence in an overexploited aquifer system: A case study of Taiyuan City, northern China
Integrating geophysical and underwater robotic surveys with transport and geochemical modeling to assess the Solotvyno salt mine hazard in the Transcarpathia province of Ukraine
abstract: The Solotvyno salt mine in West Ukraine presents significant environmental and infrastructural risks due to uncontrolled salt dissolution following mine flooding, causing ground subsidence, sinkhole formation, and transboundary contamination of the Tisza River. This study employs an innovative multidisciplinary approach to characterize subsurface conditions and contamination pathways. The UX-1Neo autonomous underwater robotic platform conducted 14 dives in two flooded mine shafts, revealing intact main shaft structures but worrying blockages in horizontal passages, distinct haloclines at different depths (60 m in ventilation shaft 9, 140 m in shaft 10), and evidence of ongoing salt crystallization. Ground geophysical surveys such as electrical resistivity tomography, very low frequency radio-magnetotellurics and horizontal loop electromagnetics identified compromised protective clay layers (“pallag”) and potential air-filled voids, explaining accelerated dissolution and surface deformation. Hydrodynamic and contaminant transport modeling quantified salt fluxes (~ 2000 m 3 /day through “pallag” zones, ~ 13–15 m 3 /day from direct mine leakage) and confirmed dissolution rates of approximately 5.0–5.5 m 3 /day of rock salt, driven by both anthropogenic influences and natural gradients toward the Tisza River. NETPATH mixing models revealed variable contamination throughout the system, with the Black Moor area showing highest vulnerability (up to 27.4% mine water contribution) while the Tisza River maintains relatively good water quality despite measurable contamination (1.97% mine water). The suggested approach provides critical insights into risk assessment and remediation planning, representing a significant advancement in monitoring and managing complex environmental hazards associated with abandoned salt mines.

title: Ascertaining controls on spring discharge: Implications for the revival of drying springs in the Middle Hills region of Nepal
Groundwater occurrence and quality in a hyper-arid desert: Insights from high-resolution electrical resistivity surveys in Tharparkar, Pakistan
abstract: The Tharparkar District in Pakistan is among the world’s most water-scarce regions, characterized by its hyper-arid climatic conditions and the absence of perennial surface water resources. Understanding the occurrence of groundwater potential and its quality is therefore critical, particularly in remote regions where hydrogeological information remains limited. This study characterized groundwater resources using 576 high-resolution electrical resistivity survey (ERS) probes up to a depth of 300 m, conducted from 2017 to 2020. Complementary hydrochemical investigations included laboratory analysis of 168 groundwater samples collected from dug wells and 672 soil samples up to a depth of 0.60 m. Results demonstrated that the water table lies at depths of 2–15 m (26% of the area), 16–30 m (23%), and 31–90 m (51%). Interpretation of ERS data revealed that approximately 10% of the groundwater resources, covering the southern parts of Diplo, Islamkot, and Nagarparkar Talukas, are suitable for drinking at a depth of 25 m, with around 3% classified as fresh and 7% as slightly saline. Groundwater salinity increases with depth, as 51% of the area shows high salinity at depths of 26–50 m and very high salinity at depths of 51–200 m. Arsenic and fluoride concentrations exceed permissible limits in 10 and 28% of the groundwater samples, respectively. These findings provide robust geophysical and hydrochemical evidence to guide targeted groundwater development, water quality mitigation strategies and inform policy interventions, aimed at enhancing water security and safeguarding the health of communities living in severely water-stressed desert regions.

title: The spatiotemporal evolution and controlling factors of the groundwater environment: Insights from long-term monitoring of Tongzhou District, China
Integrated geochemical characterization and multicomponent modeling for reservoir temperature estimation in the Boğazlıyan Geothermal Field (Central Anatolia, Turkey)
Correction: Isotopic investigations on identification of atmospheric moisture origins and evaluation of runoff source contributions to the Upper Beas River Basin in the western Himalayas
Understanding groundwater flow in a buried valley and bedrock aquifer system in Kurikka, Finland, using hydrochemical indicators and residence time tracers 3H and 14C
abstract: Growing demand for groundwater in western Finland has drawn attention to a regional network of buried valleys with high potential for domestic and municipal water supplies. This study aims at understanding the groundwater flow in the buried valley and bedrock aquifer system using hydrochemical data and residence time indicators (3 H, 14 C). A multivariate statistical analysis (hierarchical clustering on principal components) revealed six water groups reflecting the origins and different stages of groundwater evolution. Overall, a modern groundwater component (< 60 years old) and active flow system are present in all parts of the system. Longer residence times are found deeper within the buried valleys (3 H-free waters) and at greater depth in a few locations in the bedrock (14 C ages > 5000 years). The occurrence of geochemically evolved waters in the deeper, downgradient areas of buried valleys indicates suitable (in terms of quantity and quality) and safe (low vulnerability) water supply relative to demand. More broadly, the multi-tracer approach provides insights into the geochemical evolution of groundwater, revealing groundwater flow conditions, geological history and aquifer unit composition. Residence time indicators also illustrate the relative hydraulic isolation of buried valleys, which has implications on vulnerability and sustainable exploitation. To fully clarify the exchanges between bedrock and granular aquifers, a sampling scheme targeting deep flow paths beneath the Paloluoma and Kyrönjoki valleys would be necessary. This study will support the development of a numerical model of the aquifer system and contribute to informing future management decisions.

title: Towards global groundwater recharge estimation from GRACE-constrained GLDAS-CLSM data
abstract: Accurate estimation of groundwater recharge at regional to global scales is essential for sustainable water resource management, yet current methods lack consistency. This study introduces the groundwater storage fluctuation (GSF) method to derive gross recharge, total discharge (including both natural and human-related outflows that cannot be distinguished without additional data), and net recharge from GRACE-constrained GLDAS-2.2 CLSM groundwater storage (GWS) anomalies. Based on monthly GWS fluxes, the GSF method requires no seasonal templates or specific recharge-event identification. Global mean annual recharge for 2004-2024 is estimated at 16,081.5 km $$^{3}$$ /year, consistent with existing global hydrological models and multi-study averages (14,806 ± 1,721 km $$^{3}$$ /year). Recharge ranges from <100 mm/year in arid zones to >300 mm/year in humid tropical areas, with a non-significant global trend of 0.34 mm/year. Arid basins show the highest interannual variability, with coefficients of variation of 48% for the Murray-Darling Basin (Australia), 40% for São Francisco (Brazil), and 36% for Colorado (USA). Validation against an Australian chloride mass balance (CMB) dataset shows strong spatial agreement ( $$\varvec{\rho }$$ = 0.82). In the Murray-Darling Basin, CMB validation confirms this performance ( $$\varvec{\rho }$$ = 0.83 and a standard deviation, STD, of 32.1 mm/year). The underlying GWS, validated against 259 boreholes in the basin, correlates at 0.47 with an STD of 33.9 mm, within the bootstrap uncertainty limit of 38.2 mm. Results should be interpreted at GRACE’s effective resolution ( $$\sim $$ 300 km), and grid-cell estimates in data-sparse or low signal-to-noise ratio areas should be used with caution.

title: A Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD)-enhanced Bayesian physics-informed neural network for uncertainty propagation in groundwater transport modeling
How does rewetting propagate through restored peatlands? An integrated surface–subsurface modelling analysis of water–table dynamics
abstract: Peatland restoration, through drainage suppression, is widely implemented to recover hydrological and ecological functions; however, the groundwater system responses governing rewetting efficiency remain insufficiently quantified across spatiotemporal scales. Here, a boreal fen is used as a process-representative system to resolve how restoration interventions, including ditch infilling and damming, reorganise catchment-scale water-table dynamics, drawing on calibrated, fully integrated three-dimensional physics-based modelling (HydroGeoSphere). Simulated restoration elevated domain-scale median water table by ~ 23 cm, with comparable gains (~ 22 cm) in nominally undisturbed areas, revealing that drainage legacy extends well beyond visibly ditched zones. Variogram analysis confirmed a shift from fragmented, drainage-controlled conditions to hydraulically connected systems with increased spatial correlation lengths. Water-table recovery propagated according to distinct hydrogeologic response regimes depending on restoration structure and subsurface properties. Low-permeability peat infillings generated strong localised responses with rapid exponential attenuation of water-table recovery (~ 70% decline within ~ 40 m), whereas dams produced broader, plateau-like responses extending up to ~ 100 m. Geomorphic setting further modulated recovery, with peat thickness and proximity to peat–mineral margins acting as primary controls through a threshold-like response regime. Seasonal hydroclimatic forcing modulated recovery, with wet-season response nearly doubling water-table rise relative to dry subarctic winters. These results demonstrate that drainage suppression reorganises peatland groundwater systems by enhancing lateral connectivity and controlling how hydraulic responses propagate across space. While the absolute magnitudes are site-specific, the identified controls and response patterns provide a mechanistic, transferable basis for guiding restoration in comparable boreal fens.
